4d1f12e12079.text:
Tenable spent 30 days running frontier AI models against their own code to test Claude Mythos Preview as part of Anthropic's Project Glasswing. The company built an agentic code security harness powered by this frontier LLM, running it against code and service repositories with pinned commits to ensure reproducible results.

Key Findings: 1. Code security now starts with proof rather than suspicions. Frontier AI can build working exploits and prove which flaws are genuinely dangerous, making remediations confirmed issues rather than ranked lists of possibilities. 2. The durable asset is the orchestration harness around the model, not the model itself. The harness handles state management, parallelism with focus, and cross-repo reasoning—tasks a prompt alone cannot accomplish. 3. Frontier AI augments senior researchers rather than replacing them. The scarce resource remains the expert who writes threat models and judges what findings matter.

Technical Implementation: Tenable's harness operates in a loop: threat model feeds context, scopes static analysis to specific abuse cases, drives targeted exploitation against running builds, and feeds results back to confirm exploitability or eliminate false positives. The research revealed that blindly pointing coding agents at repositories doesn't work. Standard agents exhaust context mapping architecture, leaving minimal capacity for actual vulnerability hunting. The harness solves three structural problems: state management across runs, parallelism with focused attack classes, and cross-repo reasoning linking vulnerable code to reachable entry points.

Cost Analysis: The compute bill for one engineer's June 2026 usage totaled approximately $41,718 across 71 harness runs against 37 repositories: Cache writes: $24,839 (60%); Cache reads: $7,774 (19%); Output tokens: $7,266 (17%); Base input: $1,839 (4%). The median run cost $47, while the mean was $588. The most expensive single run exceeded $9,000. Frontier models are non-deterministic; three passes are recommended for adequate coverage, with each successive pass finding approximately half as many new issues as the previous run.

The Human Element: The threat model—which must come from someone with top-to-bottom system understanding—is non-negotiable. "Hand it a blank threat model, it produces confident, plausible, wrong output at machine speed," author Blake Kizer notes. The same senior researcher reads what the model surfaces, decides what's worth driving to a working exploit, triages results, and refines the threat model for subsequent passes. This person cannot be the most available person—they must be the most senior.

Triage and Action: Every candidate finding must clear a gate: Is there a reproducible proof-of-concept? Those without go to a validation queue. Those with one advance through triage questions addressing reachability, automation capability, impact level, and whether findings touch critical assets.

Implementation Recommendations: Begin with one service the best person knows thoroughly; write the threat model by hand from expert knowledge; run against pinned commits for reproducibility; route output through a triage tree ending in real tickets. The article advises against starting with the entire fleet, crown-jewel services, or allowing the frontier model to write fixes directly.

Conclusion: Frontier AI in a well-designed harness fundamentally changes code security work. Rather than removing experts, it reallocates their time from testing to threat modeling and triage. "The harness makes you faster at knowing. What you do with that knowledge is still on you," Kizer states. (Author: Blake Kizer, Published: August 3, 2026)

7c45082c5728.text:
Thirty years ago, software developers wrote code line by line, and a handful of them per company shipped anything to production. Ten years ago, DevOps engineers automated that pipeline and multiplied what each of them could deploy. Three years ago, AI coding assistants—GitHub Copilot, Cursor, Claude Code—started writing meaningful percentages of that code alongside them. Today, AI app generators let anyone with a browser tab describe an app in plain English and deploy a working version in minutes. Each wave lowered the barrier to entry, multiplied the builder population, and added a fresh layer to the attack surface without waiting for security to catch up.

The numbers under the shift: AI app-generator revenue reached $4.7 billion in 2026, projected to hit $12.3 billion in 2027. Vercel's v0 crossed 4 million users with a $340M ARR run rate by end of February 2026; 30% of apps on Vercel are now deployed by AI agents rather than humans (per CEO Guillermo Rauch). JetBrains' January 2026 survey found 90% of developers regularly use an AI coding tool at work; GitHub Copilot passed 20 million users; Cursor hit $2 billion ARR in February 2026; Claude Code adoption grew 6x in nine months. Verizon's 2026 DBIR ranked shadow AI as the third most common non-malicious insider action, a fourfold increase in a year.

The CNAPP model assumes a discrete list of cloud accounts provisioned by DevOps on a quarterly cadence - a model that breaks when builders spin up production surfaces from a prompt. Example scenarios: a developer's Cursor-generated over-permissioned IAM role goes unreviewed; a data scientist's Vercel-deployed Claude inference endpoint is set to org-wide visibility by default; a PM's Lovable-built internal tool leaves an HR API key in plaintext; a marketer uploads a customer CSV to a Claude project shared org-wide with no retention limit. None of these touch an AWS account a CNAPP would flag - they touch Vercel, Claude Enterprise, GitHub, MCP servers, and other platforms outside most CNAPP tenants.

CNAPP was built for AWS/Azure/GCP; SSPM was built for Salesforce/M365. Both assume a small, stable, centrally-owned set of accounts. Vercel and Claude Enterprise are control-plane PaaS platforms with team workspaces, deployment rules, SSO enforcement, data retention and project-visibility settings that most CNAPPs/SSPMs never inspect, despite both being mainstream (Vercel v0's 4M+ users; Anthropic enterprise deployments inside many Fortune 500 companies).

AI AppGen Security is Orca's new capability set addressing this gap. Two new integrations: Claude Enterprise (via Claude's Compliance API, detecting unenforced SSO, indefinite retention, non-private projects, sessions with no expiration, over-privileged owner roles) and Vercel (inventorying teams, users, tokens, projects, deployments, domains, env-var metadata, firewall config; detecting plaintext secret-like env vars, unauthenticated production URLs, non-expiring API tokens, disabled WAFs, org-wide public projects). Findings map to Orca's unified data model and risk scoring already used for AWS/Azure/GCP.

The CISO's real job when everyone is a builder: blocking platforms doesn't work because builders route around restrictions (shadow-AI numbers already prove this). The alternative is turning 'no' into 'I know' - seeing every builder, every platform, and every misconfiguration in one risk model. (Author: Ashleigh Lee, Published: August 3, 2026)

About Orca: Orca Security delivers security for the companies that build, providing visibility across cloud, AI, and application environments; customers include SAP, Autodesk, Gannett, Lemonade, Digital Turbine; backed by Temasek, CapitalG, ICONIQ Capital, Redpoint Ventures.

ce97a06e9eab.text:
Somewhere between a CVE's publication and your next scheduled scan, an attacker already has a working exploit. That gap used to be measured in weeks; today it's measured in hours. A record 48,177 CVEs were published in 2025, on pace for ~59,000 in 2026, while median time from disclosure to first working exploit collapsed from 56 days (2024) to 23 days (2025) and is now a matter of hours; AI-assisted attackers reportedly weaponize new advisories in 4-12 hours, and vulnerability exploitation surged 34% YoY per Verizon's DBIR, now the entry point in 1 of 5 breaches.

Why scan-driven detection cannot keep up: built-in latency from scheduled scans/signature releases; fragmented coverage across siloed telemetry; operational friction from network scans requiring IT coordination.

Introducing InstaScan: the industry's first 'scanless detection' capability, powered by Agent Insta, which continuously correlates every new vendor advisory against software/asset telemetry, exposure, and threat context Qualys already holds (from Qualys and third-party tools), detecting new vulnerabilities without a scan window. Across technologies making up 60-70% of typical enterprise vulnerability volume, InstaScan reportedly delivers over 90% of exposure detections instantly with no scan job run.

How Agent Insta powers InstaScan (five stages): 1) build a trusted software inventory from scan agents, SBOMs, registries, CMDBs, Qualys sensors and third-party inventories; 2) normalize software identity with an AI retrieval model to standard CPEs/PURLs; 3) create a canonical, confidence-scored inventory; 4) continuously monitor new CVE disclosures/advisories 24x7; 5) correlate and confirm against the canonical inventory, publishing only high-confidence findings to TruRisk and downstream workflows.

InstaScan feeds TruRisk prioritization with cleaner/faster data and feeds Agent Val for autonomous/semi-autonomous remediation, while existing Qualys Cloud Agents, network scanners, and container sensors continue running on normal cadence to independently reaffirm InstaScan findings.

InstaScan will be available within the Qualys ETM platform by the end of August 2026; organizations can contact their Qualys TAM or start a free ETM trial. (Author: Himanshu Kathpal, VP Product Management, Platform and Technologies; Published: August 6, 2026 per byline, digest-dated August 3, 2026)

42b3fcb0f44e.text:
The Herald Business reports:
Seoul Facilities Corp. has drawn criticism over its plan to offer 5,000 won [$3.50 USD] per affected user in response to a personal data breach involving about 4.62 million people, with questions mounting over whether the compensation is adequate.
Seoul Metropolitan Council member Im Gyu-ho of the Democratic Party of Korea (Jungnang District 2) said the corporation’s handling of the incident — not just the compensation amount but its entire response — was flawed, and called for more substantive victim relief and accountability.
According to Im, a security firm notified the corporation in July 2024 of signs that personal data had been leaked, but the corporation failed to immediately alert the Seoul Metropolitan Government and relevant authorities, and did not promptly notify affected users. The breach became public only after a police investigation, and individual notifications to victims were not sent until nearly two years later.
…. “It is the height of irresponsibility for an institution with data security so weak it could be hacked by a middle schooler to try to bury the matter with 5,000 won per person,” Im said. “This incident goes beyond a simple hacking case — it is a test of public institutions’ capacity to protect personal data, manage crises, and restore public trust. The corporation must transparently disclose the cause of the breach, hold those responsible strictly accountable, and put in place real measures for victim relief and prevention of recurrence.”
Read more at The Herald Business.

a702fce22e21.text:
Bill Curtis reports:
The full names and contact details for more than 100,000 police officers and staff have been leaked on the dark web after a hack, The Times can reveal.
As part of a major security breach, hackers compromised data belonging to the Ministry of Defence (MoD), the Home Office, National Crime Agency (NCA), and Crown Prosecution Service (CPS).
This means three government departments have been caught up in hacks recently after the Department for Education (DfE) had more than half a million pieces of data compromised last week.
[…]
A little-known cybercriminal group named ExfilSquad are believed to be responsible. The group has infiltrated multiple western targets in recent weeks.
Read more at The Times.
As DataBreaches previously reported, ExfilSquad informed DataBreaches that all of the victims are on their leak site were “… the result of Microsoft Power Apps/Dynamics 365 misconfigurations. We exploited improperly configured permissions on the victims’ Dataverse tables.”

04c99d2ec6e0.text:
DPA reports:
The tiny principality of Liechtenstein has fallen victim to a major cyberattack in which the data of 31,000 people were stolen, the government said on Sunday.
The country, which lies between Switzerland and Austria, has a population of around 41,000.
The government said it had convened a crisis team led by Prime Minister Brigitte Haas and Justice Minister Emanuel Schädler.
The attack had breached the protection of personal data, it said. The target was the “register of beneficial owners,” a database containing the names and other details of the de facto owners of companies, foundations or trusts.
Read more at Yahoo! News.
The news coverage does not reveal how the attack occurred or if the government has any suspects identified. The government’s website does not have any notice or press release about the breach at this time.
In 2008 stolen bank data resulted in a huge scandal about tax dodgers that went on for years (see most of the related posts, below), but we haven’t seen a lot of other breaches reported for Liechtenstein over the years.

31fda2bd3cb9.text:
The infamous ShinyHunters extortion group has leaked over 41 gigabytes of data allegedly stolen from the physical security firm Brinks Home. Headquartered in Dallas, Texas, Brinks Home provides home security systems backed by an alarm response center.

Last week, the company announced that hackers accessed a portion of its IT systems and that they threatened to leak information allegedly stolen during the incident. "We are aware that such material may be posted publicly. Brinks Home is working diligently to determine what information was involved and who may be affected," the company said in an incident notice. Noting that it would notify potentially affected individuals if their personal information was compromised, Brinks Home pointed out that customers should remain "vigilant against unsolicited emails, text messages, or phone calls requesting personal information or account credentials".

According to Brinks Home, its alarm monitoring and system functionality has not been affected, as the attackers did not access its products or services. The company has not shared details on the threat actor responsible for the incident, but its disclosure came around the same time that ShinyHunters added Brinks Home to its Tor-based leak site.

More than 4.9 million records were stolen from Brinks Home's Salesforce instance during the incident, the extortion group says. As the physical security firm did not pay a ransom, the hackers have leaked online more than 41GB of files allegedly stolen during the incident. Some of the stolen records, ShinyHunters claims, include personally identifiable information (PII). SecurityWeek has not independently confirmed the hackers' claims. (Author: Ionut Arghire, Published: August 3, 2026, 7:45 AM ET)

7af0348a7b1a.text:
AI is moving incredibly fast, and every security leader is feeling the pressure to keep up. AI platforms like Claude, Codex and Cursor are already helping security teams write detections, investigate alerts, summarize incidents, and automate repetitive work. The conversation has evolved from whether AI belongs in the SOC to where each type of AI delivers the most value.

Two kinds of AI, two different jobs: security operations can be seen as three layers. At the bottom are existing tools (SIEM, EDR, cloud security, identity, email security). In the middle is an autonomous AI SOC that investigates every alert automatically, correlates findings, applies context, and determines which alerts need human attention. At the top are AI platforms like Claude, Cursor, and Codex, where analysts collaborate with AI to write detections, create reports, hunt threats, and make decisions.

Why AI platforms shouldn't investigate every alert: they're designed to help people, not run continuously as a 24/7 investigator integrated with security tools and organizational memory. The tokenomics problem: every investigation requires context (telemetry, logs, threat intel, prior investigations) which consumes tokens; at thousands of alerts/day, fresh LLM conversations for each alert become cost-prohibitive. An autonomous AI SOC instead combines deterministic workflows, forensic analysis, organizational memory, cached context, and selective AI reasoning to keep costs predictable.

The MDR reality: many organizations rely on MDR providers who own investigation workflows and telemetry, limiting an AI platform's ability to independently investigate since it lacks access to the same data.

Investigating 100% of alerts: teams typically prioritize high-severity alerts, but analysis of 25M+ alerts from 2025 found nearly 1% of confirmed incidents originated from low-severity/informational alerts, meaning severity doesn't always reflect risk. An autonomous AI SOC can investigate every alert while escalating only cases needing human judgment.

Where Claude and similar platforms shine: once an autonomous AI SOC completes investigations, analysts can use AI platforms to ask questions about completed investigations, draft/refine detection rules, hunt for emerging threats, summarize investigations, generate reports, and make final decisions on complex cases.

Conclusion: organizations need both an autonomous AI SOC (continuously investigating alerts) and AI platforms like Claude (helping professionals work faster and decide better) working together.

d23671f243c7.text:
A previously undocumented loader framework has been found disguising Go code inside a counterfeit Python runtime, after first instructing Microsoft Defender to ignore the directory and the process it was about to abuse. According to research from Blackpoint Cyber's Adversary Pursuit Group (APG), published July 30, the intrusion hit two endpoints at a law firm and deployed two undocumented families: a Go loader tracked as HollowFrame and a pair of Rust backdoors tracked as Matryoshka.

Exclusions Before Payloads: the chain began with spear phishing routing recipients to an encrypted Mega archive containing a shortcut file named Case Documents.lnk. Executing it wrote Base64 content to a temp file, rebuilt a script via certutil, then launched an obfuscated PowerShell chain prompting for admin rights. Once elevated, it created Defender exclusions covering a staging directory and the process name python.exe before downloading executable content. The archive retrieved was named to resemble an official Python embedded distribution (though filename read amd96 rather than amd64).

Python in Name Only: launching the bundled python.exe with no arguments moved the chain into DLL sideloading. The accompanying python311.dll was not CPython but a 64-bit Go library exporting four Python-compatible function names, handing execution to HollowFrame - a modular loader offering process ghosting, module stomping, and manual PE mapping, plus persistence via scheduled task, WMI event subscription, or Startup folder.

A Dead Drop on GitHub: HollowFrame sideloaded a malicious version.dll beside a legitimate OneDrive updater for the first Matryoshka backdoor. A second Rust variant (wtsapi32.dll proxying Windows Terminal Services exports) used a private GitHub repository per victim for beacon/command/result files instead of a custom C2 server, using a OneDrive user agent. The variant could identify domain controllers, enumerate domain computers/privileged groups, and inventory network/local configuration.

Blackpoint recommends correlating unexpected GitHub API connections from non-development processes, flagging signed binaries loading adjacent DLLs from user-writable paths, constraining GitHub API access from non-dev endpoints, reviewing scheduled tasks/WMI subscriptions for update-themed names, and detonating password-protected archives/shortcuts in a sandbox. (Author: Alessandro Mascellino, Published: August 3, 2026)

03639a2da45b.text:
Qodana 2026.2 shipped with new security inspections, published benchmark results, post-quantum cryptography checks, and coverage reporting that no longer has to be pointed at the reports. The security work sits in the .NET linter and runs by default: Qodana tracks untrusted data across files in C#, JavaScript, and TypeScript, surfacing SQL injection, command injection, cross-site scripting, and path traversal that single-location rules miss. JetBrains splits the analysis into pattern rules (catching bad code at one spot) and a taint engine (following the data); teams can add custom rules in the OpenGrep format.

Benchmark Results Now Public: SABER (Static Analysis Benchmark Evaluation Runner) runs Qodana against public security benchmarks and compares findings against known expected results, covering CodeQL benchmarks for C# and JavaScript, the WebGoat.NET vulnerable app scored against Sonar's published ground truth, and a post-quantum demo project. Runs sit on a TeamCity server with open guest login.

Five-Level Crypto Analysis: Qodana for JVM flags cryptography vulnerable to quantum computers, with inspection groups following NIST's post-quantum recommendations ranging from flagging pre-quantum/legacy algorithms to flagging everything short of maximum security, addressing 'harvest now, decrypt later' attacks.

Additional features: coverage reporting no longer requires copying reports into a Qodana directory since it auto-detects default locations for JVM, Android, JavaScript, PHP, Python, Go, and .NET projects; Laravel checks are now enabled by default in Qodana for PHP; builds can fail on prohibited or unidentified dependency licenses; Kotlin and Java will receive the same pattern rules and cross-file taint analysis in a future release. (Author: Anamarija Pogorelec, Senior Staff Writer, Help Net Security; Published: August 3, 2026)

57ee2dd8bb9d.text:
Simbian has released its autonomous AI Threat Hunt Agent, which investigates potential threats and identifies malicious activity across enterprise environments. The Threat Hunt Agent represents the third pillar of Simbian's AI-driven security suite, completing coverage across the entire threat timeline: The Present - the AI SOC Agent analyzes real-time alerts and neutralizes active threats as they occur; The Future - the AI Pentest Agent probes environments from an attacker's perspective to uncover vulnerabilities before exploitation; The Past - the new AI Threat Hunt Agent finds threats that bypassed initial detection.

Huy Ly, Head of Global IT Security at Monolithic Power Systems, stated: "Every security leader lives with one question: what did we miss?" He noted the agent hunts across years of data spanning multiple tools.

Superhuman Hunting Without Silos: the Threat Hunt Agent automates hypothesis generation using business context, integrating AI SOC investigation results, verified intrusion paths, and threat intelligence. It analyzes data across SIEM, EDR, cloud infrastructure, data lakes, and MCP servers. CEO Ambuj Kumar remarked: "Threats from the past, present, or future – Simbian has you covered!" He emphasized the platform completes the SecOps loop by hunting missed threats, stopping ongoing ones, and preventing future attacks. Hunt results feed into detection engineering, enabling new rules to catch previously missed threats in the future. (Published: August 3, 2026)

ec3bcc75d6f8.text:
The UK government's corporate finance adviser has admitted that an employee left an internal file containing the names and work email addresses of dozens of officials publicly accessible for around 40 hours. The breach, first reported by The Guardian, was disclosed in UK Government Investments' (UKGI) annual report, which says it occurred during the 2025-26 financial year after a member of staff "did not follow established information security policies." The exposed document contained "high-level management information" alongside the names and work email addresses of 51 government officials.

UKGI, the Treasury-owned outfit that advises ministers on corporate rescues to billion-dollar share sales, said it voluntarily reported the incident to the ICO even though it did not meet the threshold for mandatory notification. It also informed its Audit and Risk Committee and commissioned an external review. The report offers little detail: it doesn't say when the exposure occurred, where the file was hosted, whether anyone accessed or downloaded it, or which departments employed the affected officials, nor does it identify the external reviewing firm or its specific recommendations.

The review concluded UKGI's response was appropriate and recommended further improvements to security controls and incident preparedness; "the overwhelming majority" of recommendations have either been implemented or are due soon. The mishap comes in a year when UKGI worked on major deals including offloading the government's remaining NatWest shares, small modular reactor financing, the Eutelsat capital raise, and the Royal Mail takeover. The Register has asked UKGI for further details. An ICO spokesperson said: "We can confirm UK Government Investments Ltd reported an incident and we are assessing the information provided." (Author: Carly Page, Published: Monday, August 3, 2026 at 12:02 UTC)

c99c66b9ecfa.text:
AI didn't just make defenders faster. It made attackers faster too. With speed no longer separating attackers from defenders, the deciding factor moved to whether organizations can afford to build agentic security and whether they can trust it.

Arctic Wolf launched the Aurora Agentic SOC at RSA Conference 2026 as the largest commercial agentic SOC in the industry. The Aurora Superintelligence Platform processes more than 10 trillion security events weekly. The Aurora Agentic SOC has resolved over three million security cases and run more than 200,000 weekly investigations using the Swarm of Experts.

What It Actually Costs to Build This Yourself: most AI security tools use consumption-based pricing where each additional event/investigation adds cost. Arctic Wolf built the Aurora Agentic SOC to eliminate this trade-off, offering predictable pricing, unlimited data ingestion, and unlimited investigations while managing infrastructure. Deployment takes approximately 10 days and costs roughly 12 times less than building comparable capability internally.

Why the Swarm Knows When to Ask for Help: the 2026 SANS AI in Cybersecurity Survey found nearly two-thirds of security professionals received incorrect AI-generated guidance. Arctic Wolf developed the AI Trust Engine as a validation framework governing agent behavior. The Swarm autonomously resolves over 60% of cases with high confidence; for complex cases, agents escalate to analysts. All outcomes pass through the AI Judge before reaching customers, resulting in approximately one security alert daily instead of overwhelming queues.

Arctic Wolf appeared at Black Hat USA (August 4-6) at booth 1564 and launched an Agentic SOC Cost Calculator on its website. (Author: Dan Schiappa, Published: August 3, 2026)

493be4320f33.text:
A ransomware note doesn't take down a business. The weeks of downtime after it does. Leaders ask what it costs to stop an attack; the harder question, which actually decides whether a business survives, is what it takes to keep operating while recovering from one.

The Real Cost of an Incident: senior leaders focus on prevention costs (tooling, headcount, insurance premiums) which are a rounding error next to what a major incident actually costs. Per IBM's most recent report, the average U.S. data breach now runs $10.22M, and nearly half of that doesn't hit the books until more than a year later. Forensics, legal, notifications, and fines land in the low hundreds of thousands; the costs that actually threaten the business - lost revenue during downtime, payroll burned while operations stall, slower growth the following quarter, and hits to valuation - are an order of magnitude bigger.

What Resilience Actually Means: cyber resilience is four things - anticipate, withstand, recover, and adapt. Most boards can't answer yes to these, and the gap is widening because the threat is moving faster than programs built to handle it.

Four Trends Tipping the Field Toward Attackers: faster exploitation (shrinking disclosure-to-weaponization window), vulnerabilities piling up faster than teams can review, cheaper AI models benefiting attackers as much as defenders, and rising attack payoff versus cost. Per SANS Institute's 2026 AI Survey, 95% believe attackers are using AI against them, and 78% confirmed or suspected an AI-enabled attack in the past year.

Resilience Doesn't Work Piece by Piece: seeing an attack coming doesn't help if you can't withstand it; containing an incident doesn't help if recovery still takes weeks. What decides whether an incident becomes a rough quarter or an existential one is whether anticipate/withstand/recover/adapt run as one system.

What We Built to Close That Gap: the Arctic Wolf Cyber Resilience Bundle, organized around the same four capabilities, backed by the Arctic Wolf Security Operations Warranty (up to $3M in coverage), designed to run alongside existing controls rather than replace them. Available now through Arctic Wolf and its partners; the company offers a Business Value Assessment to estimate incident costs and bundle value. (Author: Will May, Published: August 3, 2026)

6d0265711c98.text:
An unknown Chinese-speaking threat actor has been observed running a campaign targeting Apple iOS devices by leveraging a publicly leaked version of the DarkSword exploit kit. Attack surface management platform Censys said it identified the threat actor running more than 100 web properties, most of which are fake Amazon Web Services (AWS) sign-in pages on a domain that also hosts the exploit toolkit. "The hosting concentrates in Hong Kong but reaches into Japan, the United States, and Europe," according to Censys researcher Aidan Holland's analysis published July 31, 2026.

DarkSword, discovered earlier this year by Google Threat Intelligence Group, iVerify, and Lookout, is a full-chain exploit kit believed used by commercial surveillance vendors and suspected state-sponsored actors targeting Saudi Arabia, Turkey, Malaysia, and Ukraine since November 2025. The kit targets iOS versions 18.4 through 18.7, employing watering holes to trigger patched vulnerabilities that execute JavaScript facilitating GHOSTBLADE malware deployment - an information-stealing tool.

Following public source code leaks, other threat actors began exploiting the toolkit. Censys discovered DarkSword Admin panel logins matching seven hosts across three countries as of July 30, 2026, plus Singapore and Hong Kong hosts running various exploit-panel front ends. The attack flow begins when victims reach operator-controlled domains hosting AWS console or Apple ID impersonation pages, triggering malicious iframe elements that load JavaScript firing the DarkSword chain and deploying GHOSTBLADE modules. Upon successful exploitation, the implant delivers keychain, iCloud, and Wi-Fi credential-dumping modules, conducting file-exfiltration sweeps to attacker-controlled endpoints.

Holland noted this cluster runs the leaked kit rather than a reimplementation, evidenced by shared staging-page hashes plus Russian-language code comments from leaked source material. The Singaporean host previously hosted administration panels for Coruna, another iOS exploit kit predating DarkSword. Evidence suggests threat actor UNC6353 leveraged both kits against Ukrainian targets. Censys discovered an open directory listing in Frankfurt exposing operator tooling, including an SSH key comment 'jkcing@apt,' a web-content fuzzer, and references to a previously undocumented malware family 'Thorn C2.' The C2 Control Panel displayed a group name (亚太集团, 'Asia-Pacific Group') and a Telegram contact link - the first direct contact channel recovered for this operator. (Author: Ravie Lakshmanan, Published: August 3, 2026)

1dc9613beb22.text:
This essay originally appeared in Foreign Policy.

Earlier this month, two of OpenAI's models broke out of their containment sandbox and attacked another AI company. The story is kind of wild. OpenAI was running security tests on two of its models: GPT-5.6 Sol and an unreleased model that is almost certainly GPT-6. In particular, it was running the ExploitGym benchmark, which measures how good a model is at turning security vulnerabilities into working exploits: basically, offensive cyberattacks.

Since these were internal tests, OpenAI locked those models in a secure sandbox that denied them access to the internet. But it was running the models without any safety filters that would prevent them from offensive cyber-actions. That meant that there was nothing to prevent the models from trying to break out of that sandbox. And then break into AI company Hugging Face's network because they thought that they could read the answers there rather than doing the hard work of trying to solve the puzzles.

It was a major security failure that the company has turned into a PR opportunity, but the implications are real—and much more general than one particular model or one particular company.

Modern AI models exhibit genie behavior: They can do what you ask in ways that you don't expect or want. This is akin to Dionysus granting King Midas's wish that everything he touches turn to gold (spoiler: His food, drink, and daughter all turn to gold on touch), or the golem of Prague guarding a ghetto beyond all reason. It's Disney's 'Sorcerer's Apprentice' and the paperclip maximizer.

This OpenAI incident is an example of an AI genie. The goal was to satisfy the benchmark. The 'proper' way to do that is to figure out how to execute various cyberattacks. The genie way is to steal someone else's solution. But because the model didn't understand the difference, it chose the easier path.

And, of course, now that we have seen this particular genie behavior, we can specify in the benchmark prompt that stealing the test answers doesn't count. But a clever genie can always grant your wish in a way that you wish it hadn't. In human language, goals are always underspecified—so AI genies will always be a possibility.

Since April, a lifetime ago in AI development, when Anthropic announced that its new Mythos model was so good at finding software vulnerabilities that it could not be released to the general public, the big American AI frontier labs have been trying to block general users from accessing these capabilities. But nothing in this incident is exclusive to OpenAI's, or Anthropic's, frontier models.

Agentic AI systems have two important parts. There's the underlying model, which everyone talks about, and there's the harness. The harness sits between what you type and what the model sees, and what the model produces and what you see. The harness determines what the model does and how it does it. It's where bias is removed, or not. It's where controls and guardrails live. If multiple models are being used in concert, the harness is where all of that is coordinated.

The OpenAI benchmark tests were almost certainly with simple harnesses, to better test the raw models. But we know that smaller, cheaper, open-source models with more sophisticated harnesses can equal frontier models in performance. There's nothing magic about OpenAI's frontier models; lots of models could have done the same thing.

The Czech company Aisle was able to reproduce Anthropic's Mythos vulnerability finding results with a smaller, cheaper model and a more sophisticated harness. More importantly, the Chinese company Moonshot AI just released its frontier model: Kimi K3. Its performance rivals its U.S. competitors. And it's both free and open, which means it's not possible for it to have guardrails. If you, or anyone else, wants to use it for cyberattack, nothing can stop you.

Even if the U.S. frontier AI companies had some technical advantage, it's now only a few months' worth.

What this means is that all attempts at control—limiting models to a select group of users, export controls on models and chips, blocking models from answering certain types of queries, mandating kill switches on AI systems, or pausing AI research—are all futile. Most only apply nationally, not globally. Most don't affect models that users run locally and not in the cloud. And all ignore the incredible pace of AI development worldwide.

Even worse, U.S. companies limit access to their most sophisticated models, fearing being banned by the government if they do not do so. When Hugging Face was attacked, it was not able to use the frontier models from either OpenAI or Anthropic to help analyze the attack and formulate defenses. Both were blocked, because both of those companies limit their models' cybersecurity capabilities. Some U.S. companies have special access to these capabilities, but Hugging Face is an American company with French origins, and as such is probably excluded. Instead, Hugging Face turned to the GLM-5.2 model from the Chinese company Z.ai.

Artificially blocking capability also prevents cybersecurity research, again giving the offense an advantage. (For instance, Claude Fable 5 refuses to edit this essay because of the topic; it forcibly downgrades to a less capable model.) This kind of prohibition has long-term implications for cybersecurity. If we assume that these models are getting better over time, then software written by older models will be attacked by newer ones. In a world of largely AI-written software, we need the most capable models for defense.

AI cyberattack is the new normal. The models are increasingly highly sophisticated at both attack and defense, and there is no way to enable the latter without also enabling the former. And they are genies, increasingly capable of behaving in unanticipated ways.

And there really are no good answers. Any regulation needs to be global, which feels like an impossible prospect in today's world. Even U.S. national regulation will be neutered by the massive amounts of money sloshing around in these companies.

Given that reality, and in the absence of any international consensus on AI regulation, we need the best AI on the defense. The U.S. government needs to make it clear—or whatever passes for that clarity in this capricious administration—that it will not ban models with sophisticated cyber capabilities. The last thing Americans want is for the defenders to turn to Chinese and other models because the U.S. models are artificially hobbled.

(Author: Bruce Schneier; Published: August 3, 2026)

45fbf8f08dff.text:
**Title:** Pass the Passkey: A Novel Attack Surface in Passwordless Authentication
**Author:** Arie Olshtein
**Published:** August 3, 2026

This Palo Alto Networks Unit 42 research article examines three novel attack classes against Google's synced passkey ecosystem on Chrome/Windows devices with TPM:

1. Pass-ta-key Attack: Malware extracts the device identity key to authenticate without user interaction, device unlock, or privilege escalation. The attack exploits how Chrome stores wrapped identity keys accessible via standard Windows CNG APIs.

2. Silver Pass-ta-key Attack: Malware forces device re-onboarding to register an attacker-controlled UV (user verification) key during the pending state, enabling full account takeover from the attacker's environment without the victim's device involvement.

3. Golden Pass-ta-key Attack: Malware extracts the Security Domain Secret (SDS) master key from Chrome's memory during re-registration, allowing decryption of all synced passkeys for credential theft and reuse.

Critical Findings: The research demonstrates that despite hardware-backed protections, 'malware can obtain the required signature silently, without user consent' or elevation. The attacks exploit gaps between design assumptions and implementation, including inconsistent UV flag validation across relying parties.

Mitigations Recommended: Enforce strict user verification validation; validate device key attestation; harden recovery/re-registration flows; prevent sensitive key material exposure; restrict local passkey data access; implement signature counter mechanisms.

6d5a2a4a401d.text:
On March 13, 2025, Hugo Moreno-Mendez arrived at the McLennan County Probation Department in Waco, Texas, expecting a routine probation check-in. Instead, Immigration and Customs Enforcement officers were waiting to arrest him.
According to a criminal complaint reviewed by WIRED, officers drove Moreno-Mendez to a nearby ICE field office. There, one deportation officer after another approached him with the same demand.
Open your mouth.
One officer tried to take his fingerprints and swab the inside of his cheek for DNA. He refused. Then another tried. Then a third. Each time, Moreno-Mendez refused.
Four days later, Moreno-Mendez was charged with failing to register as a noncitizen and refusing to provide DNA while in federal custody—the latter a misdemeanor that, as of 2021, ICE itself said it was unaware had ever been accepted for prosecution.
Moreno-Mendez took both counts to trial. On August 18, 2025, a magistrate judge in Waco found him guilty of each and sentenced him to time served.
Moreno-Mendez’s case is part of a sweeping expansion of DNA collection from people held for civil immigration violations—a federal campaign that, backed by the threat of prosecution, funnels the genetic profiles of nearly everyone in ICE custody into an FBI database built for criminal investigations. New research from Georgetown Law's Center on Privacy and Technology estimates that the Department of Homeland Security has become the largest single source of new genetic profiles in the nation's criminal DNA system, with ICE alone potentially adding as many as roughly 920,000 profiles in 2025.
The vast majority of people in ICE custody have no criminal conviction, and residing in the US undocumented is typically a civil, not criminal, offense. Yet once the DNA profiles of detained people enter the FBI’s Combined DNA Index System, or CODIS, law enforcement agencies across the country can compare them against evidence from unsolved crimes—and against crime-scene DNA collected years or even decades from now. The physical sample, which holds a person's entire genome, sits in a federal laboratory indefinitely.
The expansion of DNA collection has extended to families held in immigration detention, sparked lawsuits over the collection of DNA from protesters and others who allege they should never have been subjected to the program, and drawn congressional scrutiny after lawmakers learned that children were being swabbed at a family detention center in Dilley, Texas.
“None of the families at Dilley have been convicted of a crime,” US representatives Joaquin Castro, Greg Stanton, and Nanette Barragán said in a joint statement to WIRED. “They do not belong in a database meant for violent criminals, especially children.”
In response to questions from WIRED, a DHS spokesperson defended DNA collection as a border-security and identification measure, saying CBP takes samples from people arrested on federal charges and from detained noncitizens who are subject to fingerprinting and not otherwise exempt. Asked about children whose profiles were submitted to CODIS, DHS pointed to a separate DNA-testing program used to verify family relationships. That program is distinct from the collection at the center of WIRED’s reporting. DHS did not address Georgetown’s estimate that ICE may have added hundreds of thousands of profiles to CODIS in 2025.
For most of the program's history, migrant DNA collection played out at the border, where Customs and Border Protection swabbed people it took into custody. ICE's own contribution was marginal. Internal training slides obtained by Georgetown through the Freedom of Information Act (FOIA) show ICE collected 3,609 DNA samples in fiscal year 2020 and 16,392 more through mid-May of fiscal 2021—roughly 20,000 in all. CBP was operating on a different scale entirely: Agency spreadsheets Georgetown obtained and analyzed show it sent the FBI the DNA of at least 1.36 million people between October 2020 and the end of 2024, more than a dozen times ICE's rate during the same time period.
Georgetown's new report suggests the program entered an entirely different phase in 2025. FBI records show the "detainee" index of CODIS—the sub-index where DHS-collected profiles are stored—reached 3,345,692 profiles by December 2025, growing by roughly 995,000 that year alone. That is more than 2,700 people a day, every day, for a year.
The FBI does not explicitly disclose which agency submitted which DNA profile. To estimate the split, Georgetown compared the total against CBP records showing the agency sent the DNA of approximately 75,215 people to the FBI in 2025. ICE has refused to release comparable data, rebuffing repeated public records requests. Based on the gap, Georgetown estimates that ICE may be responsible for as many as 919,908 new profiles in a single year.
The change tracks a broader shift. According to Transactional Records Access Clearinghouse data cited by Georgetown, CBP once accounted for the majority of immigration detentions. ICE now accounts for roughly 85 percent, CBP for 15. As of July 11 of this year, ICE was holding 65,765 people, up from 60,311 in early April, while arrests climbed toward 1,500 a day, according to Austin Kocher, a research assistant professor at Syracuse University. The largest single group in detention had no criminal history at all.
“Fun Facts”
US law enforcement’s increased DNA collection traces to a legal and regulatory shift that began more than two decades ago. Congress in 2005 authorized federal agencies to collect DNA from people arrested, charged, convicted, or detained under federal authority. For years, however, Justice Department regulations allowed DHS to exempt many people held in immigration custody when collecting samples would create resource burdens.
In 2020, the DOJ eliminated the exemption. That December, ICE issued Directive 10092.1, requiring officers to collect DNA from nearly everyone in its custody.
Internal 2021 training materials obtained by Georgetown show just how broadly officers were instructed to interpret the policy. One slide, from a May 2021 refresher course for Enforcement and Removal Operations (ERO) officers, tells them that asylum seekers and refugees who have not adjusted their immigration status are not exempt—“therefore, their DNA must be sampled.” Another instructs officers, in capital letters, to ensure DNA is largely collected after “ANY arrest.”
Under a heading reading “FUN FACTS,” a May 2021 ICE presentation counts 69 confirmed CODIS hits from samples that ERO submitted in roughly the preceding six months, matching evidence in cases involving “Sexual Offences, Homicide, Missing Person, Burglary, Larceny, Crimes of Public Order, Property Crimes, Assault and Battery, Stalking/Domestic Violence and a stolen Pinto.” The slide's author appended a note: “Editor's note: you'd care if that was YOUR Pinto!”
