Cybercriminals frequently disguise malicious files as harmless documents, exploiting users who open attachments without checking file extensions. Kaspersky experts analyzed malicious email campaigns from early 2026 to identify the 15 most dangerous file extensions.

Top 15 Dangerous Extensions: .exe, .js, .html, .dll, .bat, .vbs, .xls, .pdf, .jse, .au3, .docx, .htm, .wsf, .scr, .lnk

Executable Files: Programs like .exe, .dll, .com, and .scr can execute malicious code immediately upon opening. Attackers frequently use double extensions (e.g., "invoice.docx.exe") to trick users, exploiting Windows' default setting of hiding known file type extensions.

Scripts: Extensions including .js, .bat, .vbs, and .cmd automate command sequences. The iconic ILOVEYOU worm spread via a VBS script, infecting millions in the early 2000s.

Web Files: HTML and HTM files often contain phishing pages mimicking legitimate login forms to harvest credentials.

Archives: ZIP, RAR, and 7Z files frequently contain malware, sometimes password-protected or intentionally corrupted to bypass security scanning.

PDF Files: Despite appearing harmless, PDFs can host malicious scripts and clickable elements. A 2026 vulnerability in Adobe Acrobat allowed remote execution of malicious PDF files.

LNK Shortcuts: Windows shortcuts can masquerade as documents while directing to malicious commands. Unpatched systems execute them automatically.

Microsoft Office Documents: XLS, DOCX, and macro-enabled formats (.xlsm, .docm) can trigger malware downloads or execute embedded commands through macros.

Protection Recommendations: Install comprehensive security solutions with file scanning capabilities; never open attachments from unknown senders; verify email addresses against official sources; avoid files with double extensions; research unfamiliar file extensions; enable Protected View in Microsoft Office; keep Windows updated regularly.

Author: James Coker, Deputy Editor, Infosecurity Magazine. Published: 7 August 2026.

Approximately 1,500 UK charities have potentially experienced data breaches following a cyber incident affecting third-party CRM provider Beacon. Personal information held by these charities, particularly those in healthcare and victim support sectors, was accessed, copied, and likely exfiltrated by an unauthorized actor.

Beacon operates a specialized CRM platform serving around 1,500 voluntary sector organizations. On August 6, a company spokesperson informed Infosecurity that all customers had been notified of the incident, stating: "Our focus is now on supporting them as much as possible in any onward communication."

Since Beacon's public disclosure on August 4, 2026, numerous UK charities confirmed their databases were compromised, including Myton Hospices, Sheffield Hospital Charity, Priscilla Bacon Hospice Charity, Rowcroft Hospice, Clock Tower Sanctuary, and Victim Support.

Affected data includes names, email addresses, telephone numbers, and donation records. Beacon advised customers to "assume all data they store in its platform, including attachments, has been downloaded." Although data was encrypted, the unauthorized actor may have decrypted it.

The platform does not store sensitive patient information, payment card details, or bank account information. Customers can safely collect payments via Beacon forms but must update payment providers following the Security Incident Response Guide.

A compromised access key—more sophisticated than a simple username and password—enabled the breach. External cybersecurity experts have launched an investigation. No ongoing unauthorized access has been observed since containment.

The attack remains unattributed, with no data appearing on the dark web. Previous similar incidents have involved extortion demands.

Security expert Muhammad Yahya Patel of Huntress noted charities are "persistently underappreciated targets," explaining that donor databases contain valuable personally identifiable information enabling fraud and social engineering, while security investment in the sector remains minimal.

Author: Eduard Kovacs. Published: August 7, 2026 (6:00 AM ET).

The National Motor Freight Traffic Association (NMFTA) revealed that a 2024 safety recall for Bendix's EC80 heavy-truck brake controller quietly patched serious security vulnerabilities alongside the publicly disclosed memory corruption issue. Senior cybersecurity research engineer Ben Gardiner presented these findings at Black Hat USA 2026.

The EC80 electronic control unit manages anti-lock braking, traction control, and stability functions on heavy commercial vehicles, communicating via J2497 (PLC4TRUCKS), the industry standard for trailer ABS warning-light requirements since 2001.

In late 2024, three original equipment manufacturers issued recalls covering approximately 450,000 units after Bendix identified memory corruption problems. The company attributed the issue to line noise and shipped a firmware update.

Upon reverse-engineering pre- and post-update firmware, Gardiner discovered that the update deleted dozens of functions. Within that removed code, researchers identified multiple vulnerabilities: buffer-handling flaws enabling remote code execution and denial-of-service attacks, a hardcoded password disabling traction control, and additional crash and code execution pathways.

Potential Impact: J2497 can be accessed remotely through vulnerabilities disclosed in 2022 or via compromised trailer telematics. Testing revealed that triggering crashes caused complete CAN bus traffic stoppage, requiring battery disconnection for recovery. This resulted in loss of speedometer, steering assist, shifting capabilities, and ABS functionality—effects depending heavily on operational context.

NMFTA noted that while the outcome could create immobilization risks during cargo theft operations, the attacks don't directly prevent driver vehicle control. However, the vulnerabilities proved serious enough to warrant the recall. Notably, none of the vulnerabilities received CVE identifiers despite being fixed, potentially obscuring the security significance of the safety-framed update.

Disclosure and Completion: NMFTA coordinated with Bendix, two affected OEMs, NHTSA, and Transport Canada before public disclosure. According to NHTSA's recall-completion tracker, completion rates ranged from 0–99% as of July 16. NMFTA estimates industry-wide plateau around 80% due to equipment loss and underreporting. A comprehensive 179-page technical whitepaper was published following the Black Hat presentation. Bendix has not responded to SecurityWeek's comment request.

Author: Beth Maundrill, Editor, Infosecurity Magazine. Published: 7 August 2026.

Google's Threat Intelligence Group discovered that the BlackFile extortion operation, known as UNC6671, has rebranded itself as Redact. The group announced its retirement in 2026, citing an affiliate breakaway as justification. However, researchers identified overlapping phishing templates, target patterns, and shared infrastructure suggesting the same actors now operate under multiple brands including Pink, Helix, and Falcon.

On June 27, Redact operators published information about their new data leak site and rebrand. They claimed the original BlackFile brand had been compromised by an exiled affiliate who operated an unauthorized lookalike site and conducted unauthorized extortion campaigns using different Tox identities.

Vishing Attack Methods: The group primarily targets enterprise employees through voice phishing, impersonating IT helpdesk personnel. Researchers noted that the initial access and post-compromise TTPs have largely remained the same despite rebranding. Attackers direct victims to spoofed login portals where adversary-in-the-middle infrastructure captures credentials and MFA tokens. Once access is established, they deploy automated scripts to exfiltrate data from Microsoft 365 and Okta environments. UNC6671 reuses generic root domains across multiple organizations; domains like passkeyhelpdesk[.]com appeared in campaigns targeting separate victims claimed by different extortion brands, confirming infrastructure overlap.

Evolving Targets and Tactics: Between April and July 2026, the group shifted targeting priorities—from manufacturing, real estate, healthcare, and insurance sectors to technology, transportation, and hospitality firms, eventually focusing on high-value financial and legal organizations including private equity firms and law firms. New techniques include spoofing legitimate helpdesk phone numbers with urgent FIDO2 passkey enrollment pretexts, and using compromised email accounts to reset passwords while deleting security notifications.

Financial analysis revealed that between January 7 and May 12, 18 BlackFile Bitcoin wallets received approximately 141.65 BTC, valued at roughly $10.69 million USD.

Recommended Mitigations: Google recommended organizations enforce phishing-resistant authenticators, integrate single sign-on, enforce session controls to reduce session duration, and restrict authentication to trusted network sources. Since vishing targets personal devices, authentication should originate from corporate-managed endpoints with mobile device management and endpoint detection and response capabilities.

144673547098.text:
Author: Swati Khandelwal. Published: August 7, 2026.

Security researcher Malcolm Stagg has disclosed a new attack class called NatJack that manipulates network address translation (NAT) connection state to hijack active TCP sessions, spoof DNS responses, expose mapped ports, and exhaust NAT tables.

Presented at Black Hat USA 2026, the research found affected behavior across independently developed implementations, including Windows and Linux. Two implementation-specific flaws have been assigned CVEs: CVE-2026-56181 (CVSS score: 8.3) in Windows NAT used by Hyper-V, and CVE-2026-63913 (CVSS score: 8.2) in Linux Netfilter conntrack.

NatJack generally requires the attacker to have privileged access to a system behind the same NAT as the victim. The mitigation guidance therefore emphasizes separating untrusted workloads from trusted systems that share NAT infrastructure. There is no single patch for the broader attack class. Organizations should apply available Windows and Linux updates and encrypt traffic even within internal networks. The research also recommends Internet Protocol (IP) Source Guard where applicable.

The NatJack research targets an assumption built into many NAT implementations: hosts behind the same NAT are generally assumed not to manipulate one another's connection state. An attacker controlling a system behind the same NAT can manipulate connection-tracking entries belonging to another system.

The research describes four main attack paths: redirecting traffic from active TCP connections by replacing NAT mappings, interfering with DNS requests to enable response spoofing, disclosing externally mapped ports, or filling NAT connection tables with spoofed flows until legitimate clients cannot create new connections.

Stagg tested the techniques against dozens of real-world network infrastructure products from multiple vendors and demonstrated proof-of-concept exploitation in controlled environments. No public evidence indicates NatJack techniques have been exploited in the wild as of August 7, 2026.

Author: Ionut Arghire. Published: August 7, 2026 (5:09 AM ET).

Microsoft and Apple on Thursday announced fixes for multiple vulnerabilities across their products.

The charge was led by Microsoft, which patched over a dozen vulnerabilities across Active Directory, Azure, Entra, SharePoint, Teams, and other products, including critical-severity remote code execution (RCE) issues.

Three of the issues, CVE-2026-63508, CVE-2026-56162, and CVE-2026-65667, have a maximum severity rating of 10/10. Described as missing authentication in Planetary Computer Pro, improper authentication in Azure SQL Database, and missing authorization in Teams, respectively, they could lead to elevation of privilege (EoP) and can be exploited over the network.

Four other flaws, CVE-2026-50515 (RCE in Azure Service Bus), CVE-2026-62830 (EoP in Azure SRE Agent), CVE-2026-59115 (EoP in Entra Provisioning Service), and CVE-2026-50481 (EoP in Active Directory), have a CVSS score of 9.9/10. All four are remotely exploitable.

Other critical- and high-severity issues that Microsoft addressed on August 6 could lead to information disclosure, RCE, EoP, and spoofing. Microsoft's fresh security updates rolled out one week after over two dozen fixes landed for vulnerabilities in Office, 365 Apps for Enterprise, Edge, and Azure Cosmos DB.

Apple squashed a single bug on Thursday, tracked as CVE-2026-65400 (CVSS score of 7.5), which could allow remote attackers to bypass Screen Sharing authentication. Patches for the security defect were included in macOS Tahoe 26.6.1, macOS Sequoia 15.7.9, and macOS Sonoma 14.8.9. The updates were rolled out roughly a week after Apple fixed dozens of security defects with the release of iOS 26.6 and macOS Tahoe 26.6.

Author: Sinisa Markovic, Managing Editor, Help Net Security. Published: August 7, 2026.

OpenAI has updated GPT-5.6 Sol, the model powering ChatGPT for Plus and Pro subscribers, and released GPT-5.6 Luna to all free-tier users. The company is eliminating rate limits on text conversations for free users, enabling continuous chat without waiting for resets.

For paid accounts, GPT-5.6 Sol now combines quick replies and extended reasoning within a single model, replacing the previous separation between "Instant" and "Thinking" modes. Users can adjust how much reasoning effort the model applies to responses using a new slider.

OpenAI reports the update significantly reduces factual errors. Testing on financial, medical, and legal queries showed Luna and Sol produced substantially fewer responses containing errors compared to the previous GPT-5.5 Instant model.

Changes for free users: Free and Go tier subscribers receive GPT-5.6 Luna as their default this week. Starting next week, OpenAI will remove text chat rate limits and introduce a "Think" button for complex questions. Unlimited chats remain subject to "abuse guardrails," though limits persist for file uploads and image features.

Teen safeguards: GPT-5.6 Sol received additional training to avoid romantic roleplay, age-restricted challenges, and positioning itself as a relationship substitute. The model incorporates age-related boundaries covering sexual content, eating disorders, body image concerns, age-restricted products, dangerous activities, and violent imagery. When teenagers need assistance, the model directs them toward trusted adults. OpenAI reinforced this with system-level protections and new evaluations for users under 18.

Regarding security, GPT-5.6 Sol demonstrated strong resistance to jailbreak attempts and prompt injection attacks, maintaining performance comparable to earlier versions.

Author: Swati Khandelwal. Published: August 7, 2026.

Entra ID researcher Dirk-jan Mollema demonstrated that malware already running in a signed-in Windows session can silently use the victim's Windows Hello for Business key to authenticate to Microsoft Entra ID.

The attacker can then establish longer-term cloud access, register a device it controls, obtain a Primary Refresh Token (PRT), and add further authentication methods where tenant policies permit.

On TPM-backed systems, the attacker does not extract the private key, recover the PIN, or trigger a biometric prompt. Windows ticketing keeps private-key operations available while the user is interactively signed in, allowing code running as the user to ask Windows to sign authentication data. Administrator privileges are not required.

The technique requires code execution in the victim's signed-in session. Mollema describes the behavior as a consequence of how Windows Hello for Business works and says it was left as-is. The disclosure does not report active exploitation or victims. Mollema recommends monitoring unexpected device registrations.

The disclosure does not identify the exact Windows builds or Windows Hello for Business deployment models tested. The Hacker News found no CVE or Microsoft advisory tied to the technique in searches of Microsoft's Security Update Guide, NVD, and CVE.org as of August 6, 2026. The Hacker News has contacted Microsoft and Mollema; replies are pending.

Microsoft documents the ticketing behavior. Mollema said the ability to invoke Windows Hello for Business keys from a compromised session was presented at DEF CON 32 in 2024. That method could produce a signed assertion for a PRT, but also required access to an Entra-registered or joined device.

The new work treats the Windows Hello for Business key as a FIDO2 passkey through WebAuthn. Mollema found that the five-minute Entra ID challenge is not bound to a session, user, or tenant. An attacker can therefore request it on another host and have the compromised endpoint produce the signed assertion. ROADtools, a framework for interacting with Entra ID, can use the assertion to request tokens or open a browser session as the victim.

Mollema found that the token carries no device ID claim. A token without that device binding lets the attacker register a new device, request a PRT for it, and reach Microsoft cloud services. Microsoft documents that a PRT remains valid for 90 days and is continuously renewed while the user actively uses the device.

Mollema found that the WebAuthn sign-in can satisfy Conditional Access policies requiring Microsoft's phishing-resistant authentication strength. He said the sign-in also counts as fresh multi-factor authentication, allowing an attacker to add passkeys or Windows Hello for Business keys on the new device where policies allow. Separate device-state or compliance policies can still interrupt the chain, so the complete persistence route will not work in every deployment.

The finding exposes a limit of phishing-resistant authentication: the credential can remain hardware-bound and unexported while malware inside the signed-in endpoint session invokes it for the attacker.

Mollema published the PowerShell proof-of-concept scripts in the ROADtools repository. The Hacker News found fido_assertion.ps1 and hellopoc.ps1 in the folder on August 6, 2026. For detection, he recommended hunting for Windows Hello for Business sign-ins with an empty device ID. Legitimate incognito or non-SSO browser sessions can produce the same pattern.

Author: James Coker, Deputy Editor, Infosecurity Magazine. Published: August 7, 2026.

Ransomware attacks experienced a significant uptick in July, rising by 19% compared to June. According to analysis by Comparitech, a total of 799 claimed ransomware attacks occurred that month, representing the second highest monthly total in 2026 and the third highest in the past 17 months.

The finance sector saw the steepest increase, with attacks jumping 71% month-over-month. Technology followed at 62%, healthcare at 46%, and education at 44%. Attacks targeting US organizations also surged, climbing 31% from June.

Notable incidents included an assault on US healthcare provider AnMad that forced facility closures, and a Romanian government land registry attack resulting in complete database deletion and significant disruption to real estate operations.

Rebecca Moody, head of data research at Comparitech, emphasized: "These attacks highlight how ransomware groups hit organizations in various different ways – taking down key systems, stealing troves of data, and even deleting massive datasets."

Dominant Threat Actors: The Gentlemen and Qilin ransomware groups dominated the landscape, collectively responsible for 33% of July attacks. The Gentlemen claimed 135 attacks while Qilin recorded 125. This represents an ongoing competition for supremacy between the two groups. Other active players included DragonForce (41 attacks), INC (36), CRPx0 (33), and SafePay (30).

Author: Swati Khandelwal. Date: August 7, 2026.

Security researchers from Novee Security discovered critical vulnerabilities in coding agents from Anthropic, Google, and OpenAI that could allow unprivileged attackers to access CI/CD workflow secrets through GitHub issues.

Gemini CLI Vulnerability (CVE-2026-12537): Rated CVSS 10.0, this OS command injection flaw in the container launcher allows attackers to execute code on CI hosts before sandboxes activate. A crafted .gemini/.env file enables this attack. Fixed in Gemini CLI 0.39.1 and run-gemini-cli 0.1.22.

Claude Code Vulnerability (CVE-2026-54316): This flaw turned Hugging Face's public download counter into an exfiltration channel leaking API keys character by character. Affects versions 0.2.54 through 2.1.163. Anthropic rates it Moderate (CVSS 6.0), though NVD assigned 9.1 under v3.1 scoring.

OpenAI Codex Finding: No CVE assigned. The vulnerability involved running two Codex passes in a single job sharing one checkout, allowing the first pass to modify instructions for the second. OpenAI separated passes into different jobs and implemented read-only sandboxes.

Common Root Cause: All three flaws stemmed from "the harness," the code surrounding models that determines execution permissions. Validation occurred in one section while actual execution happened elsewhere with higher authority, creating an enforcement gap.

Remediation Status: Neither Gemini nor Claude Code vulnerabilities appear in CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog. A public reproduction lab for Claude Code flaws exists on GitHub since June 18. No confirmed real-world exploitation documented.

f063889547f4.text:
Author: Xavier Mertens. Published: 2026-08-07.

Xavier Mertens examines Atuin, a tool that modernizes Linux shell history logging by storing command records in a SQLite database rather than flat text files. Traditional shell history files suffer from limitations including lack of timestamps, unreliable command ordering, and easy user manipulation.

Atuin records contextual data for each command: execution directory, duration, exit code, session ID, and hostname. It also supports encrypted cross-machine synchronization.

Key Forensic Findings - Primary Artifacts Location: ~/.local/share/atuin/history.db (SQLite database); ~/.local/share/atuin/history.db-wal (uncommitted records - critical for investigation); ~/.config/atuin/config.toml (configuration file).

Investigation Advantages: The database structure provides a UTC timestamp (nanoseconds since epoch), the working directory, the exit code, execution duration, and other metadata per command, enabling detailed timeline reconstruction.

Investigative Cautions: Commands may appear in the database without running on that specific host if sync is enabled, and configured filters can prevent certain commands from being recorded entirely.

Author: Ionut Arghire. Published: August 7, 2026 (3:22 AM ET).

Unlimited Technology Systems is notifying over 3.8 million individuals that their personal information was stolen in a data breach.

Based in Montgomery, Ohio, Unlimited provides advanced financial and revenue cycle technology to healthcare providers and organizations. It claims to be working with more than 4,500 oncology offices and over 6,500 specialty providers.

The incident was discovered in October 2025 and involved one of the company's commercial data centers. The company's investigation determined that hackers stole certain data from its systems between October 5 and October 10, 2025.

The stolen data includes personal, medical, and health insurance information. Specifically, the hackers obtained names, addresses, phone numbers, email addresses, Social Security numbers, medical record numbers, diagnoses, dates of service, insurance policy numbers, claims/benefits information, and scanned documents such as driver's licenses and government IDs.

According to Unlimited, "The data involved in the incident does not include full patient medical records, medical imaging, or financial information, such as credit card or bank account information."

The company notes it is unaware of any attempted or actual misuse of the compromised information.

In late July, Unlimited notified the US Department of Health and Human Services that 3,803,750 people were affected. The HHS added Unlimited to its breach portal on August 6.

The company is offering affected individuals two years of free credit monitoring, fraud consultation, and identity theft restoration services.

Unlimited has not identified the threat actor responsible, and no known extortion or ransomware groups have claimed the attack.

Keepit announced AI Truth Cloud, transforming backup from a compliance requirement into the strategically valuable data asset an organization can hold.

As AI agents take on business-critical decisions, AI Truth Cloud positions Keepit as the sovereign source of truth that enterprise AI can safely build on: data that is verifiable, governed, immutable, and proven.

Author: Ionut Arghire. Published: August 7, 2026 (2:56 AM ET).

Google released Chrome 151, patching 41 critical and high-severity vulnerabilities. Over two dozen are memory safety bugs that could cause data corruption, crashes, and arbitrary code execution.

The update resolves six critical-severity flaws, including five use-after-free issues affecting WebGL, Aura, Skia, and Views components, plus an out-of-bounds write in the ANGLE graphics engine. External researchers discovered two WebGL defects; Google found the remaining four critical issues.

The remaining 35 vulnerabilities are high-severity. Google identified 25 of these; external researchers found 10. Only two bug bounty rewards were disclosed, each worth $500.

Among the 35 high-severity issues, 24 are memory safety bugs encompassing use-after-free, buffer overflow, out-of-bounds write, and uninitialized use defects. The remaining flaws involve insufficient input validation, inappropriate implementations, race conditions, and integer overflows.

The article notes that Google's use of AI drives a faster patching pace, indicating the company's accelerated vulnerability remediation efforts.

Chrome 151 rolled out as versions 151.0.7922.108/.109 for Windows and macOS, and 151.0.7922.108 for Linux. No evidence of active exploitation exists, but users are advised to update immediately.

4d44b470228a.text:
Author: Ravie Lakshmanan. Published: August 7, 2026.

A new analysis has revealed that TeamPCP, a significant cybercrime threat actor, has maintained an active presence dating back to 2020. Researchers from Oligo Security connected the group's recent operations to earlier campaigns through overlapping infrastructure, malware deployment methods, and operational techniques.

The investigation links TeamPCP to two notable 2025 campaigns: ShadowRay 2.0 (also known as IronErn), which compromised AI infrastructure to create self-propagating botnets, and TA-NATALSTATUS, which targeted exposed Redis servers to deploy cryptocurrency miners. The TA-NATALSTATUS campaign appears related to an April 2020 Trend Micro report documenting Redis server targeting for malware deployment.

TeamPCP initially gained attention when they exploited React Server Components and Next.js vulnerabilities to extract credentials and sensitive data in Operation PCPcat. Later that year, they launched systematic attacks against cloud-native environments to establish malicious infrastructure for data exfiltration, ransomware deployment, extortion, and cryptocurrency mining.

The group subsequently shifted focus toward high-profile supply chain compromises, leveraging GitHub Actions and token theft to poison open-source libraries and infect developer systems.

Evidence connecting these operations includes overlap between the IronErn GitHub and GitLab identities observed during ShadowRay 2.0 alongside command-and-control infrastructure and malware staging techniques. The threat actor repeatedly abused known vulnerabilities affecting React, Docker, Redis, and Ray platforms using automated exploitation methods.

The malware arsenal evolved continuously, including a Python script called "kube.py" deployed after Kubernetes breaches. Newer variants observed through March 2026 incorporated destructive wiper functionality. Code checked for Iranian timezone configuration; if detected, it deployed a DaemonSet named Kamikaze that wiped cluster nodes. On non-Iranian systems, it deployed CanisterWorm backdoors. For Iranian non-Kubernetes systems, malware executed "poison_pill()" routines erasing entire filesystems.

Oligo researchers concluded that TeamPCP represents the continuation of an existing operational ecosystem rather than an entirely new threat actor.

44c2ae5a41bc.text:
Author: Anamarija Pogorelec, Senior Staff Writer, Help Net Security. Published: August 7, 2026.

Internet-exposed automatic tank gauge (ATG) systems in the US dropped dramatically from approximately 4,800 addresses monthly to 2,354 by June 2026 — a decline exceeding 50% over three months. These devices, located beneath gas station forecourts and at critical infrastructure sites, monitor fuel levels and can control alarms and equipment.

Following suspected Iran-linked attacks reported in April and May, the Energy Marketers of America issued an urgent advisory on April 14. CISA and federal agencies coordinated response efforts alongside industry partners.

The data reveals genuine device removal rather than mere address churn. Port 10001 — a factory default from Lantronix adapters — showed 65% decline (4,214 to 1,466 addresses), while control port 8001 remained stable at roughly 850 addresses, demonstrating the drop wasn't scanner-related.

Researchers estimate approximately 2,260 addresses representing genuine removals between January and June. The decline remained consistent across the three-month period, suggesting sustained operator response to advisories rather than temporary attention.

However, gaps persist: port 8001 exposure remains unaddressed, devices behind network protections remain vulnerable to lateral movement attacks, and newer web-based console defaults remain exploitable.

951111871470.text:
Author: Mirko Zorz, Director of Content, Help Net Security. Published: August 7, 2026.

ShieldFont is a web font technology created by Isaque Seneda and Gabriel Abrucio that displays one set of words to human readers while serving different words to AI scrapers and crawlers. The tool launched in October 2025 with support from type foundry Playtype.

How It Works: The technology swaps words in page source code before deployment, replacing each word with another of similar type and frequency. The font then renders the swapped words to display correctly to browsers, while scrapers pulling raw HTML receive the altered text. According to Abrucio, "Mostly writers and artists, but more broadly anyone who wants to protect their creativity" are the intended users.

Word substitution happens server-side to prevent exposing the dictionary to browsers. The technique requires choosing whether to optimize for user comfort or embrace protective friction.

Limitations and Vulnerabilities: The system has documented weaknesses. Anyone with the shipped font can extract the 11,962 word pairs using an inverter. Headless browsers, OCR tools, and vision-language models reading rendered pages see unprotected text. The researchers tested effectiveness by swapping roughly 25% of words and found meaning failed in 55.8% of news passages examined.

RSS feeds leak unencrypted content by default. Screen readers receive hidden protected regions, requiring alternative puzzle-solving mechanisms to access real words.

Strategic Value: Seneda emphasizes economic deterrence: increasing scraping costs from raw HTML extraction to OCR processing represents real money, even if it is still only cents per page. Future plans include dictionary rotation and per-deploy seed variations to raise attacker expenses further.

The broader purpose centers on cultural impact. As Abrucio notes, "we see ShieldFont's trade-offs as an investment in human creativity" amid concerns that mass scraping discourages online publishing.

ShieldFont remains freely available on GitHub under open-source terms.

6ea651e55023.text:
Author: Anamarija Pogorelec, Senior Staff Writer, Help Net Security. Published: August 7, 2026.

A Brigham Young University pilot study examined whether people can distinguish between AI-generated and human-written spear phishing texts. Researchers recruited 25 volunteers who provided personal details (job, workplace, hobbies, city, recent social media posts) that informed message creation.

GPT-4 generated six messages per participant using a prompt template, while undergraduate students in a deception course created the remainder under time constraints. Participants then sorted all twelve messages, indicating which ones they would likely click.

Key Findings: GPT-4 messages succeeded 28% of the time versus 21.3% for student-written ones — a gap with substantial statistical uncertainty. The researchers note that one simple prompt achieved comparable results to screened student submissions.

Work-related messages proved dramatically more effective than hobby or social media themes, clearing the click threshold 38% versus 19% and 17% respectively.

When asked to identify AI-generated messages, participants achieved only 52% accuracy — barely above random chance. Despite having theories about stylistic indicators, people fundamentally struggled with detection.

However, a machine learning classifier achieved 88.7% accuracy after stripping formatting elements. Researchers emphasize this classifier hasn't been tested beyond this specific dataset and warns that adversaries can defeat such tools through paraphrasing.

Limitations: The study used printed cards rather than authentic mobile interfaces, compared AI against novices rather than professionals, and involved too few participants (25) for strong statistical conclusions. The researchers recommend: "Check the sender, the channel, the link, and the request against what you would expect to receive."
