Zoom did not respond to multiple requests for comment from WIRED about the A Security findings.
The bugs are now patched, with Zoom issuing both server and client-side fixes—or patches for both Zoom’s own servers and the applications that run on customer devices. But the researchers emphasize that it was alarming to contemplate bugs that could have been exploited to take over a target device simply by getting someone onto a Zoom call. Joining a call is in itself a gesture of trust, but given how ubiquitous video calling is in both personal and professional contexts—and given that Zoom in particular is also widely used for events and semipublic activities like webinars—people typically have their guard down when joining a Zoom.
“If you just get on a Zoom with us, we can take over your device,” A Security cofounder Yossi Torati told WIRED on a call. (It was, incidentally, hosted on Microsoft Teams.) “The worst-case scenario is that we can take over an enterprise just by having this vulnerability in our hands. If I’m an attacker, I can be on a call with someone from a company, take control of their computer and their credentials, and then use them to move laterally in the enterprise.”
Practitioners often call security a “cat-and-mouse game,” but as AI bug hunting proliferates, this delicate dance has become an all-out race.

808ccbb18ef5.text:
Spain's national police say they caught a cybercriminal after a momentary technical glitch exposed his face to a video identification platform.

The unnamed man allegedly made 38 attempts to impersonate 30 people and obtain digital certificates in their names, succeeding on multiple occasions.

A digital certificate uses public key infrastructure to bind a cryptographic key to a verified identity, allowing its holder to authenticate themselves and create legally recognized electronic signatures.

In Spain and other EU countries, certificates can be used to sign contracts, authorize transactions and deal with public bodies online, avoiding some of the in-person appointments traditionally required for administrative procedures.

A certificate issued in someone else's name would therefore give a scammer a powerful tool for impersonation. Police allege that the suspect planned to use the fraudulently obtained credentials in further cybercrimes.

The alleged fraudster targeted a security company authorized to issue digital certificates and bypassed its identity checks using forged documents, altered photographs, deepfake tools, and a carefully arranged lighting rig.

The verification process required a live video check comparing the applicant's face with the photograph on the identity document.

He allegedly used deepfake technology to alter his face in real time so that he could bypass the visual identity checks, and used custom lighting to recreate the appearance of each document's holograms.

"The alleged perpetrator used household spotlights with strategically placed colored bulbs to simulate the flashes and security features found on physical identity documents under real light," police said. "He then balanced the counterfeit documents in front of the webcam, perfectly recreating the official holograms. He also used VPNs to anonymize his connections and employed manipulated documents with apparent security features."

Police did not say how many of the 38 attempts succeeded, only that certificates were issued on "multiple" occasions.

His luck allegedly ran out when the face-changing software suffered a momentary processing delay. The disguise dropped for "barely a second," exposing his real face to the verification camera, police said.

Investigators eventually identified and located the suspect, who was arrested on suspicion of repeatedly forging official documents. A search of his home yielded a laptop protected by high-grade encryption, several mobile phones, storage devices, and documents, according to police.

The investigation was complicated by the use of more than 320 phone lines across 24 devices. Most had allegedly been registered under stolen identities, with police tracing their sale to outlets in the Murcia region.

(Author: Connor Jones, Published: Tuesday, August 11, 2026 // 13:27 UTC)

ce568a63dde3.text:
Researchers have found that compromised or malicious SIM cards can issue commands to some smartphones and cellular-connected devices, allowing attackers to steal information, disrupt communications, downgrade connections to 2G, and in some cases execute code.

Tomasz Piotr Lisowski and Dr Marius Muench of the University of Birmingham, working with Kristian Covic from Fuzzware, traced this to a legitimate function already built into the cellular spec.

That function is Proactive SIM. It lets a card send instructions to a device's modem instead of only answering the modem's requests. One instruction, RUN AT, tells the modem to execute an AT command, the control language modems have used since the 1980s. A SIM that shouldn't be trusted gets a direct line into the hardware.

To determine how much access this provides, the researchers developed a toolkit called CATana and tested it against 18 smartphones and eight cellular IoT devices. Two of the smartphones exposed an AT command interface to the SIM. Seven of the eight IoT devices did the same.

The testing uncovered four vulnerabilities and produced demonstrations involving code execution, file theft, denial of service, and forced network downgrades.

"The fascinating part here is that the proactive capabilities of a SIM and the resulting attack surface is explicitly defined in the technical specifications for cellular communication, resulting into 'specification-compliant' attacks," said Dr Marius Muench, Assistant Professor, University of Birmingham.

"Other researchers, cybersecurity experts, and leaked intelligence documents have shown some of the dangers of hostile SIMs before us. Yet, the resulting risks have not been fully mitigated. Potentially, this is because hostile SIMs are not included in most threat models; although we slowly see a promising shift here," added Muench.

On an AUTEL EV charger built around a Quectel EC25-AFX module, SIM-issued commands triggered a command injection flaw in the modem's Linux-based application processor, giving the researchers code execution on the cellular module.

An OPPO Reno14 F 5G accepted 198 AT commands and variants through the SIM interface, including commands that could power off the phone, stop its modem, or force the connection onto 2G. The downgrade persisted after the researchers enabled airplane mode, disabled the SIM, and changed the phone's network settings. Because 2G lacks network-to-device authentication, a device forced onto the older network can also be more susceptible to rogue base stations impersonating legitimate cellular networks.

Against a Quectel EG25-G modem, the team combined a malicious symbolic link with commands sent from the SIM to email a targeted file from the device to a server they controlled.

None of these attacks works without control of the SIM itself. The researchers describe several ways this could happen, including vulnerabilities in SIM software, physical replacement or tampering, abuse of remote SIM-management infrastructure, and modification during manufacturing or distribution.

Separately, the researchers found that affected Android versions allowed a hostile SIM to trigger the standardized LAUNCH BROWSER command and open an attacker-controlled website without user interaction, including while the phone was locked. Google tracked the issue as CVE-2025-48618 and addressed it for Android 13 through 16 in December 2025.

The team reported its findings to the GSM Association and to affected chip and device makers before publishing. Several manufacturers have already shipped patches or hardened configurations, and the wider SIM AT issue is logged by GSMA as CVD-2026-0122.

"It was great working together with the affected companies and GSMA," Muench said. "Our reports were treated seriously, and key manufacturers made software updates and hardened configurations available to their customers. This will benefit billions of future SIM-enabled devices operating worldwide, including smartphones, connected vehicles, payment terminals, routers, critical infrastructure and EV charging systems."

Kristian Covic called hostile SIMs "an overlooked attack vector" and said the team was glad to help demonstrate the risk through the project.

Patching individual bugs isn't enough on its own, the team argues. Their recommendation is to deprecate the RUN AT feature altogether and strip the related code out of modem and device firmware, rather than leaving it dormant behind a filter.

"The attacks we found only scratch the surface of what is possible with hostile SIM cards. We will keep working on bringing more of the attack surface to the public light and hope to cooperate with vendors and standardization bodies to remedy the risks in today's and future devices," Tomasz Piotr Lisowski concluded.

(Author: Sinisa Markovic, Published: August 11, 2026)

8a80890e770c.text:
A malicious SIM card can order the device it sits in to run commands of the attacker's choosing. On the cellular modules built into electric-vehicle chargers, industrial routers, and car telematics units, that is enough to take the whole device over.

Researchers at the University of Birmingham and the security firm Fuzzware tested 26 phones and cellular modules for the capability, found it switched on in 9 of them, and used it to run their own code on a commercial EV charger.

Six of the eight cellular modules they tested accepted the command. Only 3 of 18 phones did: the OPPO Find X5, the OPPO Reno 14 F 5G, and the ASUS Zenfone 9. No iPhone or Pixel was among them.

The exposure is in machine-to-machine hardware. Five of the six were Quectel parts, three of them pulled from an EV charger, an industrial router, and a car's telematics control unit.

Knowing the victim's number is not enough: every attack starts with a hostile card already in the slot, swapped by hand, slipped in as a thin interposer, pushed out by a compromised operator, or subverted in software or on the production line.

There is no single patch. Every one of the nine devices that accepted the command runs a Qualcomm communication processor. Qualcomm told the researchers it has built a hardened configuration that switches the interface off by default. Quectel says it has mitigated the file-access flaw and is still working on the interface itself. Neither has published an advisory.

The command in question is a proactive command, part of the standardised set a SIM can push back at the modem instead of waiting to be read. RUN AT asks the modem to execute an AT command, the modem control language that dates to the 1981 Hayes Smartmodem.

Marius Muench, assistant professor in computer science at the University of Birmingham, said the SIM's proactive capability and the attack surface it opens are "explicitly defined in the technical specifications for cellular communication."

Architecture is what makes the IoT side worse. Nearly every module the team examined runs a small application processor alongside the radio, usually Android on an ARM Cortex-A7, and passes up any AT command the radio does not handle itself.

The charger is a commercial Autel unit (MAXI US AC W12-L-4G). Inside it, the Quectel EC25AFXDGA module's atfwd_daemon passes attacker-controlled text into a shell call through an unsafe format string. A character blocklist was supposed to stop shell escapes; a newline got past it, and the team achieved code execution.

On an OPPO Reno 14 F 5G, the command AT+COPS=0,,,0 pinned the phone to 2G, irreversible by the owner through any normal means. Two further commands powered the handset down and shut off the modem. The team's CATana tooling found 198 AT commands reachable through the SIM on that handset.

A third case study read arbitrary files off a Quectel EG25-G by way of a TFTP daemon running as root that does not check whether a path is a symbolic link, then mailed the files out using the module's own AT+QSMTP commands.

While building up to this work, the group showed that a hostile SIM could make a locked Android phone open an attacker-controlled web page with no user interaction (Pixel 6, 8, 9 among others), patched by Google as CVE-2025-48618 in December 2025.

Muench said the team is fairly confident every module in Quectel's EC25, EG25 and RM52xN series is affected, and likely other Quectel modules built on a Qualcomm modem too, used in cars, vehicle chargers, payment terminals and other IoT devices.

The reports went to Google, Oppo, Quectel, Semtech and Qualcomm in March 2026, and to the GSMA in May. The exposed SIM AT interface is tracked as CVE-2026-57550 (Qualcomm) and CVD-2026-0122 (GSMA), though the CVE record has yet to appear in the CVE Program's published list. Semtech confirmed the findings and plans to ship Qualcomm-authored patches. Quectel confirmed them too and said the command injection was already fixed in newer firmware, though it has not published affected/fixed version numbers. As of August 10, none of the five vendors had issued a public advisory, and no exploitation has been reported.

(Author: Swati Khandelwal, Published: August 11, 2026)

32b6997c3bbb.text:
Corma emerged from stealth mode on Monday with $60 million in funding for a foundation model designed specifically for defensive cybersecurity.

Headquartered in Tel Aviv and San Francisco, Corma was founded in 2025. One of the company's founders is Alon Pluda, who serves as CEO.

The company has raised $60 million in seed funding from Sequoia Capital, Khosla Ventures, and Coatue.

Corma develops an AI foundation model exclusively engineered for defensive cybersecurity operations. The system processes large datasets of security telemetry, such as system events, audit logs, and network traffic. By analyzing this information, the technology connects subtle anomaly indicators over extended timeframes for complex threat evaluations.

This architecture powers automated agents that integrate directly into an organization's current security infrastructure. The agents operate alongside human staff to handle a wide range of defensive duties while continuously adapting to their designated enterprise environments.

Through this ongoing environmental learning, the agents detect and neutralize threats, including multi-stage intrusions.

Corma claims it ran tests using AI models from OpenAI and Anthropic, and while they were capable of conducting end-to-end attacks, they failed to defend against the same type of attacks.

"AI-powered attacks are operating at a speed and sophistication that neither human teams, better tooling, nor general-purpose AI can match," stated CEO Pluda, emphasizing the need for "a complete AI-powered defensive workforce, built from the ground up for cybersecurity."

(Author: SecurityWeek News, Published: August 11, 2026, 8:01 AM ET)

85cba639cd4c.text:
Credential vaulting has fundamentally transformed from basic password storage into a dynamic security layer. Historically, vaults functioned as "glorified password storage"—secure digital lockboxes with minimal oversight between credential retrieval and use.

Modern Privileged Access Management (PAM) has repositioned vaulting as an active control system managing the entire credential lifecycle: issuance, duration, rotation, and retirement. As the article states, "The vault is the single source of trust for every credential in the environment."

The shift represents a philosophical change: "That single change, removing humans from the business of memorizing and typing privileged passwords, closes off a huge number of attack paths."

Traditional environments suffer from credential sprawl—hardcoded passwords, shared admin accounts, and unchanged credentials that persist across years. Modern vaulting eliminates these risks through centralized management and automatic rotation.

The evolution extends beyond IT administration into engineering environments. CI/CD pipelines traditionally relied on long-lived credentials embedded in configuration files. Modern solutions replace these with ephemeral, just-in-time access: "A long-lived, broadly scoped credential sitting in a pipeline is basically a skeleton key that never gets thrown away."

This approach enables rapid deployment while maintaining security through temporary, scope-limited credentials that automatically expire.

Modern vaulting provides comprehensive inventory and audit capabilities. Organizations gain centralized visibility across all privileged credentials—human and machine-based—streamlining compliance reporting and incident response.

(Author: Jeff Carpenter, Published: August 2026)

66fd63fbb0aa.text:
Suisan City in California is continuing to grapple with an ongoing cyber-incident, amid a spate of cyber-attacks targeting local authorities in the US.

The City government declared a state of emergency after its IT network was infected by "malicious software" at roughly 5:45 am on August 7. This declaration enables the City to gain access to emergency resources and support at state and federal level.

The attack has affected 911 call routing, police and fire dispatch, records and City services.

Additionally, the authority shut down its entire IT network in an effort to contain the threat and preserve evidence for a federal investigation. This means online services and internal operations remain temporarily unavailable, while City Hall remains closed, impacting in-person meetings across all departments including planning, housing and water.

In an update published on its website on August 10, Suisan City assured its residents that its police and fire services are able to continue to respond to emergency 911 calls, which are being routed through the Solano County dispatch center.

The City also stated that there is no "imminent" threat to the public from the incident.

Suisan city is located in Northern California and has a population of approximately 30,000.

There are indications that the incident impacting Suisan City is ransomware-related, although there has been no official confirmation of the source of the attack or the perpetrators.

In a statement posted on her LinkedIn page late on August 10, Suisan City Council Member Princess Washington revealed that an emergency meeting would be taking place on August 11 regarding the continuing effects of the cybersecurity incident.

In addition, she said that the Council will consider convening a closed session to "receive information and provide direction regarding threats to public services and facilities, cybersecurity matters and anticipated litigation."

California-based news website SFGATE has reported that the emergency meeting would consider the City's response to demands from a "person or persons" behind the malware attack.

Several other US local authorities have been hit by cyber-attacks in recent weeks. On August 5, 2026, the City of Coweta in Oklahoma revealed it had experienced a "system-wide ransomware attack." On August 6, 2026, Washburn County in Wisconsin issued a press release confirming it is currently responding to a cyber incident.

Numerous US cities and local authorities have been targeted by ransomware in recent years. In August 2025, officials from the City of St. Paul, Minnesota, confirmed that the Interlock ransomware group has published employee data online after refusing the attackers' payment demands. In 2024, Clay County in Indiana and Jackson County in Missouri reported being hit by ransomware attacks that had impacted critical government services.

Commenting on the recent incidents, Seemant Sehgal, Founder & CEO, BreachLock, observed: "Municipal IT and security teams operate under resource constraints that most enterprise security organizations would find difficult to imagine." He added that "Suisun City, Coweta, Washburn County – these are not outliers, they are a pattern."

(Author: James Coker, Published: 11 August 2026)

ce16aaea4e0c.text:
Security researchers created a fake cryptocurrency startup called Ballena Azul and conducted a hiring operation to identify North Korean operatives seeking remote IT work positions. The team—comprising Mauro Eldritch of BCA LTD, Heiner García of NorthScan, and ANY.RUN—successfully hired three suspected operatives and monitored their activities on isolated virtual machines.

The first candidate claimed residency in Pasadena, Texas but provided a California driver's license and New York bank account. Researchers discovered his submitted image contained metadata indicating Google Gemini processing and SynthID watermarking. The second supplied a Texas license with a valid Social Security number and Kansas City bank account. The third submitted a New York license belonging to someone else, along with a genuine iPhone photograph with GPS coordinates removed.

Upon onboarding, all three operatives conducted reconnaissance by running system profiling commands (dxdiag, systeminfo, wmic). One installed Chrome Remote Desktop, syncing personal Google credentials and granting access to browsing history and saved passwords. He also logged into GitHub on the work machine.

The researchers observed infrastructure hosted on Vultr and Gorilla Servers, with "AstrillVPN exit nodes running throughout." Operatives used 2fa.cn for two-factor authentication relay and browser extensions including AIApply, Final Round AI, and Simplify Copilot.

A separate April case involved two U.S. facilitators sentenced for placing North Korean workers at over 100 American companies using 80+ stolen identities, generating more than $5 million for North Korea.

Researchers recommend periodic identity verification, in-person checks for remote workers, recruiter training, and blocking AstrillVPN access. A July 31 joint government advisory notes red flags including single accounts accessed from multiple addresses and profiles appearing machine-translated.

(Author: Swati Khandelwal, Published: August 11, 2026)

5080bcc2b6d7.text:
OpenAI is launching GPT‑5.6‑Cyber, its newest large language model purpose-trained for cybersecurity tasks, based on its latest frontier AI model, GPT‑5.6 Sol.

The AI company also restructured its Daybreak program to introduce two new tiers: Daybreak Blue for defensive cyber tasks and Daybreak Red for advanced defensive tasks as well as offensive cyber operations.

Members of Daybreak Blue receive access to frontier general-purpose models, including GPT‑5.6 Sol, with "system-level safeguards" to perform authorized defensive security work. This encompasses vulnerability discovery, secure code review, malware analysis, incident response and patch validation.

Daybreak Red members gain access to purpose-trained cybersecurity models like GPT‑5.5‑Cyber and GPT‑5.6‑Cyber for advanced tasks such as vulnerability research, exploit validation and security testing.

OpenAI stated that GPT‑5.6 Sol "delivers state-of-the-art performance on cybersecurity tasks" but deployed system-level safeguards to "screen cybersecurity-related requests to prevent misuse." While general users have these guardrails enabled, Daybreak Blue access removes them. GPT‑5.6 Sol will still refuse certain "highly dual-use cybersecurity prompts."

GPT‑5.6‑Cyber, exclusively available through Daybreak Red, reduces refusals and improves performance on sensitive security tasks. The model completed 95% of a set of sensitive requests involving exploit-chain development, authentication bypass, and privilege escalation. By comparison, general-access GPT‑5.6 Sol completed just 1.5% of the same tasks, and GPT‑5.5‑Cyber completed 57.3%.

OpenAI benchmarked GPT‑5.6‑Cyber against other models on cybersecurity-specific metrics and tasks including zero-day vulnerability discovery evaluation and vulnerability reporting. The new model outperformed all other OpenAI offerings on every assessment.

The company disclosed that GPT‑5.6‑Cyber identified CVE-2026-15903, a high-severity vulnerability in Chrome's V8 JavaScript engine. Researchers validated findings and reported them to Google through coordinated vulnerability disclosure, resulting in a fix.

Alex Goller, principal solution architect for EMEA at Illumio, described the two-tier system introduction as "a good first step for OpenAI to mitigate two issues." He noted that Daybreak Red restricts models from causing harm and limits exposure to model capabilities, while Daybreak Blue addresses gaps that prevented frontier model use during incidents.

However, Goller emphasized that AI model guardrails should not serve as the primary control mechanism for defense. He advocated for zero trust principles, stating: "These are agents operating inside your environment and the controls that matter follow zero trust principles." He stressed the importance of visibility into agent activities, segmentation capabilities, and sandboxing enforcement within infrastructure rather than relying on model-level controls.

(Author: Kevin Poireault, Published: 11 August 2026)

13b0b6470075.text:
The post highlights research titled "Black Box Warfare: Human Judgment and Military Decision-Making in the Age of AI."

According to the study abstract, researchers deployed a replica of an AI decision-support system used in military targeting and tested it with 2,015 Israeli military personnel. The findings challenge common assumptions about automation bias.

Key discoveries include:
- Personnel demonstrated "strong evidence of algorithmic aversion, especially in scenarios involving high collateral damage" rather than blindly following AI recommendations
- Adding "explainable AI" features reduced this aversion and improved decision evaluation
- Trust in military AI varies based on individual factors, operational stakes, and interface design
- Human agency remains critical in high-stakes military decisions

The research reveals that transparency about AI inputs increased human confidence in algorithmic recommendations, though one commenter noted tension between these laboratory findings and real-world deployment data showing operators approving AI suggestions "in as little as 20 seconds."

Commenters raised concerns about AI's integration throughout information supply chains and the difficulty of verifying data quality when sources become obscured.

(Published: August 11, 2026, blog post by Bruce Schneier)

c568b6a6bcd1.text:
A Chrome extension called "AI Sidebar with DeepSeek, ChatGPT, Claude and more" has returned to Google's Chrome Web Store after being removed in January 2026. Originally flagged by OX Security in December 2025, the extension was caught scraping ChatGPT and DeepSeek conversations and sending data to external domains. Before removal, it achieved over 300,000 installs with a 4.6-star rating.

Netskope Threat Labs discovered that as of August 2026, the extension resumed distribution through Google's content delivery network with malicious payloads. Version 1.7.2.0 (released July 20-31) appeared clean, likely to establish update credibility. Version 1.7.3.0, released two weeks later, contained "a surgical 21-line addition to a single script file" implementing an affiliate monetization scheme.

The scheme triggers on update events and uninstall actions. When Chrome reports an update, a service worker opens an affiliate link through a URL shortener directing to an AI video-generation platform. Developers' code comments specified this would generate fresh commissions per release rather than one-time payments.

Attribution points to Extchange.com, listed as developer and data controller, with domain registration in February 2024. The Chrome Web Store falsely lists "DeepSeek AI" as developer.

Netskope classified version 1.7.3.0 as Trojan.GenericFCA.Script.37952 and detected it arriving at enterprise endpoints via Google's CDN. The firm reported findings to the Chrome Web Store and recommends organizations remove the extension, warning that "the same channel could just as easily carry a more damaging payload next time."

(Author: Eduard Kovacs, Published: August 11, 2026, 7:15 AM ET)

91bb8fcd9b4a.text:
Windows Plug and Play can be abused to fetch signed vendor software for an emulated USB device and execute privileged installation components that researchers chained to SYSTEM access on a fully updated Windows 11 machine.

The same PnP path can be triggered over Remote Desktop without physical hardware when supported Plug and Play or low-level USB redirection is enabled; Microsoft says that redirection is not allowed by default.

Security researchers Alejandro Hernando and Borja Martinez described the technique in "Plug And Pwn: Weaponizing Windows PnP Auto-Install," research prepared for DEF CON 34.

They built tooling to emulate arbitrary USB devices and said that, under the required conditions, an unprivileged user can turn the PnP installation path into SYSTEM code execution. Microsoft's own driver documentation describes the underlying selection step: Windows receives hardware and compatible IDs for a device and uses them to find a matching driver package.

According to the researchers, the physical chain starts by emulating a Sierra Wireless device so Windows installs SwiService.exe, a SYSTEM service exposing a SetDNS primitive. They use it to redirect DNS, then emulate a Sony FeliCa reader whose co-installer retrieves configuration files over plaintext HTTP and derives local filenames from URL paths.

The researchers say a path-traversal flaw lets them place a DLL in System32; reconnecting the Sierra device then loads the planted DLL and yields SYSTEM.

The remote variant replaces the physical device with synthetic USB traffic over RDP. The researchers' Python client forges a USB identity and presents a phantom Intel RealSense device, causing Windows to follow the redirected device-installation path. They say the resulting RealSense software can be abused through a CRYPTBASE.dll search-order hijack from a user-writable installation directory, giving the authenticated low-privilege user SYSTEM code execution.

The remote path is configuration-dependent, not a default Windows exposure. Microsoft says Remote Desktop Services does not allow supported Plug and Play and RemoteFX USB redirection by default. Administrators that do not need the feature can leave it disabled. Microsoft also provides device-installation restrictions that can allow or block devices by hardware or compatible ID, device-instance ID, and setup class.

The research demonstrates abuse of a legitimate privileged installation path combined with weaknesses in signed third-party packages. The vendor-specific Sierra, Sony, and Intel exploit mechanics remain researcher findings and should stay attributed unless matching vendor material independently confirms them.

(Author: Swati Khandelwal, Published: August 11, 2026)

8b75efd46bab.text:
Ceva Logistics, a subsidiary of French shipping giant CMA CGM Group (the world's third-largest shipper), experienced a significant data breach affecting its European contract logistics operations. The company provides warehousing, fulfillment, manufacturing support, and aftermarket services to numerous clients.

Ceva notified affected customers on August 1, with eight warehouses impacted. According to a company statement, "No other Ceva systems globally were affected, and all other operations continue without incident."

The cyber-attack occurred between July 29 and August 1. Video game developer Valve disclosed that attackers obtained "names, email and home addresses, phone numbers and order details" from its European shipping records retained by Ceva for up to 90 days post-delivery.

Multiple high-profile organizations experienced fallout, including Dutch retailer Bol, department store De Bijenkorf, football club Ajax, and banking institution ING. Bol reported extended restoration timelines at Ceva's Veerweg facility, potentially impacting service levels.

Cybersecurity experts highlighted logistics companies' vulnerability. Joseph Perry from Arcova noted that "shipping information is highly contextual" and enables convincing phishing attempts. Anna Collard (KnowBe4 CISO advisory) characterized it as a "textbook supply chain breach" and warned customers anticipate delivery-themed phishing lures in coming weeks.

This incident mirrors CMA CGM's 2020 ransomware attack, which temporarily disabled shipping operations.

(Author: Phil Muncaster, Published: August 11, 2026)

Cloud Compliance Solutions for Enterprises: The Automation Checklist

Author: Jake Kramber
Published: August 11, 2026

Enterprise teams managing cloud environments across multiple providers and regions face significant challenges with manual compliance tracking. Spreadsheets become outdated rapidly, audit evidence collection consumes weeks of engineering time, and each new framework adds coordination complexity across departments using disparate tools.

Why Manual Processes Fail at Scale
Manual cloud compliance breaks down due to three factors: legacy systems predating current regulations, siloed teams tracking requirements independently, and frameworks updating faster than manual processes can accommodate. Most enterprises still depend on spreadsheet-based tracking distributed across finance, IT, HR, and security teams, each maintaining separate versions and audit cadences. When auditors request evidence, teams must reconcile conflicting records, often discovering gaps only during review. This fragmentation drives organizations to seek ways to "simplify multi-cloud compliance reporting," and compliance automation directly addresses this issue.

What Cloud Compliance Automation Does
Cloud compliance automation uses software to continuously collect evidence, monitor control effectiveness, orchestrate remediation workflows, generate audit-ready documentation, and integrate across cloud services without manual intervention. The five core mechanics include: Automated evidence collection pulls configuration snapshots and audit logs from cloud APIs continuously; Real-time monitoring detects control deviations immediately rather than waiting for scheduled reviews; Workflow orchestration routes findings to appropriate teams with context, triggering automatic remediation when conditions are met; Audit-ready documentation assembles evidence into structured reports aligned to specific frameworks; Cross-system integration connects compliance data across identity providers, cloud platforms, and CI/CD pipelines. Together, these mechanics reduce mean time to resolution for compliance gaps from days or weeks to hours.

Core Domains for Enterprise Solutions
A comprehensive compliance solution must cover twelve domains: Governance and risk ownership; Asset inventory and data classification; Identity and access management; Secure configuration; Network segmentation; Data protection; Logging and monitoring; Vulnerability and patch management; DevSecOps and change management; Backup and recovery; Incident response; Third-party risk.

Framework Coverage
Enterprise buyers typically need coverage across multiple frameworks. NIST SP 800-53 provides the most comprehensive federal control catalog. ISO/IEC 27001 serves as the global information security management standard. SOC 2 compliance focuses on trust service criteria for SaaS providers. PCI DSS applies to organizations handling cardholder data. HIPAA governs protected health information in the United States. GDPR sets data protection requirements for EU residents' personal data. The practical approach involves defining one internal control set and mapping it to each applicable framework. When a single control satisfies requirements across multiple frameworks, evidence is collected once and presented multiple ways.

Top Cloud Compliance Solutions for 2026
Orca Security uses SideScanning technology to read cloud workload data out-of-band without deploying agents, providing full-stack context across workloads, identities, and data stores. Wiz is a unified CNAPP providing compliance capabilities across 100+ frameworks, with a Security Graph correlating findings with data sensitivity and identity exposure. Check Point CloudGuard pairs security and compliance in a single policy engine, offering 1,000+ best-practice recommendations and automating the full compliance lifecycle. Microsoft Defender for Cloud suits Microsoft-centric and hybrid environments, syncing with NIS2, NIST CSF, GDPR, FedRAMP, HIPAA, and the EU AI Act. Palo Alto Networks Cortex Cloud provides compliance monitoring across 20+ standards with broad third-party integrations for multi-cloud and SaaS environments. Qualys Cloud Platform offers end-to-end compliance capabilities including policy audits, file integrity monitoring, and asset management with granular, asset-level evidence.

Key Evaluation Criteria
When comparing platforms, prioritize: Comprehensive framework coverage with mappings for current regulations and capacity to absorb new frameworks; Multi-cloud and hybrid visibility providing a single pane of glass across AWS, Azure, GCP, and on-premises infrastructure; Context-aware risk prioritization correlating findings with identity exposure, network reachability, and data sensitivity rather than flat severity scores; Developer workflow integration embedding compliance checks into CI/CD pipelines and ticketing systems. A critical differentiator is context-aware prioritization. A platform flagging 500 misconfigurations with identical severity ratings creates noise, while one identifying which violations expose sensitive data on publicly reachable workloads with excessive permissions enables effective action prioritization.

Continuous Compliance vs. Point-in-Time Audits
Point-in-time audits prove controls worked during a specific review window but cannot demonstrate continuous effectiveness. Cloud environments change constantly as teams deploy resources, modify access policies, and update configurations. Configuration drift occurs between audit cycles and remains invisible until the next review. Continuous compliance monitoring flags these deviations in real time, giving teams opportunity to remediate before auditors or incidents surface them.

How Orca Security Automates Cloud Compliance
Orca Security connects all compliance domains through SideScanning technology that reads cloud workload data without deploying agents. Telemetry feeds into the Unified Data Model, correlating findings across workloads, identities, data stores, and network paths. The platform maps this dataset against 180+ out-of-the-box compliance frameworks, including NIST SP 800-53, CIS Benchmarks, ISO 27001, PCI-DSS, and FedRAMP/StateRAMP. Instead of managing separate tools for CSPM and CIEM, teams get posture and entitlement data in one dashboard mapped to required frameworks. Orca's Agentic AI can generate remediation steps and execute them automatically where configured, reducing detection-to-resolution time. Customers report audit preparation shifting from multi-week scrambles to standing background processes.

Frequently Asked Questions covered difference between cloud compliance and cloud security, how automation tools differ from on-premises systems, multi-cloud/hybrid handling, CSPM vs dedicated compliance platforms, and when to start evaluating compliance automation platforms (one to two quarters before the next audit cycle).

271e41a3594d.text:
Author: Swati Khandelwal
Published: August 11, 2026

A malicious tool server connected to an AI coding assistant can quietly walk off with SSH keys, environment secrets, source code, and customer data without ever sending one obviously harmful instruction.

The trick can work even after a blunt version of the same theft is refused: split the request into fragments that each look routine, place them in channels the assistant already uses, and let the agent stitch them together and send the data back.

The attack targets coding tools that connect to outside servers over the Model Context Protocol (MCP), the open standard that lets AI assistants call external tools.

A malicious MCP server can put one fragment in a tool description and another in a tool result; some setups also support server-initiated sampling. MCP does preserve structured tool and result boundaries. But ASSET Research Group's tests show agents can still combine instructions across them in the same working context, so no single fragment has to contain the whole malicious request.

The group calls the technique GhostSplice. Its disclosure describes controlled tests in isolated projects seeded with fake credentials, not a reported real-world intrusion, and says any CVE identifiers will follow coordinated disclosure; The Hacker News found none listed as of August 10, 2026.

The sharpest result is not a simple model ranking. The same model can refuse in one coding client and exfiltrate in another, depending on the safety controls around it.

The attack also has a built-in limit. It is not a way to break into an arbitrary agent from the outside: it assumes the developer has already connected the attacker's MCP server, and that the agent can already read the files being taken.

In the group's reference implementation, a server advertises a harmless-looking tool called integrity_checker with four bland fields, alpha through delta, and no sensitive filenames. A later project-scan result supplies the missing mapping: fill those fields with the contents of .ssh/id_rsa, proprietary source, customers.csv, and .env for "server-side hash verification."

Read separately, neither piece contains the full theft. Read together, they tell the agent to collect sensitive local files and pass their contents to the attacker's tool. The public repository also includes a canonical three-channel variant that separates the project inventory, the file-to-field mapping, and the collection tool across three interactions.

Split into two pieces, average compliance rose from 42% to 82% across eleven API-tested models, the disclosure reports. Its broader results table contains 15 model rows. GPT-4o, Gemini 2.0 Flash, and Llama 3.3 70B went from 0% in the one-piece test to 100% when split in two. Claude Haiku 4.5 stayed at 0% in the API tests but reached 100% in a three-piece Cursor test. GPT-5.4 was reported at 90% in Cursor and 100% through Codex CLI, while the repository says it dropped to 0% behind Claude Code.

The headline scores need care. Claude Sonnet 4.6 and Opus 4.6 are listed at 0% across the published table, but ASSET says Sonnet still sent proprietary source containing a live hardcoded key in one test while redacting the more obvious secrets. Those numbers are the researchers' own results and should not be read as "unaffected," or as general compliance rates: each reflects the specific setup tested.

The Hacker News has reached out to the ASSET Research Group for further detail on its testing and will update this story with any response.

The simplest lure was also the hardest to second-guess. Elaborate compliance or governance stories gave the model something false to question; a plain fill-in-the-blanks template did not. To the model, the group writes, the task is just to "fill in the form the tool asked me to fill in."

The defense lands on the client. The MCP specification says clients should keep a human able to deny tool invocations and must treat annotations from untrusted servers as untrusted. OpenAI's current guidance likewise warns that unsafe MCP servers increase prompt-injection risk and tells organizations to vet custom and third-party integrations.

ASSET's prescription is tighter still: treat server output as data, not instructions, and do not let values from one tool's output flow unchecked into another tool's arguments.

GhostSplice follows Ghostcommit, a June disclosure from the same lab that hid an instruction inside a PNG referenced by a project convention file, then let a coding agent encode .env secrets into source as integers. The mechanics differ, but both point at the same weak spot: the safety boundary around the model can matter as much as the model itself.

9bd04859d964.text:
Mines, Minds, and Machines: The Journey of AI

The fourth industrial revolution traces a supply chain from mineral extraction through chip production to AI model development and embodied robotics. This progression has become a theater of geopolitical competition, with state-sponsored and criminal actors targeting each link.

The Mines
Rare earth elements and critical minerals like lithium, cobalt, and graphite form the foundation of advanced technology. China controls over 90% of rare earth element processing globally, providing significant leverage. In 2025, Beijing threatened to suspend rare earth exports to pressure Washington on semiconductor technology restrictions. Competition for minerals is expanding into challenging territories: deep ocean mining at 6,000 meters, Arctic regions losing 70% of ice since the 1980s, Greenland's critical raw materials, and Antarctica where mining remains prohibited "only until 2048." Cyber operations accompany this competition, with state-sponsored groups targeting Canadian miners and seabed mining regulators, while sophisticated intrusions plague Indonesia's nickel sector.

The Minds
The AI stack comprises five layers: energy, chips, infrastructure (data centers), models, and applications. America leads in chip design and model development, while China excels at energy production. Taiwan's TSMC dominates semiconductor fabrication, making it a systematic reconnaissance target for Chinese state-sponsored groups like RedJuliett, which targeted "85 Taiwanese organizations in a single campaign." Data centers represent the most contested layer - "the new refineries, converting gigawatts and chips into intelligence." Nations court these facilities with land and power deals, with plans emerging for orbital and lunar compute infrastructure.

The Machines
Humanoid robotics deployment is accelerating commercially. BMW reports the Figure 02 robot assisted producing 30,000+ vehicles; Unitree's R1 humanoid retails around $5,500; projections suggest "three billion humanoid robots will be in operation by 2060." China filed significantly more humanoid patents (5,688) than the US (1,483) between 2020-2025. Security vulnerabilities pose serious risks. Researchers discovered "undocumented backdoors" in Unitree models, including weak encryption enabling fleet-wide compromise through wireless propagation. These vulnerabilities enable surveillance, network infiltration, and remote hijacking.

The Future
The convergence of advancing robotics, demographic decline, and AI capabilities creates conditions for massive humanoid robot adoption. Cyber operations will intensify along every supply chain link. Cost pressures may compromise security implementation, potentially triggering corporate crises that spawn dedicated robot-security industries. Organizations must understand their exposure across the entire AI development chain: "from ore to algorithm to actuator."

Type: webapps

Vulnerability Overview
A Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) vulnerability exists in Apache Gravitino versions 1.0.0 through 1.2.1. The fetchFileFromUri() method in JobManager.java processes URIs from job template fields without proper destination validation.

Affected Components
The vulnerability impacts these job template fields: executable, scripts, jars, files, archives. The system accepts HTTP, HTTPS, and FTP schemes, downloading remote content via FileUtils.copyURLToFile() to the server's staging directory.

Attack Capabilities
An authenticated attacker can: register job templates pointing to internal or metadata URLs; trigger job execution to force server-side URL fetching; access downloaded content from the staging directory (if readable); conduct blind SSRF detection using out-of-band callbacks.

Valid Gravitino user credentials; job template privilege access; Python 3.8+ with requests library.

Example Targets
The exploit demonstrates attacks against internal configuration endpoints (http://127.0.0.1:8090/configs), cloud metadata services (AWS IMDSv1: http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/), and custom OOB callback servers for blind detection.

Vulnerability Response in the AI-Discovery Era

Published: August 11, 2026
Author: Ivan Evsyukov

Frontier AI models can now find vulnerabilities at a scale and speed humans can't match, with Mythos as the current high-water mark. That includes flaws with no CVE attached, in code that has been reviewed for decades. Access to the strongest models is restricted today, but the capability is spreading, and attackers get it too.

Here is the practical problem: finding vulnerabilities got fast and cheap. Triaging them, fixing them, and containing what gets exploited did not. If your program was already behind on its backlog, this makes it worse.

Four Shifts in the Ground Rules
1. There are more vulnerabilities than established institutions can process. CVE creation doesn't keep up with what AI can find, so some real findings will never have a CVE at all. Regardless of whether something has a CVE, if it represents a real business risk, your team owns doing something about it.
2. Exploits get faster and cheaper for attackers. The time from a vulnerability being known to it being exploited has collapsed. Mandiant's latest M-Trends report estimates "the average time-to-exploit at negative seven days." This means exploitation now begins before patches exist.
3. Risk acceptance gets harder to justify. There is an industry narrative that AI makes defense faster and cheaper, so leaving things unfixed looks less like a resource problem and more like a decision.
4. Your whole attack surface is more exposed. Software, configuration, and identity weaknesses can all be discovered and probed at machine speed.

How to Create a Program for the New Landscape: A Four-Part Plan
1. Scan and Discover: Everything found should end up in one manageable location. Scanning must pull in vulnerability data beyond the CVE catalog, including AI-discovered flaws, and feed them into the same triage and remediation process as everything else.
2. Prioritize: Three signals matter most - In-use (is the vulnerable package actually loaded and running), Exploitability (can it be reached), and Impact (real negative business impact if breached). Focus the team on the short list this analysis produces and trust the triage tooling.
3. Remediate: Fix at root (patch the base image once), automate ownership and assignment, use autoremediation where possible, block pre-production via admission controllers, and use cloud/network/identity configuration changes as remediation levers when patches lag.
4. Plan for Vulnerabilities Being Exploited: Watch workloads for indicators of compromise, measure detection/response speed and find bottlenecks, build real containment playbooks with defined escalation paths, and set up business notification processes before an incident.

Conclusion
None of this is novel - it's coverage, triage, an industrial fix pipeline, and a real plan for things that get through. What's changed is that AI has raised stakes on both ends: attackers find more, faster, but defenders have the same tools available and must learn to leverage them effectively. Discovery scaled. Now response must match.

426b0759e107.text:
From Open Lures to Cloaked Gates: How a macOS ClickFix Campaign Learned to Hide

Published: August 5, 2026
Authors: Microsoft Security Research and Srinivasan Govindarajan

Microsoft Threat Intelligence observed a macOS ClickFix campaign distributing infostealers through look-alike domains. The campaign evolved from openly serving malicious commands to employing server-side browser fingerprinting that conceals payloads from automated tools while targeting genuine macOS users.

How ClickFix Works
ClickFix is a social-engineering technique where attackers convince users to execute Terminal commands instead of downloading traditional applications. The lure typically mimics verification steps, software updates, or CAPTCHAs, with commands disguised as necessary for completion. This approach circumvents normal macOS security checks including quarantine handling, code-signing evaluation, and notarization.

Campaign Evolution
The infrastructure initially served ClickFix lures directly with malicious commands visible in page HTML. The same domains now employ lightweight JavaScript profiling (~2.5 KB) before revealing content. Simple crawlers receive empty pages; qualified macOS browsers receive the malicious lure.

Fingerprinting Gate Mechanics
The gate collects visitor data across six browser objects: navigator attributes (platform, user agent, language), display values (screen size, color depth, window dimensions), WebGL-derived GPU signals distinguishing real hardware from virtualized environments, environmental checks (timezone, touch support, iframe detection), and anti-analysis probes detecting developer tools and automation frameworks. Data submits server-side with a "mode: php" tag for evaluation. Non-qualifying requests receive benign decoys or blank pages.

Infection Chain
Qualified visitors see a GitHub-themed fake download page. Running the provided Terminal command retrieves remote scripts ultimately delivering Atomic Stealer (AMOS), which harvests credentials, browser data, cryptocurrency wallet information, and sensitive files for exfiltration.

Campaign Indicators
Over 250 domains identified following patterns like "file[word][word]" (filecopperbasket, filevelvettractor) and variations (applefilevault, cloudsendhub). The naming pattern serves as a hunting pivot alongside infrastructure behavior analysis.

Mitigation Strategies
Organizations should educate users that legitimate downloads never require Terminal commands, monitor shell sessions spawning curl/base64/osascript, detect native-tool abuse sequences, inspect outbound downloads, protect credential stores, and block shared backend infrastructure rather than individual disposable domains. macOS 26.4+ displays warnings when users attempt pasting potentially malicious commands into Terminal.

Detection Coverage
Microsoft Defender XDR provides coverage across execution, credential access, and data exfiltration tactics with specific behavioral detection rules for suspicious AMOS execution, keychain copying, and information theft activities.

New Microsoft Defender 'ShieldBreak' Zero-Day Exploit

Author: Sergiu Gatlan
Published: August 12, 2026

A security researcher known as Nightmare Eclipse has released a zero-day exploit called "ShieldBreak" targeting Microsoft Defender after the August 2026 Patch Tuesday updates. The vulnerability enables attackers to gain SYSTEM-level privileges on fully patched Windows 10, Windows 11, and Windows Server systems.

Key Details
Technical Distinction: Unlike the RoguePlanet vulnerability it bypasses, ShieldBreak operates differently. According to cybersecurity expert Kevin Beaumont, "RoguePlanet was a filesystem race condition vuln" whereas "ShieldBreak user-mode callback hook to change file contents during a Defender cloud-hydration scan via cfapi."

Exploit Requirements: Microsoft Defender must be enabled for the exploit to succeed, as confirmed by vulnerability analyst Will Dormann.

Success Rate: Nightmare Eclipse claims the proof-of-concept achieves a 100% success rate on Windows 11 25h2 and Windows Server 2025.

Broader Context
This disclosure is part of an escalating dispute between Nightmare Eclipse and Microsoft. Since April 2026, the researcher has publicly released nine zero-day exploits targeting Windows components and Defender, with only some receiving patches. Microsoft has responded with "warnings of legal action" against those engaging in "malicious activity causing real harm."

Microsoft's Statement: The company stated it "is aware of the reported vulnerability and is actively investigating" the claims, reaffirming commitment to coordinated vulnerability disclosure practices.

Microsoft Patches 400+ Vulnerabilities in August 2026 Patch Tuesday

Author: Zeljka Zorz, Editor-in-Chief, Help Net Security
Date: August 12, 2026

Microsoft released fixes for over 400 vulnerabilities in its August 2026 Patch Tuesday, including one zero-day actively being exploited (CVE-2026-68820) and three previously disclosed flaws.

Critical Vulnerabilities
CVE-2026-68820 is a use-after-free flaw in Windows Ancillary Function Driver for WinSock allowing low-privileged users to escalate to SYSTEM level. Check Point researchers revealed North Korean attackers exploited this in Operation Dream Job campaigns, deploying kernel-mode rootkits.

CVE-2026-62832 affects Windows User Profile Service, permitting authenticated attackers admin access through a specially crafted application. Researcher Nightmare-Eclipse released proof-of-concept code ("LegacyHive") enabling standard users to access administrator registry data.

CVE-2026-72971 impacts Windows Container Isolation FS Filter Driver, affecting only ARM64-based Windows 11 systems.

CVE-2026-62815 is a critical Microsoft QUIC vulnerability allowing unauthenticated remote code execution via specially crafted network packets.

CVE-2026-62878 is a stack-based buffer overflow in Windows DNS enabling remote code execution by unauthenticated attackers.

Additional Concerns
Security researcher Nightmare Eclipse released "ShieldBreak," reportedly bypassing July's Microsoft Defender vulnerability patch (CVE-2026-50656). This exploit affects Windows 11, 10, and Server 2025, using user-mode callback hooks to manipulate files during cloud-hydration scans.

Expert Guidance
Industry experts advise organizations to triage patches carefully, prioritizing actively exploited vulnerabilities and internet-facing systems while avoiding rushed rollouts that could destabilize environments.

1dc2f541e3d3.text:
Attackers Exploit VMware vCenter Vulnerability to Gain Persistent Remote Access

Author: Ravie Lakshmanan
Published: Aug 12, 2026

Threat actors have begun actively exploiting a recently patched critical security flaw in Broadcom VMware vCenter, according to findings from QUIRSO.

The vulnerability, CVE-2026-59310 (CVSS score: 9.8), is a directory-traversal flaw in VMware vCenter server that allows actors with network access to execute arbitrary code. Broadcom released patches last month.

QUIRSO discovered this activity during an incident response engagement. The attack sequence showed path traversal consistent with the vulnerability, followed by deployment of a malicious cron job establishing persistence via reverse_ssh - an open-source tool enabling SSH connections to attacker infrastructure.

As many as 361 unique victim IP addresses across 47 countries were identified, with compromised systems first contacting attacker domains on August 3 - five days after public disclosure. "The strong correlation between the time of disclosure and exploitation suggests the disclosure as the initial starting point for the campaign," QUIRSO stated.

The majority of affected systems were located in Germany, the U.S., Turkey, Iran, and France. While the attacker's identity remains unclear, activity patterns suggest an advanced persistent threat actor.

VMware appliances have previously targeted Chinese threat actors like UNC5174, who weaponized security flaws in VMware Tools and vCenter for espionage campaigns.

QUIRSO noted that reverse_ssh presence alone doesn't indicate malice, but combined with "unauthorized installation, unexpected outbound connections or execution on a vulnerable vCenter appliance," it represents a high-priority investigation indicator.

Separately, Defused Cyber reported increased scanning against VMware vCenter targeting CVE-2026-59309 (CVSS score: 9.8), suggesting potential exploitation attempts.

dde04165b928.text:
Fresh Windows Zero-Day Exploited in North Korean Cyberattacks

Author: Ionut Arghire
Published: August 12, 2026 (4:45 AM ET)

North Korean hackers have been exploiting a newly patched Windows zero-day vulnerability to take over victims' systems, Check Point reports.

Attributed to the infamous Lazarus Group APT, the attacks represent a continuation of the long-running Operation Dream Job campaign targeting job seekers with fake work opportunities at well-known companies. North Korean hackers have been mounting fake job attack variations regularly.

Active since early 2026, the new campaign has been targeting the defense sector across multiple countries, mainly aerospace and aviation organizations in Europe and India, Check Point says.

Posing as recruiters, the attackers have contacted potential victims through popular professional platforms or direct messaging applications and convinced them to download a malicious payload.

As part of one infection chain, an archive containing a PDF viewer, a malicious DLL, and an encrypted payload posing as a PDF file is served to the victim, and DLL sideloading is used to execute the Mistpen malware downloader in memory while a decoy job description is shown on the screen.

The infection chain continues with reconnaissance, persistence, and the exploitation of a previously unknown vulnerability in Windows' Ancillary Function Driver for WinSock (afd.sys), followed by the deployment of ForestTiger, a known Lazarus backdoor.

The afd.sys zero-day, now tracked as CVE-2026-68820, is a use-after-free issue that allows attackers to trigger a race condition and gain System privileges.

On August 11, Microsoft fixed the vulnerability as part of its Patch Tuesday updates, and the US cybersecurity agency CISA added it to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog, urging federal agencies to patch it within the next two weeks.

According to Check Point, a second infection chain directs users to the trojanized PDF viewer SecurityPDF, which searches for a hidden marker in any PDF file opened on the system to execute the Troy backdoor directly in memory.

Troy is a new DLL implant that supports 17 operator commands, including file enumeration/download/upload, data exfiltration, shell access, process termination, and DLL injection.

The command-and-control (C&C) infrastructure observed in these attacks includes compromised Roundcube webmail deployments and CMS platforms, many vulnerable to CVE-2025-49113, a remote code execution (RCE) flaw that has been exploited since June 2025.

"These servers are infected with RelayShell, a previously undocumented PHP webshell that functions less like a conventional backdoor and more as a communication relay between infected endpoints and the operator, exchanging commands and responses through simple text files," Check Point says.

The cybersecurity firm says that defense, aerospace, and aviation organizations in France, Germany, Brazil, and India have been targeted in the fresh campaign.

"Given the combination of a zero-day vulnerability that now has a patch, a new modular backdoor, and web-based infrastructure designed to resemble legitimate traffic, security teams in these sectors should prioritize the August Patch Tuesday update, review the indicators of compromise, and apply the same level of scrutiny to unsolicited recruiting outreach that they would apply to any unverified download request," Check Point notes.

6d749ed093f7.text: Enterprise software company Ivanti on Tuesday announced patches for four vulnerabilities in Endpoint Manager (EPM) and Neurons for MDM. The EPM update addresses three high-severity bugs, including two that could be exploited by remote, unauthenticated attackers. Tracked as CVE-2026-18129, the first is described as a cleartext transmission of sensitive information issue that can be exploited by an attacker in a man-in-the-middle (MitM) position to leak credentials for external SQL connections. The second, CVE-2026-18125, is an out-of-bounds read flaw in the EPM agent that can be triggered to crash an agent service. Both security defects were resolved in EPM version 2024 SU7, which also patches CVE-2026-18127, a high-severity input validation weakness that allows remote attackers to control filenames. An authenticated threat actor could exploit the flaw to gain full write control over an S3 bucket configured for session recording storage. "We are not aware of any customers being exploited by these vulnerabilities at the time of disclosure," Ivanti stated. Ivanti Neurons for MDM received fixes for a single medium-severity command-injection vulnerability that could be exploited remotely to disclose sensitive information. The flaw was patched in version R124 of the cloud-based SaaS platform in late June and requires no customer action. According to Ivanti, the issue did not meet CVE criteria and shows no evidence of wild exploitation. (Author: Ionut Arghire; Published: August 12, 2026)

b8f919ca0df0.text: Microsoft released 400 CVEs on August 11's Patch Tuesday, slightly lower than July's record 570 but still presenting significant patching challenges for organizations lacking automated, risk-based systems. The actively exploited zero day (CVE-2026-68820) is a use-after-free vulnerability in Windows Ancillary Function Driver for WinSock. A locally authenticated attacker with low privileges could exploit this through a specially crafted application to trigger a race condition and gain system privileges. Action1 co-founder Mike Walters noted: "Confidentiality, integrity, and availability impacts are all rated high. Exploitation has been detected in the wild." Two additional publicly disclosed but unexploited zero days were included: CVE-2026-62832 affects Windows User Profile Service, allowing authenticated local attackers to elevate privileges through loading another user's registry hive, potentially accessing sensitive data and gaining administrator access. CVE-2026-72971 involves Windows Container Isolation FS Filter Driver tampering, enabling authenticated attackers to access or modify user data and gain admin privileges through improper link resolution. The majority of addressed vulnerabilities were elevation of privilege and remote code execution flaws, with 37 of 42 critical vulnerabilities being RCE bugs. (Author: Phil Muncaster; Published: 12 August 2026)

535caba50f37.text: SAP released patches addressing CVE-2026-58231, a maximum-severity flaw in Commerce Cloud (Data Hub Adapter) affecting unauthenticated users. The vulnerability scores 10.0 on CVSS and stems from "insufficient authorization checks and input validation." The core issue involves attackers exploiting default authentication mechanisms to submit malicious input to unprotected functions, potentially enabling arbitrary code execution and compromising system confidentiality, integrity, and availability. Three Additional Critical Vulnerabilities: CVE-2026-44772 (CVSS 9.9) - Code injection in Manufacturing Integration and Intelligence; CVE-2026-34265 (CVSS 9.8) - Out-of-bounds write in SAP NetWeaver, allowing memory corruption and system information disclosure; CVE-2026-44758 (CVSS 9.1) - Code injection enabling privileged attackers to execute arbitrary operating system commands via server-side template injection and SSRF vulnerabilities. Security firm Onapsis recommends customers patch immediately and redeploy updated versions. As interim protection, organizations should configure IP Filter Sets restricting vulnerable endpoint access. Post-patch implementation requires maintaining the "Secure Transformer" property with allowlisted XSL file hosts. (Author: Ravie Lakshmanan; Published: August 12, 2026)

b0b86a16d74f.text: Cisco has alerted customers to a high-severity vulnerability impacting its Secure Firewall Adaptive Security Appliance (ASA) Software and Secure Firewall Threat Defense (FTD) Software that is actively being exploited. The flaw, designated CVE-2026-20349 with a CVSS score of 8.6, stems from insufficient error checking during HTTP request processing. This allows unauthenticated remote attackers to trigger denial-of-service conditions. "An attacker could exploit this vulnerability by sending a crafted HTTP request to the Remote Access SSL VPN service on an affected device," according to Cisco's official advisory. A successful attack could force affected devices to reload, creating service disruptions. The vulnerability affects devices with specific configurations including IKEv2 Remote Access VPN with client services, SSL-VPN capabilities, or Zero Trust Network Access enabled. Vulnerable versions span ASA 9.16 through 9.24 and FTD versions 7.0 through 10.0. Cisco has released patches for all affected versions but indicates no workarounds exist. The company discovered the issue during internal testing and became aware of active exploitation earlier this month. Researcher Valerio Brussani also independently discovered and reported the vulnerability. The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency added CVE-2026-20349 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog, mandating that Federal agencies apply fixes by August 14, 2026. (Author: Ravie Lakshmanan; Published: August 12, 2026)

9b8caf560ce3.text: PentestGPT is an open-source penetration testing agent that leverages large language models to conduct automated security assessments. The tool operates in two primary modes: autonomous and interactive. In autonomous mode, the agent executes "recon, then exploit, then walkthrough," with each phase informing the next. When switched to pentest mode, the workflow shifts to "asset discovery, vulnerability identification, report" without human intervention. The framework powers either Claude Code or Codex, making independent decisions about which tools to deploy and next steps. The original version was published by Gelei Deng and colleagues at USENIX Security 2024. Users need Python 3.12+, the uv package manager, and authenticated CLIs for Claude Code and Codex. A Docker image is available that bundles both tools, simplifying token management across team deployments. "Anonymous usage data" is transmitted to Langfuse by default, including session metadata and tool execution information. However, the developers emphasize that "command outputs, credentials, and flag values are never transmitted"-a distinction relevant for client engagements. The legacy version supports multiple LLM providers including OpenAI, Anthropic, Google Gemini, DeepSeek, and local models through Ollama, with built-in model verification. PentestGPT is available free on GitHub. (Author: Anamarija Pogorelec; Published: August 12, 2026)

a395afb55cbe.text: Cisco has released patches for a zero-day vulnerability affecting firewalls running Secure Firewall Adaptive Security Appliance (ASA) and Secure Firewall Threat Defense (FTD) software. The flaw, identified as CVE-2026-20349, relates to HTTP request processing. A remote attacker without authentication can exploit this vulnerability by sending a specially crafted HTTP request to the Remote Access SSL VPN service, causing the appliance to reload and enter a denial-of-service condition. Cisco discovered the issue internally and also received a report from an external researcher. The company became aware of active exploitation in August 2026, though details about the attacks remain undisclosed. "Cisco has urged customers to apply the available hotfixes as soon as possible." CISA added CVE-2026-20349 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on Tuesday, mandating that federal agencies patch by August 14. This marks the 12th Cisco product vulnerability with a 2026 CVE identifier added to the KEV list this year, following similar issues in SD-WAN products, Unified CM, and FMC systems. (Author: Eduard Kovacs; Published: August 12, 2026)

df2864d62994.text: Description: This vulnerability involves a use-after-free flaw in the Windows Ancillary Function Driver for WinSock, allowing "an authorized attacker to elevate privileges locally." Severity: CVSS Score 7.0 (High), Vector: CVSS:3.1/AV:L/AC:H/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H. Key Dates: Published August 11, 2026; Updated August 13, 2026; Public Disclosure August 11, 2026 at 14:00 UTC; CISA KEV Due Date August 25, 2026. f79fb4a09920.text: Bitdefender's August 2026 threat analysis examined ransomware activity from July 1-31, recording 873 claimed victims-the third-highest total in twelve months. Featured Story: CRPx0 Ransomware. CRPx0 emerged in June 2026 with minimal activity but surged to 46 victims by July. The group began targeting small dental practices but rapidly expanded to larger technology and financial services organizations, with growing victim concentration in Turkey and the United States. The group markets both Ransomware-as-a-Service (RaaS) and Hacking-as-a-Service (HaaS) programs. Notably, CRPx0 offers "100% profit-sharing model, allowing buyers to keep all profits" alongside a $10,000 subscription fee-raising questions about legitimacy versus potential scam operations. Security experts note suspicions about inflated victim claims, though the group could alternatively possess extended access to multiple data breach sources enabling synchronized attacks. CRPx0 distinguishes itself through crypto theft capabilities, employing clipper malware and wallet seed phrase extraction modules. This dual approach-combining infostealer operations with ransomware-presents an alternative to traditional encryption-focused attacks, potentially reducing detection risks. Other Notable Developments: The Gentlemen maintains top ransomware group ranking with expanding victim claims across Southern Asia. INC Ransom exploited SonicWall SMA 1000 vulnerabilities (CVE-2026-15409 and CVE-2026-15410) using KNUCKLEBALL and ORANGETAIL malware for persistence. Global Secret Group emerged with LockBit-derived code, claiming 100,000+ victims across energy and utilities sectors. LAPSUS$ announced ecosystem exit (though previous similar announcements proved temporary). Key Statistics: Top 3 Ransomware Groups: The Gentlemen, Qilin, CRPx0. Most Attacked Regions: Argentina newly ranked 8th with 21 claimed victims. Most Affected Industries: Manufacturing (1st), Technology (2nd), Healthcare (3rd). (Author: Jade Brown; Published: August 12, 2026)

4e5b12293c1b.text: Two compromised LiteLLM releases distributed on PyPI in March contained credential-stealing malware capable of harvesting cloud keys, SSH credentials, Kubernetes tokens, and database passwords. The packages remained available for approximately 40 minutes before being quarantined. Threat intelligence firm CloudSEK obtained a dataset containing roughly 434,000 files captured during the attack, mapping potential exposure to more than 2,500 organizations. However, CloudSEK emphasized this represents potential exposure rather than confirmed victim counts, as the data came from captured loot and log files rather than direct organizational assessments. Key Technical Details: The malicious versions 1.82.7 and 1.82.8 were live on March 24 from 10:39 UTC for approximately 40 minutes. Version 1.82.8 included a file named litellm_init.pth that executed during Python interpreter startup, enabling payload execution regardless of whether applications directly imported LiteLLM. The compromise originated from the broader TeamPCP supply-chain campaign linked to the Aqua Security Trivy scanner breach. Attackers retained access after incomplete credential rotation and subsequently used exposed PyPI publishing tokens to upload the malicious releases. Recommended Actions: Check for LiteLLM installations during the March 24 window (10:39-16:00 UTC); rotate all credentials accessible from affected systems; search GitHub for repositories named "tpcp-docs" or "docs-tpcp". (Author: Swati Khandelwal; Published: August 12, 2026)

b370ae548bd3.text:
During the 25 years Gerardo Pachuca has spent investigating thieves who steal cargo from semitrucks, he says he’s never seen behavior this brazen. The consultant and former Los Angeles sheriff’s detective claims that two times in recent months, robbers stole pricey hardware destined for AI data centers using a confrontational new tactic. It’s left the freight industry on edge.
The incidents involved two different shipments of high-value technology traveling from Silicon Valley to Southern California, according to Pachuca, who says he learned about the thefts from law enforcement authorities. Each truck was tailed by private security professionals driving unmarked escort vehicles, which were supposed to ensure the goods made it to their destinations safely. But hours into one journey, another driver rear-ended the escort in a hit-and-run, forcing it to stop. In the other case, the escort stopped after another car nudged it into a tailspin, a ploy commonly known as a PIT maneuver, and then fled.
Everyone familiar with the “accidents” believes the escorts were deliberately immobilized, according to Pachuca. Once the semitrucks lost their escorts, the drivers proceeded without halting—but not to their planned destinations. They were never heard from again, Pachua says, and millions of dollars in data center gear remains unaccounted for.
WIRED attempted to independently confirm Pachuca's accounts with five state and local law enforcement agencies, but could not because he shared limited information to avoid jeopardizing what he describes as ongoing investigations. But two other people in the cargo industry provided corroborating information.
J.J. Coughlin, chairman of the Southwest Transportation Security Council, a nonprofit intelligence-sharing group, says one of the affected escort companies notified him as soon as its vehicle was attacked while it was guarding “high-value technology.” Danny Ramon, director of intelligence and response at the freight-monitoring software developer Overhaul, says he learned about the rear-ending incident from law enforcement sources days after it happened. He describes the situation as a “coordinated assault” affecting a shipment of “AI hardware.”
Pachuca, Coughlin, and Ramon all say that no one was hurt in the attacks—they assume the truck drivers were in on the scheme, an increasingly common issue—and the perpetrators have yet to be caught. They are all concerned that the isolated cases could turn into an alarming trend—a violent spin on freight crime, now enabled by cyber-based scams and hacks, and targeting the very equipment powering the bleeding edge of the internet.
“It’s the worst I’ve seen,” Pachuca says of cargo theft nationwide. “The methods they are using, the value they are getting, the frequency these crimes are occurring.”
Escort companies are a final line of defense and are increasingly in demand. Michael Duffy, CEO of Solutions Group International, says his escort business used to be busy primarily ahead of the holiday shopping season, but it has now picked up year-round, with companies moving liquid cooling parts, servers, and computer chips emerging as his biggest clients. “Now that the values have shot through the roof, we’re getting called all the time,” Duffy says. He estimates his company has protected 13,000 shipments over the past four years, without a single loss.
High-value cargo and their escort vehicles have been targeted in Mexico and other countries for years. The suspected attacks in the US are now prompting escort operators to find ways to beef up their security, and some are encouraging personnel to call 911 at the first sign of suspicion. “We’ve been trying to come up with a game plan,” says Rachel Fruchtenicht of Shadow Freight Security.
