AI Heists
Cargo theft has been on the rise since the start of the Covid pandemic, when more consumers turned to ecommerce and delivery for their daily needs. More recently, the booming AI data center industry has created a new target for would-be thieves: Total spending on their construction in just the first half of this year surpassed the total for all of 2025. While the overall number of thefts reported last quarter fell 26 percent year over year, the value of the goods taken more than doubled as criminals are increasingly targeting expensive cargo, according to new data released this month by Verisk CargoNet, an analytics and risk assessment firm.
Some of the most commonly stolen goods include metals—especially copper—and enterprise-grade computer and networking equipment, according to Verisk CargoNet. These shipments are typically transported according to standard procedures, creating “a significant mismatch between their financial value and their ordinary transportation and security profile,” Verisk CargoNet said in an announcement accompanying the new data.
In April, for example, thieves allegedly made off with 34,560 optical transceiver cables and 96 network switch modules—parts used in data centers—that were supposed to be traveling from Olive Branch, Mississippi, to Richardson, Texas, according to a notice issued by private investigators to freight industry partners seen by WIRED.
In some cases, law enforcement has succeeded in recovering the lost goods. In May, authorities in Southern California announced the seizure of $4 million worth of allegedly stolen cargo, including data center cooling equipment developed by the company Deepcool AI. One person was arrested in connection with the case. Deepcool AI did not respond to a request for comment.
In June, California Highway Patrol received a tip from a prospective buyer who believed a deal was “too good to be true,” sergeant Omar Morales tells WIRED. He said CHP went on to recover more than $2.2 million in merchandise allegedly stolen in three separate incidents, including eight pallets of “server switches” manufactured by Celestica for Meta valued at $550,000 in total. Meta declined to comment. Celestica did not respond to requests for comment. Morales says the investigation is ongoing.
The same day as the Meta recovery, authorities in the Chicago area discovered a reportedly stolen trailer filled with about $1 million in equipment bound for data centers.
Hacking, Now Ramming
For the most part, today’s cargo heists are relatively simple—they don’t involve snipping locks, breaking down truck doors, or PIT maneuvers. Instead, thieves take advantage of the fragmented and sometimes impersonal nature of the freight industry, in which hundreds of thousands of independent truck owner-operators can sign up to transport shipments posted online.
Criminals sometimes hack into a truck operator's email address using social engineering or phishing, allowing them to essentially take over their business and sign up to transport loads using its legitimate motor vehicle registrations. GPS trackers on stolen trucks can be spoofed or deactivated, leaving no trace.
In another version of the scam, freight industry experts say, legitimate business owners illegally sell off their motor carrier numbers—the unique identifiers assigned to trucking companies by federal regulators—allowing fraudsters to operate as a real business with a long-standing permit, phone number, and email address.
Both of the recent thefts that targeted escort vehicles involved recently sold motor carrier numbers, Pachuca says. Morales says the Meta data center switches seized in California were stolen using a similar technique. To acquire their loot, the thieves posed as a real trucking company, including falsifying the legitimate motor carrier’s documents.
“These are very sophisticated, very organized criminal organizations,” says Ben Wilkens, director of cybersecurity at the National Motor Freight Traffic Association, a trade organization.
A new federal system, called MOTUS, is designed to crack down on some of these impersonations and scams by making it easier for trucking companies to manage their federal registrations, and for customers to confirm their legitimacy. Regulators released a bulletin in March reminding the industry that registration numbers could only be sold as part of corporate transactions, and that those sales must be reported.
Georgia-based shipper FLS Transportation Services detects a scammer trying to steal one of its loads every day, says Jaclyn Giles, the company’s director of operational support. Employee training and a paid monitoring service have helped FLS fend off most shady carriers. But every month or so, “our employees get sloppy,” Giles says, and a thief makes off with cargo.
Most recently, Giles says FLS lost $650,000 worth of tools. Last year, she adds, the company had to change insurers over concerns about insufficient coverage for stolen loads. Some carriers don’t report thefts partly because of fears that their insurance costs will skyrocket, according to Wilkens. Others are buying supplemental insurance or splitting loads across many trailers to reduce potential losses.
Giles says FLS now attaches GPS trackers directly to high-value shipments such as LEGO toys. Pachuca says one of his California freight clients, which moves a lot of tech gear, adopted Flock license-plate cameras and discovered would-be thieves casing their location to identify trailers with the highest-value products. He says another client has begun catching fake drivers’ licenses by scanning them. In June, WIRED reported that Tesla had enhanced driver identity checks after trailers with millions of dollars in batteries were taken right from its loading docks.
Authorities haven’t publicly disclosed much information about where stolen AI hardware may end up. US export controls on chips and other high-value tech have created incentives to steal and smuggle the goods to countries like China. Based on location pings when some parts are activated, some freight industry experts, including Pachuca, suspect that many stolen shipments are taken overseas.
Preventing these crimes has been complicated by a decades-long history of deregulation and patchwork enforcement. “Reporting structures and standards vary from one state to another, and the prosecution rates are low enough that this is a very high-reward, low-risk crime,” says the freight trade body’s Wilkens. “It’s easy money.”

e1efec36abd7.text: Researchers from Tracebit discovered that placing prompt injections alongside stored secrets on AWS can effectively disable AI hacking agents. The technique, called "context bombing," embeds prompts that trigger guardrail violations-such as requests for bioweapon instructions or politically sensitive content-causing the LLM to shut down rather than continue with malicious tasks. The research showed that when attacking LLMs encounter these forbidden commands, they cease following their existing instructions. Examples include prompts ordering development of dangerous biological materials or, for Chinese models, references to Tiananmen Square events. However, Schneier notes a critical limitation: "this only works against agents that have guardrails." As locally-run AI models without safety restrictions become more prevalent, attackers will increasingly leverage unconstrained systems immune to context bombing tactics. The article emphasizes that this defensive approach represents an interesting but potentially temporary advantage in the evolving AI security landscape, as adversaries adapt their strategies to circumvent such protections. (Author: Bruce Schneier; Published: August 12, 2026)

b391413b22fa.text: More than 2,500 organizations and over 430,000 CI/CD pipelines were affected by the LiteLLM supply chain attack, according to CloudSEK's investigation. The compromise occurred after LiteLLM's CI pipeline automatically installed a compromised version of Aqua Security's Trivy vulnerability scanner. Two malicious LiteLLM versions (1.82.7 and 1.82.8) were subsequently published to PyPI, exposing sensitive data accessible to the library. TeamPCP, the threat actor responsible for multiple open-source software compromises, did not directly target LiteLLM. Rather, the attack exploited a chain of vulnerabilities: "one unrevoked token, three tools deep" created ecosystem-wide exposure. Despite the malicious packages remaining live for only 40 minutes, the automated nature of modern build systems enabled rapid propagation across 434,000 pipelines. Major organizations impacted include Nvidia, AWS, Samsung, Salesforce, Cisco, ServiceNow, Siemens, FedEx, Volkswagen, and others. Compromised data included package publishing credentials, cloud keys, SSH keys, tokens, and AI provider keys. CloudSEK emphasized that affected organizations should rotate all potentially compromised secrets and review logs to determine exposure scope. The firm cautioned that AI infrastructure represents an attractive future target due to its connections across data, identity, compute, and autonomous systems. (Author: Ionut Arghire; Published: August 12, 2026)

0390860fa85c.text: Poland's CERT released findings from a December 2025 cyberattack on a combined heat and power plant serving 50,000 residents. The incident represented "the first known documented attack in which threat actors have accessed an OT network through a private Access Point Name (APN)." Attack Timeline: Adversaries compromised a FortiGate VPN and firewall at a wind farm, then leveraged a Teltonika cellular router to target a private APN network managed by a distribution system operator. The attackers discovered a WAGO PFC200 programmable logic controller protected only by default credentials, gaining access to the facility's OT network. Impact: The actors located and compromised three Siemens PLCs, forcing them into STOP mode. This resulted in "shutdown of a steam turbine and the water treatment system," halting cogeneration operations. Attackers subsequently sabotaged Moxa network devices, destroyed logs, and reset multiple systems to complicate recovery efforts. CERT.PL Recommendations: The Polish CERT advised organizations to audit private APN configurations, implement network segmentation between APNs and OT environments, change default credentials, monitor inter-network traffic, and include these systems in penetration testing programs. (Author: Phil Muncaster; Published: 12 August 2026)

f59c085459fe.text: ConnectSecure has announced that Microsoft 365 Auto Remediation and AI-powered Training Assessments are now live on the ConnectSecure platform. The capabilities help managed service providers (MSPs) address supported M365 security findings, create and measure assessments, support client training and strengthen security posture from one platform. The launch advances ConnectSecure's focus on proactive, unified protection for MSPs. M365 Auto Remediation helps teams act on supported Microsoft 365 security findings, while Training Assessments streamline the creation, assignment and measurement of assessments for compliance, onboarding, third-party due diligence and security awareness. CEO Peter Bellini stated: "MSPs are under pressure to do more than point out problems. They need to help clients fix gaps, prove progress and build stronger security habits over time." M365 Auto Remediation supports a subset of ConnectSecure M365 Security Inspection findings that can be addressed through conditional access policy enforcement or reporting. Supported findings include administrative users with no multifactor authentication enforced, legacy authentication, risky sign-ins, user risk, device registration, security information registration, self-service password reset and Microsoft Secure Defaults. Training Assessments adds an AI-assisted workflow for building and distributing assessments across companies. Users can generate assessments from topics, source text, uploaded content or templates, then review and edit generated questions before publishing. The module includes configurable settings for question count, difficulty level, time limits, expiration settings, maximum attempts, pass thresholds and question types. Training Assessments also include multilingual support. Patch 360, a patch management capability, is also now available on the ConnectSecure platform, offering MSPs greater control through pilot-first validation, risk-based prioritization, staged rollouts, approval workflows, lifecycle visibility and integrated rollback. (Published: August 12, 2026)

856443aab0db.text: CBTS has launched Penetration Testing as a Service (PTaaS), merging autonomous penetration testing with security expertise to enable organizations to continuously identify exploitable risks, validate attack paths, and prioritize remediation as their environments evolve. Enterprise attack surfaces are expanding faster than traditional testing cycles can manage due to cloud environments, SaaS applications, connected systems, third-party relationships, and AI systems. Industry breach data shows vulnerability exploitation now surpasses stolen credentials as attackers' primary entry method, with AI reducing the gap between disclosure and exploitation from months to hours. Tim Mackie from Horizon3.ai noted that "organizations can continuously validate exploitable risk, prioritize remediation based on evidence, and strengthen security posture." The PTaaS offering, built on NodeZero, performs autonomous penetration tests across live production environments without operational disruption. CBTS security experts review assessment results, providing customer-specific context and remediation guidance. This transforms penetration testing from an annual checkpoint into continuous practice. Key service features include: validated exploitability through environmental testing; attack path analysis demonstrating how weaknesses chain together; expert review from penetration testing professionals; customized reporting for remediation prioritization; flexible testing frequency options (daily, weekly, monthly, quarterly). The approach aligns with Continuous Threat Exposure Management (CTEM) programs, helping security teams focus on exposures most likely to create business risk. (Published: August 12, 2026)

66eb91712bd6.text:
Crytica Security has developed a patented solution that delivers rapid, deterministic threat detection for operational technology (OT), protecting the embedded systems and connected devices that underpin critical infrastructure, national security, and healthcare without disrupting operations.

The need is becoming increasingly urgent as cybersecurity moves toward machine speed. IBM's Cost of a Data Breach Report 2026 found AI-driven attacks increased 56% year over year, while 50% of organizations with security operations centers (SOCs) have already deployed AI agents in production. As attackers and defenders increasingly operate at machine speed, confidence in the underlying security signal becomes more important.

Cybersecurity technologies provide essential visibility into networks, communications, assets, vulnerabilities, and behavior. Crytica complements those technologies by addressing what external visibility alone cannot determine: whether a device itself remains in a trusted operating state.

Crytica's Rapid Detection, Alert, and isolation (RDAi) system operates from inside each protected device, detecting unauthorized changes to the device's instruction sets and providing deterministic evidence of those changes. This high-confidence evidence augments existing SOC, SIEM, XDR and AI-assisted security workflows without requiring organizations to replace their existing cybersecurity investments.

"Cybersecurity has become extraordinarily good at observing what is happening around and external to a device, but ultimately, for detection to be truly effective, it must take place inside" each device, stated Dr. C. Kerry Nemovicher, CEO of Crytica Security.

Nemovicher explained that the company installs a lightweight "Probe" agent (under 100 KB) within protected devices to monitor instruction set integrity, known as iNSiM. This approach proves particularly critical in sectors where compromised devices could impact physical operations, essential services, and human safety.

C. Lloyd Mahaffey, Executive Chairman, noted that "customers and technology partners aren't looking to replace the security investments they already have" but rather seek faster threat detection capabilities.

Current OT and IoT cybersecurity solutions observe devices externally and infer threats. RDAi immediately detects threats from within devices and issues high-fidelity alerts that security operations personnel can trust and act upon.

55007e5229e1.text:
Google Chrome has implemented comprehensive measures to combat abusive web push notifications. The browser automatically revokes notification permissions for inactive websites and those identified by Google Safe Browsing as engaging in abusive or deceptive practices. Users retain the ability to review and restore revoked permissions through Chrome's Safety Hub if they choose to trust a particular site.

Google employs a multi-layered defense strategy combining Chrome Security, Firebase Cloud Messaging (FCM), and Safe Browsing to detect and block abuse throughout the notification lifecycle. During the first quarter of 2026, these protections "blocked more than 7 billion unwanted notifications per day on Android."

The company developed behavioral detection technology to identify networks of websites coordinating abusive notifications by analyzing service worker activity. This allows Google to proactively remove permissions from persistent bad actors distributing malware, scams, and malicious content.

Additionally, Google limits abusive websites to 1,000 push messages per minute through FCM. Those exceeding this threshold receive HTTP 429 responses, with repeat offenders facing stricter rate limits until demonstrating sustained non-disruptive behavior.

Chrome's updated permission model includes a redesigned Android permission prompt and a one-tap unsubscribe feature enabling users to quickly revoke notification permissions from problematic websites.

cd59cc0adc99.text:
The episode was recorded from Vietnam and contained some technical challenges. Troy mentions wind noise, connectivity issues, and YouTube synchronization problems, but emphasizes the impressive scenery.

The primary focus shifts to discussing the Brinks Home FAQ, which Troy found particularly noteworthy this week. He criticizes the company's FAQ for failing to adequately answer the questions it poses.

Troy acknowledges that Brinks is genuinely a victim of criminal extortion and deserves sympathy. However, he expresses frustration with how overly legalized language obscures straightforward answers to basic incident response questions.

He outlines a common pattern in these situations: attackers obtain data through social engineering (vishing and OAuth manipulation), demand ransom, then release data when payment doesn't materialize. This triggers numerous class action lawsuits, forcing companies to hire extensive legal representation. Customers receive notification only "where legally required," which is often not mandated.

2c0e800b7815.text:
Spanish police have arrested a man in Murcia accused of using deepfake software to trick a certificate provider's video identity checks in an attempt to obtain digital signatures he could use for financial fraud.

According to the police, the man made 38 attempts using this method on more than 30 citizens. Police haven't said how many of those attempts succeeded before the scheme was uncovered.

The National Police said the investigation started after a company that issues electronic certificates flagged a string of suspicious verification requests.

Investigators say the suspect appeared in the company's video calls holding a forged national ID card, while AI software altered his face on screen so it matched the photo on the document.

The fraudster ran out of luck when the digital mask glitched for a moment during a live verification call, exposing his true face on screen.

"The alleged perpetrator used household spotlights with strategically placed colored bulbs to simulate the flashes and security features found on physical identity documents under real light," police explained.

"He then balanced the counterfeit documents in front of the webcam, perfectly recreating the official holograms. He also used VPNs to anonymize his connections and employed manipulated documents with apparent security features."

Tracing the suspect's communications and payment trail, investigators identified more than 320 phone lines linked to 24 mobile devices. Most of those lines were registered using stolen identities and bought at physical points of sale in Murcia, which police were able to geolocate.

When officers made the arrest, they also carried out a search that turned up a laptop protected with high-level encryption, along with phones, storage devices, and other records tied to the case. He faces charges over a continuing offense of falsifying official documents.

205b46275d3c.text:
SonicWall announced patches for eight vulnerabilities across two products on Tuesday, including critical-severity remote code execution bugs.

The company released fixes for six security defects in Global Management System (GMS), its centralized management, monitoring, and reporting platform that was retired in October 2025.

Two vulnerabilities warrant particular attention: CVE-2026-66147 (CVSS 9.4) and CVE-2026-66145 (CVSS 9.1). Both could allow remote, unauthenticated attackers to execute arbitrary code. The former is a command injection issue in the GMS Dispatcher Service exploitable via crafted requests. The latter represents an RCE bug leading to sensitive data disclosure and arbitrary file write via zipslip.

These vulnerabilities affect GMS versions 9.5.1 and earlier (Virtual Appliance and Windows), resolved in version 9.5.2. The update also addresses high-severity insufficient certificate validation and insecure handling of serialized objects bugs.

Additionally, SonicWall released fixes for two high-severity code injection flaws (CVE-2026-66149 and CVE-2026-66150) in Email Security that could enable OS command execution with root privileges. These affect Email Security Appliance models 5000, 5050, 7000, 7050, 9000, VMware, and Hyper-V, resolved in Email Security version 10.0.36.

SonicWall reports no evidence of exploitation in the wild but urges immediate patching.

eb3d0eb4227e.text:
In this Help Net Security interview, Christopher Smith, CEO of Quantus, discusses what cryptographic inventories turn up in banks and hospitals, including default passwords and admin keys still held by former employees.

He explains where post-quantum key sizes break old size assumptions in IPsec, SSH, TLS and libp2p, why migrating user keys makes blockchains hard to upgrade, and what a silent quantum break would look like from outside. He also gives the argument for funding work whose payoff stays invisible.

On hidden cryptography in organizations: Smith notes that security teams typically understand their known vulnerabilities. The most surprising discoveries include "a default password nobody knew was there, or a hidden admin key that is sometimes still held by a former employee." He also mentions finding password hashes on user devices, including one recovered from a deceased client's laptop.

On size constraints: Post-quantum algorithms require larger keys and signatures, which breaks legacy assumptions. "IPsec, SSH, TLS can carry small-size assumptions and sometimes don't have friendly error messages when these assumptions are violated." Libp2p needed updates for post-quantum primitives.

On cryptographic agility: Smith explains that achieving cryptographic agility requires inserting abstraction layers across organizational boundaries. "Blockchains remain among the hardest systems to update" because migrating user keys requires every user to participate.

On detecting quantum breaks: He stresses that evidence of remote key compromise wouldn't come with explanation. A hardware wallet compromise demonstrated this—forensics found a weak RNG, but without such evidence, a mathematical break remains ambiguous given modern software's complexity.

On funding invisible security: Smith compares it to insurance pricing: "Cryptographic failure is quantifiable, although many decision makers haven't thought very deeply about what the numbers are." Organizations must migrate faster than threats emerge.

6dcf49c1a7d5.text:
Based on 338 million attack simulations, the report reveals enterprise defenses have improved at network edges but remain weak internally.

Perimeter vs. Interior Defense Gap: Prevention effectiveness reached 69% at the perimeter, but dropped dramatically to 37% post-compromise. "Inside the domain, defenses stop roughly one action in three" while allowing others to proceed.

Quiet Attacks Evade Detection: Organizations successfully block 85-90% of loud lateral movement and privilege escalation attempts, but only stop approximately 10% of reconnaissance activities and 22% of credential-harvesting attacks from memory.

Same Tool, Different Results: The credential-theft tool Mimikatz demonstrated stark variance: "Dumping credentials from LSASS process memory...was blocked 94% of the time" versus only 3% when reading from the local registry—identical behavior, different detection rates.

Malware Prevention Declining: Malware prevention fell to 50%, down from 60% in 2025 and 71% in 2024, reflecting structural limitations in indicator-based detection amid massive daily file volumes.

Detection Remains Problematic: Only 14% of simulated attacks generated alerts despite logging improvements, indicating organizations struggle converting collected data into actionable intelligence.

8261c5a6ac75.text:
A seller on a cybercrime forum is offering a ready-made scam kit for $500, complete with an admin panel that tracks victims, checks their crypto wallets for value, and inflates fake balances to squeeze out more money, Malwarebytes found.

Researchers discovered the scam project on May 16 and described it as an example of how social engineering, phishing, and financial fraud can be combined into a single operation.

The account behind the kit goes by xrep. It has been active on the forum since March 2026 and has built a reputation there, with other cybercriminals leaving positive feedback on its threads.

Xrep's specialty is packaged tools built around X. Instead of making buyers write their own code or set up their own servers, xrep hands over something close to a finished product.

"It is a complete scam-in-a-box," Malwarebytes said. "The technical infrastructure, phishing functionality, fake investment dashboard, victim tracking, and administrative controls are bundled together into a ready-to-use package."

Scammers use fake $TSLA presale to steal cryptocurrency: The kit Malwarebytes examined builds a fake presale page for a token called $TSLA, styled to look like it comes from Tesla. It supports several languages and works on phones as well as desktops.

The scam starts with a fake "eligibility check" that asks visitors for their X username, then pulls their profile photo to make the offer feel tailored to them. From there the page piles on pressure. A progress bar climbs on its own, a countdown clock ticks down, and warnings claim the token price is about to rise, all built to make people move fast and skip questions.

Once someone believes the offer is genuine, the site gives them two ways to lose their money.

One asks them to connect a crypto wallet to claim a bonus. The form that opens up asks for a 12-word recovery phrase, the words that control everything in a wallet. Whoever has that phrase can empty it.

The other skips wallets and just asks for a transfer, in Bitcoin, Ethereum, USDT, or Dogecoin, sent straight to an address the scammer owns.

"Victims may believe they have made a legitimate investment, but no real tokens are being purchased. Instead, the scammer simply receives the cryptocurrency while the victim sees a fake balance displayed on the website," researchers noted.

Admin panel gives scammers control over victims: "What makes this operation particularly concerning is the level of control provided to the scammer," researchers noted.

Beyond watching victims move through the site and pulling in their X usernames, locations, and any recovery phrases they enter, the panel lets the operator check whether a stolen wallet is worth draining further before bothering to chase it. And the fake balance a victim sees isn't set once and left alone. The operator can raise it whenever they want, so the investment looks like it's paying off and the victim sends more.

The panel also lets the scammer manage fake purchase orders and message victims directly. If someone has already sent money, the operator can follow up claiming there's a delay and that an extra network fee is needed to release the funds, a second attempt at the same wallet.

"Someone who may not have the skills to build a phishing website, develop an administration system, or create convincing investment interfaces can potentially purchase the kit and begin targeting victims with minimal effort," Malwarebytes concluded.

a37ff5e7b3e2.text:
A critical zero-day vulnerability (CVE-2026-50656/"RoguePlanet") in Microsoft Defender's Malware Protection Engine (mpengine.dll) enables local users, including standard, low-privilege accounts, to escalate privileges to NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM using a race condition and improper link resolution. Microsoft initially issued a patch (Engine v1.1.26060.3008) in July 2026. However, on August 12, 2026, a new exploit chain, "ShieldBreak," was released by the same researcher (alias "Chaotic Eclipse"), which publicly demonstrated a full bypass of Microsoft's patch and restored SYSTEM-level access. This means even up-to-date Defender environments remain at risk.

The threat impacts all current Windows platforms using Defender, including Windows 10, 11 (25H2, Canary), and Windows Server 2025. The vulnerabilities allow authenticated users (i.e., any code run on an endpoint) to obtain full administrative control, disable security controls, persist post-infection, steal sensitive data, or move laterally. The exploit chain is entirely local – there are no network-based IOCs – and detection relies on host-based behavioral patterns.

The attacker, Chaotic Eclipse, is notorious for multiple high-impact Windows zero-day releases in 2026, targeting core system security features. The RoguePlanet/ShieldBreak vulnerabilities represent a severe risk window for all industries, especially given the rise in ransomware and targeted attacks affecting healthcare, federal, and public-sector agencies.

Initial weaponization of RoguePlanet appeared in early June 2026, was patched after nearly a month of public exposure, and has now been bypassed, necessitating urgent and layered mitigations. There is currently no official fix for the ShieldBreak bypass as of this alert.

Recommendations for CVE-2026-50656:

1. Immediate Host Inventory and Patch Validation: Review your entire IT estate for the Microsoft Malware Protection Engine version. All versions < 1.1.26060.3008 are vulnerable to RoguePlanet.

2. Deploy Layered Compensating Controls: Block or warn on execution of vulnerable Defender binaries/apps using Defender Vulnerability Management or EDR policies where feasible. Restrict local administrative rights to reduce available privilege for local attackers. Enforce application allowlisting to limit execution of untrusted local binaries. Enable Tamper Protection and least-privilege controls for Defender.

3. Implement Proactive Defense-in-Depth Strategies: Deploy and test Attack Surface Reduction (ASR) rules; use audit mode first, then move to block mode as safely as possible. Enable runtime detection (e.g., eBPF-based tools) for unusual Defender activity on unpatched or high-risk systems. Regularly review audit trails for MsMPEng.exe and User Profile Service events, focusing on child process creation, token duplication, junctions/symlinks, and hive mounting behaviors. Validate Group Policy and registry settings for Defender to ensure real-time protection, automatic remediation, and exclusion policies are secured.

Temporary Workarounds: Block Vulnerable Apps using Microsoft Defender Vulnerability Management for systems pending a patch. Apply scoped CVE exceptions with care for operational constraints. Restrict Local and RPC Access via network segmentation and Group Policy controls. Enforce ASR rules and application control policy in audit-only mode first. Develop and deploy Incident Response Playbooks for rapid containment. Enable and enforce Defender's Tamper Protection features (requires Intune or equivalent). Deploy Secure Boot and Microsoft's rollback protection policy (VBS Rollback Protections) to prevent attackers from reverting patched binaries.

Limitations: These workarounds are not a substitute for a patch; they may impact legitimate business applications or cover only some exploitation vectors.

d1bc4a42ae9d.text:
Attempts to exploit a critical vulnerability (CVE-2026-71362) in Adobe's Commerce and Magento e-commerce platforms have been detected, potentially allowing attackers to hijack customer accounts.

The flaw is described as an incorrect authorization vulnerability that could be leveraged to "gain elevated access to sensitive resources" without authentication and is one of the seven issues that Adobe addressed in a security update yesterday.

Although the software vendor states in the advisory that it is not aware of exploits in the wild for any of the fixed flaws, eCommerce security company Sansec says that its Shield web application firewall (WAF) is already blocking CVE-2026-71362 exploitation attempts.

According to Sansec, exploiting the vulnerability requires "no existing account, administrator privileges or user interaction."

After analyzing Adobe's patch, the researchers pinned the problem to Magento improperly handling customer identity in an account session.

"Sansec reviewed the patch and confirmed that the vulnerability lets attackers switch a customer session to another customer account. This gives them access to the victim's account and private customer data," the security company explains.

Four of the other flaws Adobe fixed with yesterday's updates received a high-severity score, and the other two are medium and low severity:

CVE-2026-48414 (7.7, high severity): Stored cross-site scripting vulnerability that could result in arbitrary code execution. Exploitation requires authentication and administrator privileges.

CVE-2026-48413 (8.7, high severity): Stored cross-site scripting vulnerability that could result in arbitrary code execution. It requires authentication but not administrator privileges.

CVE-2026-48415 (7.6, high severity): Incorrect-authorization vulnerability affecting Adobe Commerce B2B that could enable a security-feature bypass. It requires authentication but not administrator privileges.

CVE-2026-48416 (7.5, high severity): Incorrect-authorization vulnerability that could enable a security-feature bypass. It requires neither authentication nor administrator privileges.

CVE-2026-48411 (6.5, medium severity): Incorrect-authorization vulnerability that could enable a security-feature bypass. Exploitation requires authentication and administrator privileges.

CVE-2026-48412 (2.7, low severity): Incorrect-authorization vulnerability that could result in privilege escalation. Exploitation requires authentication and administrator privileges.

Website administrators are advised to apply the August 2026 security update for currently supported Commerce, Commerce B2B, and Magento release lines as soon as possible.

According to Sansec, these monthly fixes are distributed as isolated patch files rather than a new security release or updated Composer packages.

Website admins must first ensure they're running the latest -p release available for their supported release branch before applying the corresponding isolated patch.

df7c200b13d4.text:
The North Korean threat actor group known as Lazarus has been linked to exploiting a newly patched Windows vulnerability to deliver an unprecedented backdoor targeting defense and aerospace firms in France, Germany, Brazil, and India.

This activity represents part of Operation Dream Job, an ongoing cyber espionage and social engineering initiative by Pyongyang-backed hackers designed to pursue professionals through fraudulent recruitment offers from companies like Lockheed Martin and Enveil on platforms such as LinkedIn.

The attacks exploit CVE-2026-68820 (CVSS: 7.0), a privilege escalation flaw in Windows Ancillary Function Driver for WinSock ("AFD.sys"). Microsoft released patches in August 2026. Check Point Research disclosed the vulnerability to Microsoft in late July 2026, though exploitation began in June.

Victims receive deceptive recruiter communications and are manipulated into opening malicious PDFs or installing compromised PDF viewers, which subsequently deploy a backdoor called Troy. The malware grants remote system access and circumvents security mechanisms.

Two infection pathways have been identified:

DLL Side-Loading Chain: Victims download encrypted archives triggering DLL side-loading. A malicious DLL ("libmupdf.dll") displays fraudulent job descriptions while covertly downloading MISTPEN, a lightweight downloader. MISTPEN communicates through Microsoft Graph API and OneDrive, retrieving reconnaissance modules and executing the AFD.sys exploit before deploying ForestTiger for remote access.

Trojanized SecurityPDF Viewer: Victims obtain SecurityPDF from websites impersonating Enveil. Upon opening documents containing a specific marker, the application decrypts and launches the Troy backdoor directly into memory, supporting seventeen operator commands for file operations, shell access, process manipulation, DLL injection, and configuration updates.

MISTPEN loads four modules: GetInfoPlugin (host profiling), PvPlugin (reconnaissance), OneScreenCapture (screenshot capture), and an LPE loader using ML-KEM post-quantum cryptography.

The attack chain employs an updated kernel-mode rootkit called FudModule 3.1, repeatedly deployed by Lazarus since 2022. This rootkit achieves SYSTEM privileges through AFD.sys exploitation and injects elevated MISTPEN instances into SYSTEM processes. The updated version additionally tampers with Windows Smart App Control by "setting VerifiedAndReputablePolicyState to zero and invoking NtSetSystemInformation class 0xA4 with option 0x10000000, triggering an in-place reload of the code integrity policy."

Attackers created three domains impersonating Enveil for SecurityPDF distribution: envell[.]xyz, enveil[.]online, and uxtramine[.]org.

Rather than establishing dedicated infrastructure, the campaign hijacks compromised WordPress, SharePoint, and vulnerable Roundcube webmail servers as ForestTiger command-and-control servers. Multiple Roundcube instances were vulnerable to CVE-2025-49113, enabling attackers to implant RelayShell, a previously undocumented PHP web shell facilitating command exchange via text files. One breached France-based organization was leveraged to transmit phishing messages to additional targets.

Check Point director Sergey Shykevich stated: "What makes this campaign so dangerous is not only the zero-day vulnerability – but also how Lazarus wove legitimate, trusted infrastructure into every stage of the attack."

The findings demonstrate Lazarus continues refining malware capabilities and tradecraft while maintaining Dream Job's fundamental approach in targeting critical sectors worldwide.

5af03b4e35b8.text:
Over on DysruptionHub, Joseph Topping has introduced a new resource for exploring cyber disruptions, following incidents over time, and uncovering the connections between them:
The registry is a research resource focused specifically on cyber disruptions. Each incident profile brings together what is publicly known about what happened, who was affected, the operational impact, the available evidence, and any connections to organizations, locations, ransomware groups or critical infrastructure sectors.
The records are meant to change as the incidents do. Active incidents will receive the most frequent updates, but older records can also be revised when new information becomes available. A report does not have to remain frozen at the point where the original article ended.
The registry also allows readers to approach the reporting from different directions.

91d06c21e618.text:
A SharePoint vulnerability (CVE-2026-55040) patched by Microsoft in July is now being actively exploited in the wild. The attacks began shortly after Rapid7 released technical details and a proof-of-concept exploit on August 11, 2026.

The vulnerability is described as "a weak authentication issue that allows an attacker to bypass a security feature over a network." Microsoft noted that exploitation could "disclose files and modify data," and "an unauthenticated attacker could bypass authentication and make an anonymous connection."

Threat intelligence firm Defused reported on August 12 that honeypots detected exploitation attempts leveraging Rapid7's PoC script.

Additionally, Rapid7 discovered CVE-2026-63520, a separate SharePoint flaw that could be chained with CVE-2026-55040 to achieve unauthenticated remote code execution. This vulnerability was addressed in Microsoft's August Patch Tuesday updates with "no indication that it too is being exploited in attacks."

CVE-2026-55040 marks the fifth SharePoint vulnerability exploited during summer 2026. CISA previously urged organizations to update SharePoint instances but has not yet added this vulnerability to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog, which currently contains over a dozen SharePoint flaws.

c167609c9aa3.text:
Most security stories start with something broken. This one starts with everything working as designed.

Researchers at Reco have been tracking a campaign they call City-Forum, named after a domain registered in 2002, abandoned, and now resolving to a generic rented server from a German hosting provider. From that server, someone has been pulling records out of Salesforce and ServiceNow portals around the world.

The activity has not stopped, and there is more of it than there was. Every request Reco has seen from this address arrived as a guest. The targets they can see span telecom operators, banks and financial-services firms, enterprise-software vendors including security and data-privacy companies, and public-sector portals.

What passive DNS establishes is that the domain has resolved to this address since at least March 2025, so the infrastructure has been standing for a while. When the scanning started is a different question.

Here is the part worth sitting with: no software was exploited. No credentials were needed. There is no vulnerability here to patch. The attacker visited public customer portals as an anonymous visitor and asked them, politely and repeatedly, for their contents. The portals answered.

The guest in the room

Salesforce gives every Experience Cloud site its own standing account called the guest user, and every ServiceNow instance has one too. It is a real user with a profile and permissions like any other. When an unauthenticated stranger loads your support portal or your knowledge base, that is who they are browsing as. The guest user is not optional, it cannot be deleted, and it arrives with permissions that somebody, at some point, configured.

Nothing came out of these portals that they had not been configured to hand over.

Nitay Bachrach, Security Researcher at Reco, describes the underlying problem: "The core issue is that 'what is public' and 'what should be public' are two different things, and that's exactly what the attacker exploited."

Why this one stands out

Attackers have been abusing over-permissioned Salesforce guest users for a while, and there are off-the-shelf tools for it. This operator did not use them.

They built their own instead. Most of the resulting traffic still went down the well-trodden route: Salesforce's older Aura framework, whose guest user has been a documented target for long enough that Reco has written up a previous campaign working the same way. That is where the bulk of this operator's Salesforce effort landed. The busiest single target Reco observed logged over 560,000 events from this one address across the campaign window, almost all of it Aura enumeration.

What makes the campaign worth reading about is the rest of the toolkit, pointed at two places nobody had bothered to look. The first is the data layer behind Salesforce's newer site framework, which the existing attack tools ignore entirely. Reco's phrase for it is an offensive blind spot. The second is a ServiceNow portal search endpoint so undocumented that ServiceNow publishes no reference for it. Reco worked out how it behaves by reading the code behind the search box on a stock portal. Obscurity is not what makes it dangerous, though. The endpoint is public by design, and what it hands back depends entirely on how the sources behind it are configured.

One of the two most common sources that ship with the platform checks whether you are logged in before it goes near data. The other has no such check at all. It relies entirely on who has been granted read access to each knowledge base, which is a configuration question with nothing in the code to warn you either way.

The two behave nothing alike. On the Salesforce side the new work was thin next to the Aura flood, a few requests against each API version on each subsite it found, which is roughly what you would expect while Aura sites are still the more common target. On ServiceNow it was the opposite: once the tool found a portal, almost everything it did there went at that one search endpoint. Both halves show the same homework. They point to someone who sat down with these platforms, learned them properly, and went looking for doors no scanner was checking.

Who that someone is, Reco will not say. The activity resembles the ShinyHunters Experience Cloud campaign, guest enumeration of Salesforce over Aura and GraphQL, and Reco's position is that a campaign not matching a group's last known fingerprint tells you nothing on its own, since actors rewrite tooling and rent new boxes constantly. One thing is unlike those campaigns, offered as a soft signal rather than a finding: this operator has held a single address for at least seventeen months, with no rotation at any point.

The uncomfortable bit: you cannot see what left

Suppose you go looking and find this traffic in your own logs. You will learn less than you would like.

On ServiceNow, the transaction log records that a search happened and roughly how much came back, but not the search terms. Response size is the one thing there that speaks to what came back, and the last section below has what to do with it. Salesforce gives you more, though not enough to close the question. As Bachrach describes it, "Salesforce is somewhat better for what was attempted (which Aura actions, LWR GraphQL version-sweep URIs, self-reg probes). Event Monitoring doesn't show which records/fields were returned."

So the logs tell you what was tried, not what was taken. On the obvious follow-up, Bachrach says: "It is not possible to determine what was leaked based on the audit logs. An organization would need to simulate the requests internally and analyze the responses."

In other words, to find out what an anonymous visitor could read, someone on your side has to go and be an anonymous visitor.

There is a catch in doing that, at least on ServiceNow. The portal search endpoint answers an anonymous request with the same HTTP 201 whether or not it has anything to hand over. A portal that is leaking and a portal that is shut look identical from the outside, and the only thing separating them is whether the body that comes back is empty. A probe that returns cleanly has told you nothing until you read what it returned. The operator faced the same ambiguity and turned it into a method, mapping each portal's contents by noting which search terms produced a response with anything in it.

Bachrach's position on when this crosses into something customers hear about: "If the data contains PII or other private data, customers should be notified." The records were technically reachable by anyone. Whether they should have been is the part that determines the phone calls you make afterwards.

The same mistake, on both platforms

Asked which misconfiguration turns up most often, Bachrach points to one: "The most frequent misconfiguration was guest/anonymous over-permission. It was the root cause on both platforms."

He also separates the highest-impact fix from the most common problem: "Salesforce guest sharing rules are the highest-impact fix, but not necessarily the most common misconfiguration." Sharing rules are where the leverage is, so start there, but do not stop there and assume the job is done.

None of this is glamorous work, and on ServiceNow it is more than a permissions screen. But it is a finite job, and the server on the other end has been sitting there since at least March 2025.

You found the traffic. Now what?

Bachrach offers guidance for the first hour. First, confirm it is this pattern.

In Salesforce, check Event Monitoring AuraRequest and Sites entries with USER_TYPE = 'Guest', looking for high volumes of getItems and getConfigData, /webruntime/.../vNN.0/graphql version sweeps, and hits on /SiteRegister and /CommunitiesSelfReg.

In ServiceNow, check syslog_transaction for /api/now/sp/search requests made as guest. Then sort those rows by output length. An empty result set has a small and consistent size, so anything sitting well above it is a search that came back with records. Start there.

Then remediate. On Salesforce: Tighten guest sharing rules. Strip guest object and field permissions. Disable "Access Activities" and "API Enabled" on the guest user. Disable self-registration if it is not needed. Disable guest file access and member visibility. On LWR sites, disable "Allow guest users to access public APIs" if it is not required.

On ServiceNow: Map guest portals to their search sources, and those sources to their scripts. Review knowledge base "Can Read" user criteria for unconstrained "Any User" access. Review the enabled scripted search sources (sp_search_source) for the portal. Detach bad kb_uc_can_read_mtom links rather than editing shared criteria.

65de41792f5b.text:
North Korea's Lazarus group employed post-quantum cryptography in a sophisticated attack campaign targeting defense and aerospace organizations across Europe and India. The malware negotiated command channels using post-quantum key exchange before deploying a Windows zero-day exploit.

Check Point Research discovered the vulnerability and reported it to Microsoft on July 28, publishing their analysis on August 11 - the same day Microsoft released a patch.

The flaw, designated CVE-2026-68820, is described as "a use-after-free race condition in AFD.sys, the driver handling network sockets in the Windows kernel." Microsoft identified it as the sole vulnerability in their August Patch Tuesday release experiencing active exploitation.

This campaign represents the latest phase of Operation Dream Job, wherein Lazarus approaches defense industry employees with fraudulent job offers. Targeted organizations work on surveillance sensors, drones, and robotics, with activity spanning France, Germany, Brazil, and India.

Attack Infrastructure and Methods

The infection chain utilized MISTPEN, an in-memory downloader communicating through attacker-controlled OneDrive files via the Microsoft Graph API. Following reconnaissance and persistence establishment, a dedicated module retrieved the privilege escalation exploit.

The module requested four public keys from the command server, then generated fresh cryptographic material using Kyber/ML-KEM - the key encapsulation scheme NIST standardized in 2024 for quantum resistance. A second encryption layer using GOST-CBC operated atop MISTPEN's AES transport encryption.

The delivered payload was FudModule, Lazarus's kernel rootkit (version 3.1), which disables telemetry, removes minifilters, terminates logging services, and blinds 94 Event Tracing for Windows providers. New capabilities include tampering with Smart App Control policies.

Infrastructure and Delivery Tactics

The group operated infrastructure primarily on compromised machines, exploiting Roundcube webmail servers through CVE-2025-49113 using credentials from dark web leaks, alongside compromised PrestaShop installations.

Each server hosted RelayShell, a previously undocumented PHP webshell functioning as a message relay rather than conventional command shell. Check Point identified at least 17 compromised relay servers.

Delivery tactics shifted toward three impersonating websites for Enveil (a privacy technology vendor). Check Point confirmed Enveil faced neither compromise nor targeting. These sites distributed trojanzed PDF viewers delivering Troy, a previously undocumented backdoor supporting 17 operator commands.

3a3ca0e6d057.text:
Gunra ransomware actors are exploiting two Fortinet vulnerabilities to target government and critical national infrastructure organizations, according to a joint advisory from US and Republic of Korea authorities.

Gunra operates as a ransomware-as-a-service targeting known vulnerabilities in internet-facing devices like firewalls and VPN appliances for initial access. Once inside networks, affiliates employ sophisticated persistence and lateral movement techniques to exfiltrate large data volumes from Microsoft 365 services.

The FBI, CISA, and other US government agencies collaborated with South Korea's National Police Agency on this advisory.

Targeted Vulnerabilities

Gunra specifically exploits two legacy Fortinet authentication bypass flaws:

CVE-2024-55591: A critical vulnerability allowing remote attackers to gain super-admin privileges through crafted Node.js websocket requests

CVE-2025-24472: A high-severity flaw permitting unauthenticated attackers with device serial number knowledge to obtain super-admin access via crafted CSF proxy requests when Security Fabric is enabled

Operational Tactics

The group establishes persistence by exploiting default credentials on SSL-VPN appliances lacking account lockout controls and downloads OpenSSH for external connections. They bypass multi-factor authentication by modifying authentication processing files on corporate VDI servers.

Gunra conducts activities between 10:00 PM and 6:00 AM victim timezone, coinciding with offline administrator hours. The ransomware filters files to target user data, maximizing encryption efficiency.

The group successfully exfiltrated "tens of terabytes of data" through malicious executables targeting Microsoft OneDrive and SharePoint, compressing sensitive archives for transfer to Mega file-sharing services.

Ransom Demands

Negotiations typically begin with demands reaching "tens of millions of dollars," with victims given five to seven days to engage via Tor-based portals. Direct email contact with management staff has occurred, with threats of publishing exfiltrated data if negotiations fail.

Defense Recommendations

Organizations should prioritize: Patching known exploited vulnerabilities in internet-facing systems. Implementing offline, immutable backups in physically separate, segmented locations. Network segmentation to restrict lateral movement from compromised devices.

79c2438191e4.text:
Researchers at Reco have identified a sophisticated campaign dubbed "City-Forum" targeting both Salesforce and ServiceNow through a custom multi-platform toolset. The primary targets include telecommunications companies, financial institutions, enterprise software vendors, and public-sector portals.

The campaign represents the first observed in-the-wild exploitation of Salesforce's UI-API guest surface, affecting both Aura and LWR implementations. Notably, "one Go binary hit Salesforce over both Aura and LWR and hit ServiceNow, from the same box," indicating a unified custom toolset rather than off-the-shelf solutions.

The attacks exploit unauthenticated guest user access, which cannot be deleted from Salesforce Experience Cloud instances. As researchers explain, "if the guest can read a record, so can anyone on the internet." The campaign operates from a single IP address (158.220.87.79) resolving to city-forum.com, which has remained constant since March 2025.

The enumeration activity is substantial - one target logged over 560,000 events, predominantly guest Aura enumeration. ServiceNow attacks target an "effectively undocumented search endpoint" to detect and exfiltrate sensitive content.

The exfiltration method employs protocol-legitimate, high-volume traffic, making detection challenging. Critically, "every byte the attacker retrieved was something a site owner had exposed to anonymous users," indicating no breach of the platforms themselves.

Researchers recommend immediately disabling self-registration to prevent unauthenticated guests from upgrading to authenticated users, along with reviewing guest user permissions and monitoring detailed indicators of compromise provided in Reco's research blog.

b001143950ce.text:
The US National Institute for Standards and Technology (NIST) is looking to modernize its National Vulnerability Database (NVD) to address challenges posed by AI and incorporate more automation and AI workflows.

In a request for information (RFI) published on August 12 in the Federal Register, NIST encouraged stakeholder input on opportunities, challenges and priorities for modernizing the NVD in "an evolving cybersecurity landscape increasingly shaped by AI and machine-consumable security data."

The Institute is particularly interested in receiving "forward-looking perspectives, practical recommendations and innovative models" that will improve the NVD's scalability, automation, interoperability, transparency and utility.

Today, the NVD automatically ingests common vulnerabilities and exposures (CVE) records within about an hour, after which analysts add information such as severity scores and affected product versions. These enriched records are available through the NVD website and automated tools.

However, NIST noted that traditional methods based on "periodic scanning, static prioritization, and manual remediation" are becoming inadequate.

The RFI highlighted how vulnerability management is changing rapidly due to AI-enabled tools, faster technology cycles, growing vulnerability volumes and increased demand for automation and near-real-time data.

The Institute presented AI as an opportunity to modernize vulnerability management, while recognising risks such as AI-assisted vulnerability discovery and exploitation.

It seeks community input to create a system that is "continuous, contextual, and automated" and capable of responding effectively to emerging threats and organisational priorities.

The RFI includes a list of 30 questions inviting stakeholders to assess what the NVD should change and how it should integrate AI tools and automation workflows.

Tyler Reguly, associate director of security R&D at Fortra, said that AI can be beneficial for vulnerability discovery, particularly when analyzing source code, as it can identify "all sorts of obscure vulnerabilities" that human researchers might overlook.

However, he warned organizations against relying too heavily on AI for remediation, especially in critical or production systems. Reguly said, "I would not trust the remediation of vulnerabilities in critical systems to AI just yet," stressing that "human-in-the-loop is still so critical."

He added that AI remediation may be suitable in test environments and laboratories, but "In production systems... not yet."

Stakeholders have until October 13 to submit their input.

89ea97f6f296.text:
A proof-of-concept (PoC) exploit for a critical Microsoft SharePoint vulnerability, published by cybersecurity company Rapid7 on Tuesday, is already being used in attacks.

Tracked as CVE-2026-55040, this authentication bypass security flaw in the JWT token validation pipeline can be exploited by attackers without privileges to perform operations as a SharePoint site user or administrator.

Microsoft patched the vulnerability as part of the July 2026 Patch Tuesday updates, when it warned customers to patch systems running SharePoint Enterprise Server 2016 and SharePoint Server 2019.

According to Microsoft's assessment, "The authentication feature could be bypassed as this vulnerability allows impersonation. Exploiting this vulnerability could allow an attacker to disclose files and modify data, but the attacker cannot impact the availability of the system."

A detailed technical write-up on CVE-2026-55040 was published by Rapid7 security researcher Stephen Fewer on Tuesday, together with a PoC exploit on GitHub.

Earlier today, threat intelligence company Defused reported that Rapid7's exploit code has already been weaponized in attacks targeting its honeypots. The company warned that "Attackers are now using the @rapid7 POC for CVE-2026-55040 against our SharePoint honeypots."

Internet threat watchdog Shadowserver currently tracks over 8,500 Microsoft SharePoint servers exposed online. However, there is no information on how many of them are honeypots or have already been patched.

While Microsoft has labeled this security flaw as an attractive target for attackers, it has not yet flagged it as successfully exploited in the wild.

The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) warned network defenders on July 15 to secure their SharePoint servers against potential CVE-2026-55040 attacks.

CISA urged security teams to avoid directly exposing SharePoint servers on the Internet unless necessary and to review Microsoft's official SharePoint Server security-hardening guidance. The agency also recommended blocking external access to SharePoint Central Administration and restricting farm and database communication to required systems. Where Internet exposure is necessary, CISA recommends placing servers behind a Layer 7 reverse proxy or similar application-layer security control.

Since November 2021, CISA has flagged 14 actively exploited Microsoft SharePoint vulnerabilities, with eight of them also exploited in ransomware attacks.

On Tuesday, CISA also confirmed that a high-severity Microsoft SharePoint remote code execution vulnerability (CVE-2026-45659), flagged as actively exploited since early July, is now also being exploited by ransomware gangs.

cdfd372ddcdb.text:
Qualys has launched Real-Time CSPM, integrated into the Qualys Cloud Platform, to address the gap between continuous cloud infrastructure changes and traditional periodic scanning approaches. The solution provides instant detection and remediation guidance for security risks across multi-cloud environments.

Key Problem Addressed: Traditional CSPM tools rely on periodic scans that run every few hours or days, creating dangerous blind spots. As one security analogy illustrates: "an air traffic controller working with a screen that refreshes every 15 minutes" cannot respond to immediate threats.

Core Capabilities: Instant Risk Detection of IAM policy changes, exposed storage, and configuration drifts. Agentless Coverage across 200+ cloud services without performance overhead. Integration with the Qualys Enterprise TruRisk Platform for contextual prioritization. Automated Remediation workflows connected to ticketing systems like Jira and ServiceNow.

Real-World Impact: A healthcare provider reduced manual review effort by 40% and maintained 95% posture adherence. An e-commerce company used anomaly detection to identify cost savings and security exposures within minutes.

Future Roadmap: Planned enhancements include real-time risk scoring, automated remediation capabilities, and LLM-powered detection and remediation workflows.

Availability: Included for TotalCloud CSPM subscribers; 30-day free trial available.

d5fba9733cc2.text:
Security researchers at Group-IB discovered a coordinated attack combining two malware tools-WindRelay and SpyNote RAT-to commit financial fraud against Android users.

Attack Method: The scheme begins with social engineering. An attacker impersonates a bank employee and calls the victim with claims of payment card issues. The victim is instructed to sideload SpyNote RAT disguised as a legitimate app and grant it Accessibility Service permissions. To build trust, the malicious app label is personalized with the victim's name.

Once remote access is established, the attacker installs WindRelay without the victim's knowledge. The attacker then uses the banking app to take out loans in the victim's name. When the victim taps their payment card against the phone and enters their PIN, WindRelay converts the device into a fraudulent contactless reader, relaying "live NFC (near-field communication) exchange, including the card's transaction-specific authentication data" to the attacker's device for use at legitimate payment terminals.

Key Details: The entire attack sequence occurred within a 13-minute phone call. Group-IB identified approximately two dozen WindRelay samples submitted to VirusTotal between November 2025 and July 2026, with targeting focused on Czechia, Slovakia, and Slovenia.

Recommendations: Users should avoid sideloading APKs outside Google Play, remain cautious with apps requesting NFC access, and verify bank calls by hanging up and dialing official numbers.

0a5b0ad6901c.text:
Suspected Chinese cyber operatives used publicly available AI tools to compromise Taiwanese government systems before expanding the attack to its nuclear safety agency, supply-chain vendors, and at least seven energy companies in what security researchers called a "near-autonomous attack."

Over the first four days of July, AI agents compromised 85 government user accounts and extracted more than 2,500 personnel records, according to Dream, an Israeli cybersecurity firm. Researchers uncovered evidence of the attack in a 160 MB online archive containing 1,395 files documenting the operation.

Dream, in research published on Wednesday, detailed the intrusions and said that the suspected Chinese hackers hit "government entities in Asia" - but declined to say which government had been attacked. A person familiar with the attack confirmed to The Register that Taiwan was the target. The Financial Times first reported on Dream's research and identified Taiwan.

While the security firm doesn't attribute the agentic attack to the Chinese government or a specific hacking group, the operational documentation "points to a Chinese-language operator," the researchers said.

According to Dream, the attack framework, built on open source Hermes and OpenClaw AI agents, deployed up to eight sub-agents, each assigned to its own targets and attack techniques, across 12 "attack waves" between July 1 and July 4.

First, the agents mapped the entire government ecosystem, extracting embedded URLs, API endpoints, OAuth client IDs, and Keycloak configuration objects from a single government portal. This portal allowed the agents to identify 21 connected government systems and every supported authentication flow.

"On one target alone, it discovered 36+ API endpoints spanning account management, user data retrieval, file upload, and administrative functions - many completely unauthenticated," the Dream threat researchers wrote. "Critically, it found that one of the systems exposed its entire user database without any authentication - thousands of employee records including names, departments, and SSO account IDs."

After mapping the government's attack surface, the agents found multiple entry points including three hidden API endpoints that accepted any request body and returned a valid authenticated session without requiring user credentials. Using employee usernames harvested from an unauthenticated API, the agents broke into a government department's office automation portal, solving its CAPTCHAs with 100 percent accuracy. The agents also tested predictable password patterns based on each employee's ID, and cracked 85 accounts across multiple password-spray rounds.

Eighty-four of the 85 cracked accounts successfully authenticated to the department's internal information system, giving the attackers access to internal dashboards, equipment management interfaces, and personnel statistics pages. In total, the illicit access allowed the agents to exfiltrate a ton of government information, including more than 2,564 personnel records, a full JSON export of all department system users, seven SSO client secrets, six internal database credentials across MSSQL, Oracle, and Sybase, and internal network IP ranges.

The agents then pivoted to the Taiwanese government's supply chain. "It expanded the operation to government IT supply chain vendors, a nuclear safety agency, a government email system, and 7+ energy sector companies - scanning them all in parallel for misconfigurations, exposed admin interfaces, and exploitable vulnerabilities," the researchers wrote.

Notably, the attack framework implemented what the AI tools called "learning cycles." These are autonomous sessions where the models search vulnerability databases, GitHub repositories, and other security research for specific techniques, CVEs, and common weaknesses to exploit in the targeted government's infrastructure. Additionally, when the AI framework made a mistake, it "self-corrected," according to Dream, catching errors and fixing them through its own verification process.

This near-autonomous attack comes as frontier model makers OpenAI, Anthropic, and Meta all admitted that their agents went rogue, escaped from their training environments, and autonomously hacked other organizations and people.

OpenAI technical staffer Michael Dalton, in a Black Hat briefing last week about the Hugging Face attack, said "AI orchestrated, fully automated offensive attacks are real now." "In the near future, we should expect that threat actors will intentionally deploy, optimize, weaponize, and use offensive agent collectives in the manner that you have just described here," he added.

It appears that the future is now.

fd8b4d446056.text:
If you thought that the famous Spectre security vulns were a relic of 2018, think again. Certain RISC-V chips are still very much subject to this hair-raising hole, researchers say.

Spectre refers to a family of vulnerabilities related to speculative execution, a performance optimization technique based on predicting the flow of data before instructions have been executed. Incorrect predictions get rolled back without affecting running applications but nonetheless leave traces that can be recovered and exploited to violate memory protections and access secrets.

Spectre flaws have dogged x86 and ARM chips for years, leading computer scientists to develop a series of defenses, including Indirect Branch Restricted Speculation (IBRS), Indirect Branch Prediction Barrier (IBPB), and Single Thread Indirect Branch Predictor (STIBP).

Researchers affiliated with academic institutions in Belgium and Germany say that it's been popular to assume that the RISC-V chip architecture isn't affected by Spectre vulnerabilities because it's too simple.

That assumption is incorrect, according to a paper accepted at the 35th Usenix Security Symposium, "Spectre on RISC-V Silicon: Attacks and Defenses on Commercial Out-of-Order Processors." It says that commercially available out-of-order RISC-V processors (SiFive P550 and T-Head Xuantie C910/C920) are vulnerable to all major Spectre variants.

RISC-V processors that process instructions in-order (SiFive U74, Xuantie C906, C908) do not appear to be vulnerable.

Prior research has shown that RISC-V processors used for academic research (e.g. BOOM, RiscyOO, RSD, Proteus, NaxRiscv, and NutShell) can be affected by one or more of the Spectre variants, but hasn't addressed commercial silicon.

"We demonstrate proof-of-concept attacks on both processors using Spectre-PHT, Spectre-BTB, SpectreRSB, and Spectre-STL, achieving up to 100 percent recall with more than 97 percent precision," the paper states.

Spectre-PHT involves mistraining the Pattern History Table; Spectre-BTB poisons the Branch Target Buffer; Spectre-RSB attacks the Return Stack Buffer; and Spectre-STL (Store To Load) exploits mispredicted store-to-load forwarding.

To demonstrate the risk to RISC-V, they created a proof-of-concept Spectre exploit that leaks arbitrary Linux kernel memory on the Xuantie C910 at a rate of 338 B/s.

Software-based defenses have been developed for these vulnerabilities on x86 and ARM hardware. Unfortunately, the researchers say, these don't necessarily transfer. They also call out RISC-V hardware for its lack of introspection interfaces, necessary to observe and reason about microarchitectural features. In addition, the authors argue, the diversity of the RISC-V hardware ecosystem means that no single mitigation strategy is likely to be effective across all systems.

"RISC-V inherits the software and threat model of mature architectures without their accumulated hardening," the authors conclude. "Closing this gap is not a matter of porting individual mitigations, but of building the architectural primitives, hardware transparency, and ecosystemwide tooling that effective Spectre defense presupposes."

The authors say they disclosed their findings responsibly last December. Three of their patches have been merged into mainline Linux and two others are under review. SiFive is said to have dealt with P550-specific findings and T-Head (Alibaba) is said to have committed to publishing ad-hoc speculation barriers for their processors at some point.

The authors say they decided not to delay publication because Spectre has been around for eight years now.

The paper was written by Lukas Gerlach (CISPA Helmholtz Center for Information Security), Marton Bognar, (DistriNet, KU Leuven), Daniel Weber and Michael Schwarz, (CISPA Helmholtz Center for Information Security), and Jo Van Bulck (DistriNet, KU Leuven).

c44c5d66705c.text:
Black Hat 2026 occurred shortly after five cybersecurity agencies-CISA, the UK's NCSC, Australia's ACSC, Canada's CCCS, and New Zealand's NCSC-NZ-released a joint warning that artificial intelligence is fundamentally changing cyber risk dynamics. The statement emphasized that the window between vulnerability discovery and active exploitation continues to narrow, requiring organizations to adapt within months rather than years.

This backdrop dominated conversations throughout Black Hat. For the past decade, security teams have prioritized speed: detecting threats faster, responding more quickly, and resolving alerts with greater efficiency. However, this approach assumes adversaries operate at human pace. That assumption no longer holds.

AI has transformed breach timelines by reducing the cost of generating phishing campaigns, probing exposed systems, and chaining exploits together. Simultaneously, organizations face alert fatigue, staffing constraints, and mounting operational expenses. Despite years of investment in faster detection systems, breach rates continue climbing, and security teams struggle with insufficient resources.

According to the author's organization's 2026 AI & Cybersecurity Trends Report, approximately 70% of security leaders believe undetected threats have already compromised their environments.

Key Themes

Scale Enables Better Decision-Making: Processing over 10 trillion security events weekly allows organizations to distinguish between genuine threats and false alarms. The article notes that volume at this magnitude improves the accuracy of autonomous security systems.

Value Removes Economic Barriers: Traditional AI pricing models charge per event or investigation, which becomes prohibitive when defending at enterprise scale. The author describes an alternative approach offering predictable costs and unlimited investigations, reducing implementation expenses by approximately 12 times compared to in-house solutions.

Trust Validates Autonomous Action: The article explains that approximately two-thirds of practitioners receive incorrect AI-generated guidance. Therefore, autonomous systems should escalate decisions when confidence drops below acceptable thresholds rather than guessing. This human-in-the-loop approach resolves over 60% of cases without human intervention while routing complex matters to analysts.

Mean Time to Trusted Action (MTTA): The author introduces this metric as superior to traditional speed measurements like Mean Time to Detect. MTTA evaluates how quickly organizations receive actionable guidance they can confidently implement, whether autonomously or through human teams.

Cyber Resilience as Business Capability: Since incidents remain inevitable, organizations must prioritize recovery and operational continuity alongside prevention. This reframes cybersecurity from purely technical function to core business responsibility requiring leadership accountability.

The article concludes that organizations combining autonomous speed with human judgment, supported by comprehensive security operations, build defensible resilience against evolving AI-enabled threats.

4d138601de6d.text:
Security researchers at Socket discovered over 737 malicious browser extensions on the Chrome Web Store impersonating legitimate VPN and proxy services. These fake extensions, including counterfeit versions of Proton VPN, NordVPN, Surfshark, ExpressVPN, and Cloudflare's 1.1.1.1 DNS resolver, routed all user traffic through SOCKS5 proxies controlled by a single operator.

The campaign involved 40 publisher accounts and a shared analytics account. The extensions were downloaded approximately 75,000 times, predominantly by Russian users attempting to access blocked services.

Key threat behaviors identified: 520 extensions configured Chrome to route all traffic through the operator's SOCKS5 proxies on port 1082. 104 extensions used DNS-over-HTTPS to obscure proxy destinations. Extensions advertised nonexistent premium servers in Japan, Singapore, Canada, Australia, and Turkey for subscription fraud.

Socket explained that "with all browser traffic forced through it [the relay], the threat actor's server is positioned to read every destination, every TLS SNI value, the victim's source IP" and HTTP request bodies.

The campaign showed multiple deception indicators including brand impersonation, nonfunctional payment mechanisms, and misleading store disclosures. While Google removed over 200 extensions, more than 500 remained available on the Chrome Web Store at the time of reporting.
