934f7d28bd19.text:
This episode discusses two major cybersecurity threats: "Poison Claude," a fraudulent AI service offering discounted access to Anthropic's Claude model, and "Greatness," a phishing-as-a-service platform using device code authentication.

Poison Claude Scheme: Poison Claude offers Claude access at 5-15% of official pricing by exploiting Amazon AWS's free credit system. The operation creates fraudulent AWS accounts to collect promotional credits ($100-$200 per account), pools them together, and resells access to paying customers using cryptocurrency. As Cluley explains: "When you pay Poison Claude 5 to 15% of the normal price to use Claude, you're not really getting a discount. What you're doing is you're getting Claude access that Amazon is unknowingly paying for." Key risks include: all user prompts pass through Poison Claude's servers; potential data harvesting or credential theft; security vulnerabilities (exposed API endpoints discovered); approximately 900 users have signed up.

Greatness Phishing Attack: Greatness bypasses traditional phishing defenses by leveraging legitimate Microsoft authentication flows: uses genuine Microsoft login pages and valid certificates; exploits device code authentication designed for IoT devices; requests OAuth approval for attacker-controlled applications; users unknowingly grant full account access without entering passwords. Potter notes: "Because it's OAuth, they don't need your password. You've just essentially handed them a VIP pass into your accounts." Defense recommendations: disable device code flow if unused; implement role-based OAuth application restrictions; monitor OAuth consent events; verify you initiated any login before completing it.

Guest Information: Lianne Potter (Chief AI Security and Ethics Officer, NovStar Intelligence) also discussed her dissertation work on de-radicalizing synthetic incel personas using AI companions and behavioral science techniques.

Sponsors: Arctic Wolf, NordLayer, Vanta.

Pick of the Week: Graham: Tailscale and RustDesk (secure remote access tools). Lianne: League of the Lexicon (word game).

Author: Graham Cluley. Published: August 13, 2026 (episode dated Aug 12/13, 2026).

194e88abb873.text:
AI dominated the conversation at Black Hat USA 2026, from wide-ranging explanations of risks faced today through to a vast array of presentations claiming that AI was, in some way, responsible for the cyberthreat plaguing us.

The conference opened with keynotes followed by a fireside chat and a panel featuring mainly senior US government officials. First up was Sean Cairncross, the White House National Cyber Director, who set out the case that regulation of AI would both stifle innovation and development and struggle to keep pace with the speed at which AI is currently moving. It was clear from the discussion that there is an AI ownership race, with Mr. Cairncross claiming that "AI is a tremendous story of American innovation" and making various other comments on how America leads the world in this field. I am sure there are many of you who, like me, read this point of view with a shrug of the shoulders.

The internet at large is a global resource that no individual, or group of people, can claim is their invention or innovation – and this is certainly true also for the rise of AI. During the opening talks there was even the mention of some companies that have been instrumental to the innovation of 'AI made in America.' One of the companies mentioned is based in London, which made the claim even more preposterous. Mr. Cairncross also noted that the US government is looking at ways to build a US open-source infrastructure that the rest of the world can benefit from.

The second part of the opening keynote included Nick Andersen, Acting Director, CISA; Katherine Sutton, Assistant Secretary of War for Cyber Policy; and Brett Leatherman, Assistant Director, Cyber Division, FBI. The FBI pointed to the success of 'Operation Riptide' that resulted in the arrests of over 200 people allegedly engaged in cybercrime.

In a wider discussion, the panel examined the fast-paced situation we are faced with as vulnerabilities are being discovered by AI-powered systems in vast quantities and at speed. This prompted the CISA representative to call for "ruthless prioritization" and stress the importance of industry collaboration.

The Assistant Secretary of War for Cyber Policy made a fabulous analogy when pressed on the struggles regarding resourcing in the cybersecurity industry: you don't want a pediatrician performing heart surgery. This drives an excellent point in that cybersecurity teams around the world lack the granular specializations needed, especially in this AI moment, to protect against the sophisticated threats being unleashed by cybercriminals.

The conference highlights for me included the numerous discussions on the fast-growing numbers of vulnerabilities being uncovered in current or past software with the help of AI, as well as the detailed insight delivered by the OpenAI team into the Hugging Face incident.

The main takeaway for me is a view that I have mentioned in various presentations of my own in the past few months and that was also conveyed by several presenters at Black Hat. One of them, David Weston from Microsoft, said, in summary, that "AI agents authenticate, invoke tools, and inherit permissions in the same way a human employee does, but without the oversight, policy and governance needed to make them accountable."

This message is an important one. We talk about autonomous AI attacks and how AI did something, but behind AI are humans setting the tasks and guardrails. The technology is within our control, and we need to take full responsibility for it.

Author: Tony Anscombe. Published: 12 Aug 2026.

5d743e5d0912.text:
Security teams running containerized workloads across EKS, GKE, and AKS clusters face a persistent coverage problem. Agents protect the hosts they're installed on, but ephemeral containers, auto-scaled nodes, and serverless functions routinely spin up and terminate without ever registering with an agent. That gap leaves real vulnerabilities undetected in production.

This article breaks down what a complete workload and container scanning tool should cover, profiles six tools worth evaluating in 2026, and provides a concrete feature checklist for making a selection. It also compares agentless and agent-based approaches head to head.

Effective container security scanning tools address risk at every stage: image scanning (known CVEs referencing NVD), configuration scanning (misconfigurations in Dockerfiles, K8s manifests, Terraform), runtime scanning (live anomalous behavior/drift/exploitation), dependency and supply-chain scanning (SBOM generation), and secrets scanning (hardcoded credentials/API keys).

Top tools profiled: Orca Security (agentless SideScanning technology reconstructing a full file-system view via out-of-band cloud storage/API telemetry, covering all five layers with no agent); Wiz (agentless CNAPP correlating vulnerabilities, misconfigurations, permissions, and exposure via its Security Graph); Aqua Security (full lifecycle pre-deployment plus runtime detection, policy enforcement/RBAC); SentinelOne (image/environment/config scanning extended via Singularity cloud security bridging EDR and CWPP); Sysdig (unified CNAPP with Falco-based syscall visibility, heavier footprint); Falco (CNCF open-source runtime engine monitoring Linux syscalls, mature rule ecosystem but noisy defaults).

A features checklist is offered: multi-cloud/runtime compatibility, detection rate and accuracy (90-95%+ CVE detection, false positive reduction via reachability analysis), runtime coverage beyond build-time scanning, a unified platform correlating all five layers, and compliance framework mapping (NIST SP 800-53, CIS Benchmarks, PCI-DSS, SOC 2).

Agentless vs. agent-based comparison: agent-based requires per-host software with ongoing maintenance but gives continuous telemetry; agentless collects the same data out-of-band via cloud APIs/storage reads with zero performance impact and full coverage of ephemeral containers regardless of lifespan, though it's periodic/snapshot-based rather than continuous.

Orca's SideScanning is described in depth as reading cloud storage volumes in a virtual read-only snapshot with no code execution inside the workload, mapping to 185+ compliance frameworks and eliminating up to 90% of alert noise via contextual risk scoring (reachability, exploit availability, business criticality).

FAQ section distinguishes container scanning (image/layers) from broader workload scanning (VMs, containers, serverless, runtime state), situates scanning within a CNAPP strategy, recommends rescanning at every build/push plus continuous runtime rescans, confirms agentless approaches can detect vulnerabilities in ephemeral containers, and advises prioritizing runtime scanning for long-running, internet-facing, or audited workloads.

Author: Tyler Woo. Published: August 12, 2026.

1f6a3e34fd65.text:
Google announced that Chrome's anti-abuse systems have reduced unwanted notifications on Android by more than 7 billion daily during Q1 2026. The company detailed its multi-layered approach to combating notification abuse, which has become a vector for scams, malware, phishing, and fraudulent payment schemes.

Google employs a "Swiss cheese" defense model with overlapping systems designed to stop abuse at different stages. "Our goal is to ensure that if abuse slips through one layer, another is there to catch it," the company explained, aiming to halt abuse at the source while maintaining utility and security balance.

Chrome automatically revokes notification permissions from inactive websites and sites triggering suspicious warnings. Users can review revoked permissions in Safety Hub and restore them if desired. Chrome also enables direct unsubscription from Android's notifications panel.

The browser analyzes behavior across related website networks, including coordinated service-worker activity, to identify groups distributing malicious notifications. Chrome considers factors like notification volume, user engagement time, and permission-prompt frequency.

Disruptive sites face rate limits of 1,000 messages per minute, with excess requests receiving HTTP 429 errors. Restrictions escalate for repeat offenders and reset only after demonstrating non-disruptive behavior.

Chrome modified notification permission prompts on Android to be less intrusive, reducing unnecessary background activity and improving battery consumption while ensuring users receive only valued notifications.

Author: Mayank Parmar. Published: August 11, 2026.

8aaa74a81abb.text:
Elastic Security Labs presents a comprehensive guide to auditing AI coding agent activity using Cursor hooks and Elastic Agent. The initiative emerged from a practical problem: after deploying an AI agent capable of executing shell commands, editing files, and calling Model Context Protocol servers to hundreds of developers, the organization realized it lacked visibility into the agent's actions.

The solution involves a 280-line dependency-free bash script triggered by Cursor's lifecycle hooks that records every tool call as JSONL (JSON Lines). The Elastic Agent—already deployed on endpoints—ships these logs to Elasticsearch. Since May's rollout, this system has captured over 13 million tool-call events from 1,100+ machines.

The hook system fires at defined points in the agent loop: session start/end, before/after shell execution, before/after MCP tool calls, file operations, and sub-agent spawning. The collector script answers blocking hooks immediately—"Answer blocking hooks first. A sensor-only collector still registers the blocking events, because they carry the richest telemetry"—ensuring that logging failures never interrupt the agent's workflow.

The script identifies which surface executed the hooks (IDE, CLI, or remote session) by examining environment variables and promotes queryable fields to the top level of log entries, including hook_event_name, tool_name, command, file_path, and mcp_server, with the complete hook payload preserved under a raw key.

Two significant gotchas emerged during deployment. First, the script cannot reside in paths containing spaces—Cursor splits command paths on spaces without warning. Second, Cursor reads hooks.json only at startup, requiring operational coordination to restart running instances after deployment.

For Linux workstations without device management coverage, Elastic implemented self-installing hooks through Cursor's Cloud Distribution feature, embedding a gzipped, base64-encoded script with SHA-256 verification directly in the command.

The Elastic Agent integrates hook logs using Custom Logs (filestream) with JSON field decoding. ES|QL queries reveal operational insights: file reads outnumber shell executions by roughly four to one across the fleet, contrary to expectations. The analysis discovered over 300 distinct MCP servers in use, with 86% deployed by only one or two users.

Elastic implemented field-level security restricting ai_hooks.* namespace access to specialized teams, treating hook logs similarly to DNS logs. The collector records metadata only (command lines, file paths, tool names) while explicitly excluding prompts, file contents, and model responses.

Analysis of 13 million events from nearly 900 users showed CLI surfaces account for approximately 20% of events despite lower installation counts. The approach operates within a trust model typical of endpoint security—administrators with sufficient privileges could remove or modify hooks—and coverage depends entirely on hook events vendors expose, meaning prompts and model reasoning remain invisible. Only enterprise Cursor tenants receive Cloud Distribution hooks.

Author: Wieger van der Meulen. Published: August 11, 2026.

ffd00d043591.text:
Microsoft has released security patches addressing a Windows zero-day vulnerability called "LegacyHive," which was disclosed following the July 2026 Patch Tuesday updates.

A security researcher using the handle "Nightmare Eclipse" disclosed the flaw in protest of Microsoft's bug bounty and vulnerability disclosure practices. The researcher published a proof-of-concept exploit hours after July's security updates, claiming it targets the Windows User Profile Service.

The LegacyHive PoC requires additional credentials, making weaponization more challenging for threat actors compared to previous exploits from this researcher.

"Microsoft is aware of the reported vulnerability and is actively investigating" the validity of these claims, according to a Microsoft spokesperson.

Vulnerability analyst Will Dormann explained that non-admin users could leverage the exploit to modify the registry and achieve automatic code execution when an administrator logs in.

Kevin Beaumont published detection queries for Microsoft Defender for Endpoint and confirmed the exploit's effectiveness one day after release.

Microsoft patched the vulnerability as part of August Patch Tuesday updates, tracking it as CVE-2026-62832. The company attributed discovery to an anonymous researcher rather than acknowledging Nightmare Eclipse. The flaw stems from improper link resolution in the Windows User Profile Service, potentially allowing local attackers to gain administrator privileges through specially crafted applications.

ACROS Security released free unofficial patches on July 20 for Windows 10 2004 and later, plus Windows Server 2022 and later.

Nightmare Eclipse has disclosed multiple zero-day flaws since April 2026, including ShieldBreak, RoguePlanet, YellowKey, BlueHammer, RedSun, GreenPlasma, MiniPlasma, and UnDefend affecting Microsoft Defender, BitLocker, and other Windows components.

e2844b13208c.text:
Hackers started targeting a fresh critical-severity Adobe Commerce vulnerability immediately after public disclosure, webstore security firm Sansec reports.

Tracked as CVE-2026-71362 (CVSS score of 9.1), the security defect is described as an incorrect authorization issue that allows unauthenticated attackers to elevate their privileges.

Adobe resolved the flaw on August 2026 Patch Tuesday, saying it had no evidence of in-the-wild exploitation, but warning that threat actors have targeted Commerce before.

Shortly after Adobe's advisory was published, Sansec warned that it blocked the first exploitation attempts targeting the CVE.

According to Sansec, the flaw can be exploited by remote, unauthenticated attackers to take over other customer accounts. "Sansec reviewed the patch and confirmed that the vulnerability lets attackers switch a customer session to another customer account. This gives them access to the victim's account and private customer data," the firm noted.

Adobe resolved the underlying issue by modifying how Commerce and Magento handle customer identity in account sessions, according to Sansec.

The vulnerability impacts all Commerce, Commerce B2B, and Magento Open Source versions up to and including those running the July 2026 patches.

On Tuesday, Adobe rolled out an isolated patch to fix the critical flaw and six other security defects in all three products. Adobe urged merchants to apply the latest security updates as soon as possible, stating that successful exploitation could lead to arbitrary code execution, security feature bypass, and privilege escalation.

8b1ce1118968.text:
During conversations at Black Hat, a critical question emerged: Who is actually vetting AI's code? Developer adoption of AI coding tools continues accelerating due to genuine productivity gains, yet open source remains foundational to enterprise applications. As AI assistants auto-complete dependency suggestions instantly, security teams and maintainers face a pressing challenge: code generation has vastly outpaced traditional ingestion review processes.

When unvetted or hallucinated dependencies enter codebases at machine speed, post-commit Software Composition Analysis scans struggle to keep pace. Securing this pipeline requires governing what enters environments at the selection point, before imports trigger builds—not restricting open source or slowing developers.

The Mechanics of "Slopsquatting"
Large language models recommend libraries based on statistical probability and historical patterns, not real-time registry verification. When models suggest non-existent package names, this creates a supply-chain vulnerability called "slopsquatting."

A USENIX Security study analyzing sixteen popular code-generation models across 500,000+ code samples revealed: a measurable percentage of AI-suggested package names do not exist in public registries; nearly half of suggested dependencies that resolve to real packages contain known CVEs or outdated releases.

Attackers monitor public LLM output and repositories to identify hallucinated names, then register them on PyPI or npm with malicious payloads, waiting for automated environments to fetch them.

Early 2026 tracking identified a single hallucinated npm package name spreading through 230+ repositories before human detection—demonstrating absent ingestion controls.

Open Source Ecosystem Impact
The same AI assistants generating unvetted suggestions inside enterprises also generate automated pull requests to community repositories, straining volunteer maintainers: major projects including Kubernetes, Linux kernel, LLVM, and Godot have published diverging AI contribution policies; AI-co-authored contributions carried 70% more defects than human-authored code, per CodeRabbit's review of 470 open-source pull requests.

The Governance Gap
Recent telemetry shows adoption vastly outpacing controls: 85% of organizations use AI coding assistants; 38% use AI for PR-stage code review; only 9% have dedicated AI AppSec controls.

Traditional workflows scan code after writing or pull requests open. Machine-speed generation creates backlog noise engineers ignore.

Securing the Pipeline
Rather than waiting for hallucination rates to drop, organizations are moving defense leftward: restrict developer workstations and AI agents from querying unvetted public endpoints during code completion; route newly introduced dependencies into isolated sandboxes for automated analysis before primary branch access; shift from reactive CVE counting to proactive source curation, pre-vetting against malicious typosquats.

A curated catalog functioning as an enterprise ingestion gateway can intercept hallucinated package risks at selection boundaries, allowing teams to eliminate slopsquatting vectors without disabling AI assistants.

Conclusion
Disabling AI coding tools is impractical and uncompetitive. However, integrating AI purely for productivity without updating software supply chain ingestion rules leaves production builds vulnerable to automated compromise. Modern pipeline security requires ensuring every selected package is governed by default before builds execute.

1d9018d25624.text:
A critical-severity VMware vCenter vulnerability has been exploited within five days of disclosure by Broadcom, with attackers deploying an open-source reverse shell to hold access to compromised systems.

The threat research team at German firm Quirso discovered the campaign during an incident response engagement and published its findings on August 10.

The digital forensics company assessed a suspected advanced persistent threat (APT) actor was responsible, counting 361 victim IP addresses across 47 countries while cautioning that an IP address does not necessarily correspond to a single organization.

The vulnerability, CVE-2026-59310, is a critical directory traversal flaw in the vCenter Syslog server rated CVSS 9.8. Broadcom said an unauthenticated attacker with network access to vCenter can exploit it to execute arbitrary code, turning a service built to collect logs into a route into the operating system.

Five Days From Advisory to Compromise
Broadcom published an advisory relating to the flaw on July 29, stating in an accompanying FAQ that it had not observed exploitation. It revised the advisory on August 3 to add 8.0 U2f express patches.

Quirso's team said they first observed compromised systems contacting attacker infrastructure on August 3. The following day brought 151 further victim IPs, and by August 5 roughly 95% of the 361 total had appeared. Germany, the United States, Turkey, Iran and France accounted for 185 of them.

While the attacker may have had prior knowledge of the flaw, "the strong correlation between disclosure and exploitation points to the advisory as the campaign's starting point."

Two Clocks to Manage
For persistence the actor deployed reverse_ssh, an open-source SSH-based reverse shell framework built for penetration testing.

Because it dials outward rather than accepting inbound connections, it can bypass controls designed to block unsolicited inbound access. Quirso stressed that its presence alone is not proof of compromise.

Jason Soroko, senior fellow at certificate lifecycle management provider Sectigo, said patching would not resolve the incident by itself. "There are therefore two clocks to manage," addressing both closing the vulnerability and evicting anyone who entered before the patch.

Broadcom has not published a workaround. Fixed vCenter releases are 9.1.0.0300, 9.0.2.0100, and 8.0 U3k or 8.0 U2f depending on the deployed branch, and address both critical vCenter flaws in the advisory.

c6f1dceb7e68.text:
Threat actors have begun exploiting a critical Microsoft SharePoint flaw following the release of proof-of-concept (PoC) exploit code by Rapid7.

About CVE-2026-55040
Tracked as CVE-2026-55040, the vulnerability was patched by Microsoft as part of its July 2026 Patch Tuesday updates.

Microsoft stated that "the authentication feature could be bypassed" and that "exploiting this vulnerability could allow an attacker to disclose files and modify data, but the attacker cannot impact the availability of the system."

Rapid7 researcher Stephen Fewer published an in-depth technical analysis with proof-of-concept exploit code. According to Fewer, "a remote unauthenticated attacker can leverage CVE-2026-55040 to bypass authentication on a vulnerable SharePoint server" and perform operations as a site user or administrator. The vulnerability stems from issues in the JWT token validation pipeline.

Threat intelligence firm Defused warned that attackers are now using the Rapid7 PoC against SharePoint honeypots. While Microsoft has not yet confirmed wild exploitation, the company flags this flaw as a likely target.

When paired with CVE-2026-63520, this vulnerability could lead to unauthenticated remote code execution, according to NHS England Digital.

CISA is urging administrators to harden SharePoint deployments. The agency recommends avoiding direct internet exposure and, if necessary, placing servers behind Layer 7 reverse proxies requiring authentication.

e7b9386dd9bc.text:
WordPress announced patches for a high-severity vulnerability allowing authenticated attackers to execute arbitrary code remotely. Tracked as CVE-2026-65640 with a CVSS score of 8.8, the flaw can be exploited by attackers with Author-level user or higher permissions through malicious Postscript file uploads.

The vulnerability affects only installations using Imagick and Ghostscript. According to WordPress' advisory, successful exploitation requires that an attacker has file upload rights. "WordPress version 7.0.4 has been released, containing a fix for the vulnerability, and as a courtesy to users on older branches, the fix has been backported to all branches back to 4.7."

The vulnerability stems from how ImageMagick and WordPress handle files differently. While WordPress examines file extensions, ImageMagick inspects file contents. When an uploaded file is passed to ImageMagick based on its extension, ImageMagick detects PostScript content and calls Ghostscript to render it, enabling code execution.

Patchstack notes that some upload methods lack content checks, creating an exploitation pathway. WordPress addressed the defect by modifying the load() function to verify file contents before passing them to Imagick, preventing PostScript execution and blocking filename manipulation tactics.

The security firm emphasizes that "an Author uploading a booby-trapped 'image' is a genuinely realistic threat, not a theoretical one" for multi-author publications, membership sites, and installations with contributors or open registration.

e5a510150abc.text:
How one "cybersecurity expert" published 445 books on Amazon in a single year — and what that means for anyone trying to learn something real in the age of AI slop.

A recent article in The Atlantic ran under the blunt headline, The End of Reading Is Here. According to the piece, research from the National Endowment for the Arts (NEA) found that fewer than 50% of American adults read even a single book in 2022, and only 38% read a novel or short story.

At the same time, the U.S. book market keeps breaking its own publishing records year after year: in 2025, for instance, the number of new titles topped four million — up a third from 2024. A huge chunk of that, 3.5 million titles, came from self-publishing, and one of its most powerful engines is Amazon's Kindle Direct Publishing (KDP).

In the summer of 2026, New York Times tech journalist Kashmir Hill learned that a biography about her had been published on Amazon a year earlier, titled 'The Biography of Kashmir Hill.' Nobody had ever contacted her to research it. The listed author, John Crane Miller, used a generic stock photo and left no contact details; his profile showed he had published biographies of nine other American journalists in a single week in summer 2025. The hardcover cost $26.99 for 90 pages and contained fabricated 'facts,' including a false claim about Hill's coffee-making ritual. After Hill left a comment asking the author to contact her, all of Miller's books vanished from Amazon.

That led her to Bill Johns, a retired cybersecurity consultant whose Amazon author page lists 445 books. Johns retired in 2024 and began using ChatGPT in 2025, producing his first book, 'Ghosts in the Machine,' about hacking history, then generating 444 more books over the following year, including a 13-book cybersecurity series covering topics like Zero Trust and OT/ICS security, alongside books on sports, bridges, alcohol, biographies, military aviation, and philosophy. His process involves planning chapters with ChatGPT and writing them piece by piece; he aims for 10 books a week, Amazon's maximum publishing rate. His author photo is also AI-generated.

The economics work because Amazon's Kindle Direct Publishing uses print-on-demand, meaning books are only printed once ordered, so listing hundreds of titles costs almost nothing. Johns says he sells a few hundred books a month, earning roughly $6,000 in one holiday season. Some AI books earn far more — an AI-generated biography of Charlie Kirk became an Amazon bestseller after his assassination before being pulled following complaints calling it 'mind-numbing' and 'a disgrace.'

The post concludes by urging readers to seek trusted, human-written sources for cybersecurity information rather than relying on AI-generated content flooding marketplaces like Amazon.

c71bcda83309.text:
Ukrainian authorities conducted a major law enforcement operation this week, shutting down 94 fraudulent call centers operating across the country. The coordinated effort involved the National Police, Ukraine's Security Service, the Prosecutor General's Office, and German police, resulting in 411 searches.

The call centers operated investment scams and schemes designed to steal money or gain unauthorized bank account access. Tactics included posing as bank officers threatening account freezes, convincing victims to apply for loans and share payment card details, and tricking people into installing remote access software on their devices.

Seized Assets
During the raids, authorities recovered: 1,794 equipped workstations; 3,336 computer equipment units; 1,346 phones and 5,200 SIM cards; 90 bank cards; access credentials to 20 cryptocurrency wallets; 22 vehicles; "$2 million, 64,000 euros, and Ukrainian hryvnias in cash"; 1 kilogram of bank gold in bars and jewelry.

Twenty-six individuals were formally identified as suspects.

Investigative Findings
Investigators discovered that some call centers targeted foreign citizens, particularly in the European Union, promoting fake investment platforms. Other operations targeted medical fraud schemes and conducted systematic victim identification for investment solicitation.

Suspects face charges under Ukrainian Criminal Code provisions carrying penalties up to 12 years imprisonment and property confiscation.

bd3e4708f161.text:
An Akira ransomware affiliate disabled endpoint detection and response (EDR) solutions on a compromised system by restarting the machine into Safe Mode with Networking.

The attack began on August 4 after a hacker obtained initial access through an exposed SonicWall VPN device lacking multi-factor authentication. According to Huntress, approximately two hours after a successful VPN login, the attacker connected to the domain controller via RDP, enumerated Active Directory users and computers, and moved to an application server.

The attackers used WinRAR to archive mapped file shares and the s5cmd command-line tool to upload stolen data to an attacker-controlled S3 bucket before installing AnyDesk for remote access.

Using AnyDesk, the attacker forced the compromised host to boot into Safe Mode with Networking and disabled both the Huntress agent and Microsoft Defender's real-time protection. "For 10 minutes while in Safe Mode, the host had no working EDR, and AV was blinded," according to Huntress.

The attackers also added AnyDesk to the Windows Safe Mode registry to maintain remote access after reboot. However, when attempting to launch the main ransomware payload (akira.exe) in Safe Mode, execution failed due to low virtual memory and out-of-memory errors.

A scheduled Defender scan eventually detected the Akira executable, and the tool successfully quarantined it after the attacker rebooted into normal mode and real-time protection was restored.

Despite failing to encrypt files, the Akira operator still stole credentials and files for data extortion within five hours of initial access. This marks the first observed use of this Safe Mode tactic in an Akira attack, though ransomware families like Snatch and AvosLocker have employed this technique for years.

Huntress recommends implementing MFA for all VPN accounts, deploying credential-spraying detection measures, and monitoring for Safe Mode boot configuration changes or remote-access tools being added to the Safe Mode service registry.

d589aa80b3b7.text:
The Jewelbug hacker group has been carrying out espionage operations targeting governments and militaries while also engaging in cryptocurrency fraud.

Although the threat actor has targeted government agencies and organizations in critical sectors, including defense, telecommunications, education, and aviation, its cryptocurrency-related activity suggests that they may also operate as a hack-for-hire group that seeks to profit from cybercrime.

In a recent operation, Jewelbug (also known as Earth Alux and REF7707) compromised webmail accounts belonging to 15 government tenants as part of a campaign targeting a country in the Middle East.

Researchers at Symantec found that the espionage campaign and the cryptocurrency fraud were conducted from the same control panel.

The China-based hacker group gained write access to the shared webmail installation and inserted a malicious script into its common template. The script then ran on login pages and mailbox views across 15 tenants.

After execution, the script established a WebSocket connection to the attacker's command-and-control (C2) server, exfiltrated webmail cookies, and retrieved the user's email address to determine whether it belonged to a targeted government domain.

Valuable targets would receive a fake Adobe Flash update prompt, which installs the main payload on Windows, the Antino backdoor, and browser tooling.

Apart from Antino, the threat actor also uses the XG-Web remote-access and data-theft framework for managing campaigns and victim information.

According to Symantec, Jewelbug delivers Antino through malicious HTA files and fake Adobe Flash/Adobe installers, and then uses it to deploy additional payloads.

One of the payloads is a malicious browser extension for Chrome and Firefox, named PDF Viewer, which steals cookies and credentials, intercepts traffic, injects JavaScript, and remotely exposes browser functions.

Symantec traced Antino infections to Jewelbug's infrastructure and then obtained visibility into the group's C2 management platform, database, server logs, source code, and operator files.

The data showed that the hackers ran a large-scale espionage operation and "an industrial-scale cryptocurrency fraud business."

"Jewelbug's victim database holds more than one million implant check-in rows, more than 580,000 stolen browser cookies, several thousand captured credentials, and more than 2,300 exfiltrated email bodies," Symantec researchers note.

Regarding the espionage part, Jewelbug targeted government and military organizations across the Middle East, Southeast Asia, and South Asia.

"Runtime server logs recorded roughly 1.1 million geolocation events against approximately 4,300 distinct source IP addresses: approximately 87,200 connections from a Southeast Asian country (targeting state telecom and military networks), approximately 53,100 from a Middle Eastern country (across the national carrier's ranges, including Starlink-connected addresses in the capital), and approximately 15,000 from a second Southeast Asian country (including government ministry infrastructure)," Symantec says.

The researchers explained that the threat actor obtained write access to the webmail installation used by multiple government ministries and agencies after compromising a shared web-hosting platform operated by the state telecommunications provider and national services agency.

By injecting a single script tag, the threat actor ensured that the JavaScript payload opened a WebSocket to the C2 every time a user on one of nine government domains logged in.

"A single campaign spanned more than 15 government webmail tenants, with the hook firing on the login page and every mailbox view," Symantec says.

The cryptocurrency theft operations are backed by AI-generated articles driving traffic to fake crypto exchange sites and click-fraud bots that manipulate search rankings.

According to the researchers, the threat actor relies on an automated attack pipeline that scrapes keywords, generates thousands of fake download pages using AI, and publishes them "across a 44-server content-management fleet and hundreds of lookalike domains" impersonating OKX and Binance. Using click bots, Jewelbug manipulates rankings to promote their fraudulent pages.

The fraud uses other lures, as well: sports betting, pirated livestream portals, and private detective scams.

Symantec researchers have high confidence attributing Jewelbug's financially-motivated activities to a Chinese company that advertises SEO services.

Jewelbug also uses a Rust-based implant called 'ClientKing' that targets Linux servers, ARM64 devices, and ASUS routers, and supports command execution, SOCKS proxying, DNS tunneling, and in-memory kernel module loading.

The hackers used public Google Docs to host obfuscated payloads retrieved and executed by their implants, helping the malicious traffic blend in with legitimate Google services.

Symantec published indicators of compromise related to observed Jewelbug activity, as well as a detailed technical report describing the threat actor's tooling and tradecraft, their financial operation, and the infrastructure used in attacks.

3331217cd7a6.text:
Welcome to this week's edition of the Threat Source newsletter.

The author opens with literary quotes about experimentation and avoiding rabbit holes, then reflects on "Hacker Summer Camp" and a podcast segment called "Make Hazel a Hacker" where security concepts are explored spontaneously. He emphasizes how multiple perspectives on security questions can all be valid simultaneously, even when different. The piece encourages readers to seek diverse opinions when making decisions about threat hunting, patching, and professional development.

The one big thing:
Cisco Talos discovered "JWR," an undocumented real-time phishing framework likely related to "The Outsider" phishing-as-a-service platform. JWR operates via WebSocket connections enabling attackers to monitor keystrokes and steer victims through fake checkout flows. Deployed through SMS impersonating toll and postal authorities, it captures payment data, 2FA codes, identity documents, and device fingerprints. The threat is particularly dangerous because attackers can bypass MFA by requesting 2FA codes in real-time.

Top security headlines included:
- Ransomware attack on Colombian Justice Ministry
- FBI investigation into North Korean remote IT staffer at U.S. agency
- Microsoft SharePoint authentication bypass exploits in active attacks
- Signal's new Automatic Key Verification feature
- Ceva Logistics data breach affecting retailers and banks

The newsletter concludes with podcast recommendations, Microsoft Patch Tuesday coverage, AI weaponization analysis, upcoming conferences, and malware telemetry data.

7b68da7b4f7d.text:
A market for removing AI watermarks has sprung up days after Anthropic disclosed switching on invisible marks in everything Claude writes, spanning a GitHub project with over 4,500 stars, a cluster of newly registered web tools, and at least one established AI detection evasion service.

None of the claims about defeating the text watermark can currently be checked, though, because Anthropic has not yet published how it works or released the detector that would show whether a cleaned document still carries the mark.

Who is offering what
Among the largest is watermarks-remover, an MIT-licensed tool from software developer Guillaume Meyer, founder of Memo. It began as a Claude-only agent skill and now advertises coverage of Claude, Gemini and SynthID-Text, OpenAI provenance surfaces, and open-weight models using Kirchenbauer-style marks.

Alongside it sit repositories including claude-watermark-cleaner, remove-ai-watermarks, and noai-watermark, plus a cluster of web tools: claudewatermark.com, claudewatermark.rip, gptcleanup.com and claudewatermarkremover.app.

StealthGPT, which sells AI detection evasion, added a Claude watermark remover to its use-case pages. Another, Human Writes, advertises bypassing Turnitin and GPTZero on essays and assignments, claims to strip Claude's watermark, and carries a footer noting compliance with academic integrity policies.

What 'watermark removers' actually do
The tools do three different things, and only some of it is verifiable. Stripping hidden characters from text works and can be counted: zero-width characters, bidirectional controls, Unicode tag characters and lookalike spaces. Stripping C2PA, EXIF and XMP metadata from files works too, across PNG, JPEG, SVG, PDF, DOCX, ODT, HTML and Markdown. File metadata does not survive a re-save, a format conversion or a screenshot anyway.

The hard part is the watermark itself. It does not live in hidden characters. The watermark lives in which words the model picked, which means the only known way to remove it is to rewrite the text heavily, using a second model.

Meyer is unusually candid about this, posting that his tool removes metadata only for now, and that stripping the actual marks may come later but is not available today. His README goes further, arguing that a rewrite swaps the original model's word choices for the cheaper model's, and questioning why anyone paying for a premium model would then run its output through a worse one.

The commercial sites are less careful. Several promise clean, undetectable output, and the scores some of them return are measured against ordinary AI detectors rather than against Anthropic's watermark, for which no public detector exists.

Independent testing has already found gaps. Pasquale Pillitteri cloned the main projects and read the code rather than the READMEs, finding that one popular text cleaner let the most common hidden-payload technique through untouched. The hidden payload decoded back intact after the tool had supposedly cleaned the text.

Why Claude is marking text at all
Anthropic published a support page this week setting out its approach. Text from models launched on or after August 2, 2026 carries an imperceptible watermark woven into the wording. Supported file types get signed C2PA metadata. Marking is applied at the model level, so it appears across the API, claude.ai, Claude Code, Claude Cowork and Claude Tag, and through AWS, Google Cloud and Microsoft Foundry.

The trigger is Article 50 of the EU AI Act, enforceable since August 2, with penalties reaching 15 million euros or 3% of global turnover.

A detected mark also means less than it appears to. Anthropic acknowledges that it indicates content was processed by Claude, not necessarily written by it. Run your own prose through the model for a grammar pass, a translation or a summary and the output comes back marked.

Anthropic's page lists the ways a mark disappears, including heavy editing, paraphrasing and translation. The company says it will support third-party detection as the EU transparency rules require and will publish technical documentation later.

The reaction online has been less charitable. Responding to Meyer's post, one user called watermarking a "compliance checkbox, not a real defense." Meyer agreed on the first half, replying that it is "pure compliance to stay in the EU market."

The part that should worry defenders
watermarks-remover ships as an agent skill, installed by symlinking a directory into a local skills folder and invoked with a slash command. Its optional scoring setup clones a third-party research repository and pulls a roughly 220MB artifact.

That is the pattern worth watching. Whatever the merits of the underlying argument about provenance and privacy, a fast-moving category of tools that people wire directly into agent pipelines, and then feed their documents through, is a supply chain surface.

The projects currently in the space are at least open and readable, even where they ship no license at all. The next wave, arriving into a market with over four thousand stars of proven demand and no way for buyers to verify any claim, may not be.

989bcba63502.text:
One dashboard for misconfigurations. A separate one for identities. Neither tells you what an attacker can actually reach.

Most cloud security teams operate with fragmented visibility. Misconfiguration alerts fire from one tool, identity findings from another, and compliance reports from a third. The result is triage by volume, not by actual risk, which means the findings that matter most often sit buried under noise.

This article walks through six practical steps to improve cloud security posture using CSPM, with attack path visualization as the connecting thread: achieve full visibility, detect misconfigurations with business context, map identity risk, visualize the attack path, prioritize by reachability, and maintain continuous compliance.

Step 1 — Achieve Full Visibility Across Cloud, Identity, and AI Assets: Non-human identities like service accounts, API keys, and automation tokens now outnumber human users in most organizations, and AI/ML workloads and shadow AI deployments add further blind spots.

Step 2 — Detect Misconfigurations With Business Context, Not Just Rule Matches: A public storage misconfiguration on a bucket containing marketing images differs from the same misconfiguration on a bucket holding encrypted database backups with an adjacent service account with decryption permissions. Context transforms a rule match into an actionable finding.

Step 3 — Map Identity Risk and Entitlements Before They Become Exploitable: Compromised credentials remain one of the most common initial access vectors; the IBM Cost of a Data Breach 2024 report found stolen/compromised credentials were the most prevalent initial attack vector, taking an average of 292 days to identify and contain. Pairing CSPM with CIEM surfaces excessive permissions, unused entitlements, and cross-account trust.

Step 4 — Visualize the Attack Path From Exposure to Breach: Attack path analysis connects visibility, misconfiguration, and identity data into directed graphs showing how an attacker could move from initial exposure to a high-value target, illustrated via a cross-account example involving an unpatched VM, cross-account role assumption, and an unencrypted S3 bucket with PII.

Step 5 — Prioritize Remediation by Reachability, Not Just Severity: Reachability asks whether an attacker can actually get there, and attack-based vulnerability management lets teams filter to findings on confirmed attack paths rather than sorting by CVSS score alone.

Step 6 — Maintain Continuous Compliance and Monitoring: Compliance and posture monitoring are often run as separate workflows; effective programs map controls from frameworks like ISO 27001, HIPAA, PCI DSS, NIST SP 800-53, CIS Benchmarks, and FedRAMP to the same continuously updated asset/configuration data feeding attack path analysis.

How Orca Security Operationalizes Attack Path Visualization: Orca maps each step to platform capabilities — a Unified Data Model with agentless SideScanning™ for visibility, contextual misconfiguration detection, CIEM for identity/entitlement mapping, attack path graphs, reachability-based risk prioritization, and continuous compliance updates from the same data model. RSA Security consolidated its cloud security tooling onto Orca's platform as a case study example.

FAQs cover the CSPM vs. CNAPP distinction, CSPM vs. CIEM, when to move from manual reviews to automated CSPM, whether CSPM alone can stop a breach (it cannot, and works best paired with runtime protection), and how often CSPM tools should rescan environments (continuously or near-continuously).

89687e456f41.text:
Author: Indrani Das, Product Evangelist, Qualys. Published: August 13, 2026.

The article emphasizes that modern application security programs face a critical vulnerability: unknown APIs that attackers can identify before security teams do. Das argues that traditional inventory approaches—spreadsheets, CMDB exports, and manual lists—fail to capture the full API landscape.

The Core Problem: The article notes that '31% of breaches now start with software vulnerabilities' and threat actors leverage AI to accelerate attacks. APIs now serve as connective tissue across web apps, mobile applications, cloud services, and AI endpoints, making comprehensive discovery essential.

Why Manual Inventory Fails: Das explains that 'A catalog is only as good as its sources,' requiring integration from gateways, cloud platforms, specs, traffic analysis, scanners, and external exposure signals. Single-source discovery produces incomplete lists that create false security confidence.

The Attribution Gap: A critical insight: discovered APIs without assigned owners remain unremediable. The article stresses that 'An unattributed API produces findings nobody is accountable for closing.'

OWASP Recognition: The OWASP API Top 10 includes improper inventory management as a core risk, validating endpoint sprawl as a security concern.

Qualys TotalAppSec Solution: The platform aims to shift from assumed inventory to live, attributed, testable API catalogs through continuous discovery, owner attribution, and integrated testing workflows.

1149a55ddc0d.text:
Author: James Coker, Deputy Editor, Infosecurity Magazine. Published: 13 August 2026.

A compromised AWS access key exposed personal information held by approximately 1,500 UK charities served by CRM provider Beacon. The software company determined that the credentials were 'potentially exposed in public Javascript build artifacts,' indicating a development error.

The attacker leveraged valid credentials to access and download all data from the CRM platform, including attachments. Although data was encrypted at rest in AWS, the valid credentials allowed the threat actor to retrieve readable, decrypted copies of the information.

The malicious activity occurred on July 27 from 01:20:16 UTC for approximately one hour and 27 minutes, correlating with significant data download increases. Beacon found no evidence of attacker persistence or data publication online.

Impact Details: Affected charities operate in sensitive sectors including healthcare and victim support. Compromised data included names, email addresses, telephone numbers, and donation records—creating social engineering risks for supporters. Patient information, payment card details, and bank account information were not affected.

Organizations including The Survivor's Trust, Shrewsbury and Telford Hospital Charity, the British Deaf Association, and Yorkshire's Brain Tumour Charity confirmed breaches. The ICO determined charities bore no responsibility for the incident.

189fa4dacb4e.text:
Zack Whittaker reports:
The U.S. government will for the first time allow vetted private companies to launch offensive cyber operations against international criminal gangs and hackers, the White House said on Wednesday.
In a newly published presidential memorandum, the Trump administration said the move will allow the federal government to use “innovative capabilities of the private sector” to combat cybercrime and threats targeting Americans, such as ransomware attacks, financial scams, and sextortion.
The memorandum allows private companies participating in the government’s program to conduct surveillance, like using spyware to collect intelligence, as well as make disruptive attacks aimed at the destruction of criminals’ data or systems.
The policy change marks a seismic shift in the U.S. government’s long-standing position under U.S. federal computer hacking laws, which broadly prohibit private companies from conducting cyberattacks or disruption operations without a court-authorized approval.

3dcee49570bd.text:
Author: Eden Abergil. Published: August 13, 2026.

Organizations increasingly rely on GitHub to develop and store proprietary source code, internal documentation, and software assets. GitHub Personal Access Tokens (PATs) have become attractive targets for attackers, as compromised tokens can provide access to private repositories and expose secrets such as cloud credentials, API keys, and private keys enabling further compromise.

The Wiz Customer Incident Response Team (CIRT) investigated a coordinated campaign using compromised GitHub PATs for repository reconnaissance and mass exfiltration across multiple organizations between mid-May and early June 2026. The campaign progressed through distinct stages: reconnaissance, access validation, and large-scale repository cloning with attempts to leverage exfiltrated credentials.

Investigation Timeline - Phase 1 Repository Reconnaissance (May 15): The threat actor queried the /repositories/{id}/readme endpoint from AWS IP address 13.221.167.217 (us-east-1) using a standard Chrome browser user agent. These requests generated api.request events visible only through GitHub Enterprise Log Streaming.

Phase 2 Low-Volume Validation (May 29-31): Limited git.clone operations occurred from 107.174.201.183 (HostPapa, US) using git/2.25.1 user agent, testing a small subset of repositories across multiple victims within seconds of each other.

Phase 3 Mass Exfiltration (June 1): Between 09:14-14:55 UTC, the actor used 102 AWS IP addresses in ca-central-1 to clone thousands of repositories per organization using git/2.43.0 user agent with highly parallelized, automated tooling.

Six-Step Investigation Playbook: Step 1 Contain the Compromised PAT (revoke tokens, remove SSO authorization, remove affected users, restrict access). Step 2 Expand Investigation Timeline (baseline user activity, review security logs, pivot on IOCs, engage GitHub Support). Step 3 Identify the Leaked PAT Source (search code, configs, env vars, cloud resources; in this case the initial access vector remained unidentified). Step 4 Assess Blast Radius (7-day audit log retention for Git events, identify cloned repos, review for exposed secrets and sensitive data). Step 5 Rotate Exposed Credentials ('Any credential present within an exfiltrated repository should be treated as potentially compromised'). Step 6 Hunt for Unauthorized Credential Use across AWS, GCP, Azure, GitHub, GitLab, and internal services.

The investigation reconstructed a complete attack chain but could not definitively identify how valid PATs were compromised across multiple unrelated organizations.

Threat Detection Rules: Wiz Defend includes detection rules such as Mass Clone Operations, Private Repository Cloned from Low Reputation IP, Personal Access Token Used from Unusual ASO, Unusual user access through third-party VPN, Automated High Volume Activity from Non-Bot User, Personal Access Token Used After Long Period of Inactivity, Private/Internal Repository Enumeration, Repository Access from Unusual ASO, and Workflow Log Deleted.

Indicators of Compromise: User agents include a standard Chrome browser UA (reconnaissance), git/2.25.1 (validation phase), and git/2.43.0 (mass exfiltration). Network IOCs include 102 AWS IP addresses in the ca-central-1 region plus earlier IPs from us-east-1 and HostPapa.

Conclusion: GitHub PAT compromise can escalate rapidly from reconnaissance to mass exfiltration to credential abuse across cloud environments. Wiz recommends streaming GitHub audit logs—preferably enterprise-level—alongside cloud provider logs to enable cross-platform threat correlation.

Author: Connor Jones. Published: Thursday, August 13, 2026.

President Trump signed a memo authorizing government agencies to contract with private cybersecurity companies to conduct operations against cyber-enabled transnational criminal organizations (CE-TCOs). These operations would include surveillance and network disruption activities.

Scope of Operations: The memo permits 'Cyber Effects Operations,' defined as activities involving 'the manipulation, disruption, denial, degradation, or destruction of information systems' and related infrastructure. Surveillance missions would gather intelligence while attempting to remain undetected, though some system manipulation is acknowledged as necessary.

Important Limitations: Excludes entities operating directly on behalf of foreign governments. Prohibits operations causing 'critical outcomes' (loss of life, serious injury, or acts constituting armed attacks under international law). Requires participating companies to maintain minimum $1 million bonds, forfeitable for contract violations.

Regulatory Framework: Companies must undergo 'rigorous vetting' and demonstrate technical capabilities through annual evaluations. The Justice Department will authorize operations targeting U.S. residents or raising domestic legal concerns. Operational procedures must be established within 60 days.

Legal Considerations: Legal experts note the Computer Fraud and Abuse Act (CFAA) may require amendment or clarification. However, a CFAA provision potentially exempts 'lawfully authorized' government activities—though no court has definitively ruled whether this protects private contractors acting under government direction.

To our Patients,Some of you have or will receive a letter from Grant County Public Hospital District 2 describing a security incident involving one of our third-party vendors. It is important to us that you understand some facts regardin this incident. First, we were notified of the incident on July 7, 2026, and promptly took steps to communicate the information that we were provided.The letters which we authorized to be sent were mailed on August 5, which is within the 30 day notification period allowed for these types of events.Quincy Valley Medical Center did not experience a security incident. The security incident occurred at Aesto, which hosts archived data for Grant County Hospital District 2.As stated in Aesto’s communication to us, they have no evidence that any of the information has been misused; however, we have passed this information on to you out of an abundance of caution.If you still have questions after reading the Aesto letter, please reach out to Compliance@quincyhospital.org. We are happy to talk and help you better understand the event reported to us by Aesto.Sincerely,The Compliance Team at QVMC
Aesto provides healthcare data migration and archiving services for its Covered Entity clients. On or about December 18, 2025, Aesto experienced a network security incident that impacted a limited portion of our Amazon Web Services infrastructure. Upon detecting the unauthorized activity, we immediately contained the incident and commenced a thorough investigation. As part of our investigation, we engaged leading cybersecurity experts to identify what personal information, if any, was involved.
After an extensive forensic investigation and manual document review, on May 26, 2026, we confirmed that between on or about December 2, 2025, and December 18, 2025, certain protected health information belonging to patients of various Covered Entity clients stored within Aesto’s network may have been accessed and/or acquired by an unauthorized actor. The information included full names, full names, dates of birth, medical information, driver’s license numbers, financial account numbers only, health insurance information, individual taxpayer identification numbers, other government identification numbers, and Social Security numbers. The elements of information varied per individual, and Social Security numbers were also potentially involved for a limited number of individuals.
We have no evidence of any identity theft or financial fraud related to this incident. However, out of an abundance of caution, commencing on June 26, 2026, Aesto notified its Covered Entity clients whose patient information was included in the files potentially accessed or acquired by the unauthorized party.
Aesto is committed to maintaining the privacy of personal information in its possession and has taken many precautions to safeguard it. Aesto continually evaluates and modifies its practices to enhance the security and privacy of the personal information it maintains.
If you have any further questions regarding this incident, please call our dedicated and confidential toll-free response line that we have set up to respond to questions at 833-918-8060. This response line is staffed with professionals familiar with this incident. The response line is available Monday through Friday, 8 am – 8 pm Central Time (excluding major U.S. holidays). Be prepared to provide your engagement number: B167683. This Notice is being provided on behalf of the Covered Entities, including those identified below.
They “confirmed” on May 26, but the 60-day notification clock starts when first discovered, not when confirmed. It sounds like they first discovered the breach on December 18, 2025. If so, notification to clients should therefore have been much earlier than June 26, 2026.

Author: Alessandro Mascellino, News Reporter. Published: August 13, 2026.

Google Cloud has structured its post-quantum migration according to interim deadlines, with the first major risk domain targeted for completion by the end of 2027.

The roadmap, published August 12, organizes work into three risk domains based on Google's quantum threat model. The company aims to address store-now-decrypt-later (SNDL) risk—where adversaries harvest encrypted data today for future decryption by quantum computers—by the end of 2027.

Two additional objectives run through 2028: strengthening digital signatures against forgery and reconstructing key management for cryptographic agility. These timelines align with the 2029 deadline Google previously established with Cloudflare and Microsoft.

Completed Implementations: Google Cloud API endpoints including google.com and *.googleapis.com now support quantum-safe key exchange using NIST-standardized ML-KEM in hybrid mode. Application and proxy load balancers offer hybrid key exchange for TLS 1.3, initially opt-in to allow customer validation. Cloud KMS reached general availability for ML-KEM, ML-DSA, and SLH-DSA, while quantum-confidential ALTS (Google's internal traffic protocol) completed in 2025.

Upcoming Deployments: Cloud VPN and Interconnect deployment is scheduled for 2026-2027, Private CA for 2027, and Cloud IAM with quantum-safe Cloud HSM for 2028.

Certificate Challenges: Post-quantum signatures present performance challenges for certificate chain validation. Google is addressing this through Merkle Tree Certificates, which 'replaces multiple large signatures with one compact inclusion proof,' according to Jason Soroko of Sectigo.

The company emphasizes that customers must update client-side software and manage asymmetric key lifecycles independently. Hardware transition timelines may extend beyond 2029, depending on natural equipment replacement cycles.

Author: Guy Matthews. Published: Thursday, August 13, 2026 at 16:00 UTC.

This sponsored feature examines critical gaps in Microsoft's data protection capabilities for M365 and Azure environments. The article argues that organizations commonly misunderstand Microsoft's shared responsibility model and overestimate the company's commitment to data recovery following ransomware attacks.

Microsoft's Limited Role: The article emphasizes that Microsoft focuses on service availability rather than data restoration. According to Brent Torre, GM of cyber resilience, 'Microsoft has no responsibility' for recovering deleted data when attackers compromise systems. Native Microsoft tools address accidental deletion and governance but are 'not a backup solution' for ransomware protection.

Three Contributing Factors to the Gap: 1. Evolving Attack Methods - Criminals now prioritize identity compromise over infrastructure breaches. Entra ID has become a primary attack vector, allowing threat actors to access mailboxes, OneDrive, SharePoint, and Teams once credentials are stolen. 2. Hybrid Deployment Challenges - Organizations mixing on-premises, SaaS, and cloud workloads often fail to protect all data equally, creating inconsistent recovery capabilities. 3. Compliance Pressures - New regulatory requirements mandate cyber resilience procedures that many organizations lack.

Recommended Solution: The article advocates for independent, cloud-to-cloud backup solutions stored outside the primary Microsoft tenant. This approach enables recovery even when production environments are compromised and supports rapid business restoration.

The article is sponsored by Datto, which offers SaaS protection products designed to address these recovery gaps.

Author: Sinisa Markovic, Managing Editor, Help Net Security. Published: August 13, 2026.

President Trump signed a National Security Presidential Memorandum on August 12 allowing vetted private companies to run offensive cyber operations against foreign threat actors, under the control and oversight of the US government.

'The American private sector is the most innovative and technologically advanced in the world, and its scale, speed, and capacity secure a critical offensive cyber advantage for the United States,' the White House said. 'Yet, American businesses' innovative capabilities have historically been underutilized in efforts to identify and disrupt criminal networks operating in cyberspace. Thus, it is the policy of the United States to use all instruments of national power, including the innovative capabilities of the private sector, to combat cybercrime.'

The memorandum targets transnational criminal organizations (TCOs) that run ransomware, phishing, and sextortion campaigns against Americans from abroad. It builds on an earlier executive order Trump signed in March 2026 addressing cybercrime and fraud targeting American citizens.

According to the White House, American consumers reported losing more than $20.8 billion to cyber-enabled crime in 2025.

The Homeland Security Task Force's National Coordination Center will run the program, led by two Executive Directors, one designated by the Attorney General from the Department of Justice and one designated by the Secretary of Homeland Security.

Companies that opt in are encouraged to form agreements with other private entities and with federal, state, local, tribal, and territorial agencies to gather intelligence on criminal networks and propose operations against them.

Operations: The memorandum sets out two kinds of operations. A Cyber Surveillance Operation involves accessing a target's systems without authorization, with intent to remain undetected, for the purpose of collecting information or intelligence, including information that can be used for future Cyber Effects Operations. A Cyber Effects Operation results in the manipulation, disruption, denial, degradation, or destruction of information systems, networks, or infrastructure. Both require written approval and direction from the Program's Executive Directors before a company can act. The Executive Directors may approve operations after coordinating with each other, but they cannot approve operations resulting in 'Critical Outcomes,' defined as an action likely to cause loss of life or serious injury, or to rise to the level of use of force or armed attack under international law.

Requirements and safeguards: Companies must maintain a bond or escrow of at least $1 million as a condition of taking part, forfeited if they fall into non-compliance with their contract. They also face at least annual review to remain in the program. If a company discovers it has unintentionally targeted a US person, a system residing in the US, or a system under the control of a US person, it must cease the operation, run minimization procedures, and immediately notify the National Coordination Center, which then notifies the Department of Justice. Any activity directed at a US person requires prior authorization before an operation can be approved.

'This memorandum shall be implemented consistent with applicable law and subject to the availability of appropriations,' the White House noted.

Author: The Orca Security Team. Published: August 13, 2026.

Shadow AI is any use of artificial intelligence inside an organization that no one approved, registered, or monitored. It covers consumer chat tools, AI features switched on inside approved software, desktop agents installed on laptops, and model endpoints running in unregistered cloud accounts. One thing has changed since the category was first written about: Shadow AI now includes standalone agents running on a user's own device and model endpoints inside cloud accounts, neither of which reaches the browser proxy that used to catch this.

What is Shadow AI: A system counts when it touches company data or acts on company systems with no register, owner, or approval behind it. Three questions decide scope: consumption vs. production, standalone vs. embedded, and human-initiated vs. agent-initiated. Microsoft's shadow AI documentation defines the category as 'consumer-facing AI applications and standalone agents deployed across your organization without IT visibility or approval,' noting these agents 'can operate autonomously on user devices, creating blind spots.'

Shadow AI vs. Shadow IT: Shadow IT is an access problem you can close (cancel a license, take back the stored copy); shadow AI is a disclosure problem you can only bound, since you cannot retract a prompt once it reaches a provider governed by its own retention/training terms.

Common Examples: AI features inside approved SaaS (no new login/invoice), desktop AI applications (e.g. ChatGPT Desktop, Ollama Desktop, Claude Desktop), personal model API keys committed to repos, cloud-hosted model endpoints in unregistered accounts, and OAuth grants for MCP servers/agent connectors.

Primary Risks: which data classes reached which provider under what retention terms; who holds the credential and what else it opens; whether the system can act or only read; incident scope on provider breach disclosure; and what evidence can be shown to an auditor.

Entry Paths and gates that miss them: vendor-enabled AI features (vendor change management), free tiers (procurement threshold), OAuth consent (app consent policy), AI SDKs as transitive dependencies (dependency review), models pulled into container builds (image provenance), and personal accounts on corporate devices (device policy).

Detection: An inventory row should carry system identity, surface, authenticating identity, data classes reached, action authority, owner, and last-seen date, filled by merging identity/OAuth logs, SaaS admin consoles, network egress/DNS, cloud AI service inventories, repository secret scanning, endpoint inventory, and procurement records—no single source covers all fields.

Management: Each inventory entry gets a disposition of sanction, sanction-with-conditions, restrict, or block. Five controls shift defaults: admin-approval consent policies, egress/DNS control for model endpoints, managed key issuance, device policy for AI apps, and procurement thresholds covering free tiers. Microsoft's blocking capability is currently limited to Intune-enrolled Windows devices and only one of seven listed agents.

Governance: A usable policy names scope, permitted/prohibited data classes, an approved register with a named maintainer, an exception route with expiry, a decision owner per tier, a review cadence, and record retention, ideally aligned to ISO/IEC 42001:2023 and the CSA AI Controls Matrix v1.1 (247 control objectives across 18 domains).

Orca's role: Orca's AI security posture management builds an AI inventory/bill of materials for cloud-deployed models (Azure OpenAI, Bedrock, SageMaker, Vertex AI, 50+ AI packages) via agentless SideScanning, detecting exposed keys/tokens in repos, but explicitly does not cover desktop agents, personal-account browser sessions, or SaaS-embedded AI toggles, which remain endpoint/SaaS problems outside cloud-side scanning.

Author: Industry News. Published: August 13, 2026.

SelectHub has announced the launch of DataGrout, its specialized AI research lab introducing an LLM inference optimization platform and AI governance solution for enterprises. DataGrout's mission is to drive token reduction for agentic workflows, chatbots and AI tools, while equipping IT and FinOps leadership with a policy-driven, auditable LLM payload and cost monitoring system to track company-wide AI utilization.

As enterprise users increase LLM usage through context-intensive chat sessions and coding tools such as Claude Code, Cursor and Replit, uncontrolled token waste and hidden API expenses are putting significant strain on corporate budgets. This is especially impactful as organizations also begin expanding agentic workflow deployments across diverse use cases such as customer service and sales outreach.

DataGrout addresses this challenge through a unified connection layer that enables agents to securely access all enterprise applications with built-in dynamic context pruning, alongside a symbolic inference layer that reduces calls to the underlying LLM. Early tests have shown promising results with token reduction averaging 60% for data-intensive tasks involving ERP and CRM integration, without compromising workload accuracy.

CEO Venkat Devraj stated: 'Through DataGrout, IT and Finance teams gain precise token tracking and visibility' into LLM consumption patterns, enabling leadership to measure AI investment value while systematically eliminating waste on a per-call basis.

Enterprise leaders echoed support for the solution. Deepak Dodani, CIO at AFS Logistics, noted that 'most companies cannot accurately assess the extent to which their LLM resources are driving business value' versus unnecessary projects. Bharath Prabhakaran, Chief Digital Officer at University of Cincinnati, emphasized that 'AI line items can quickly become one of their fastest-growing operational expenses.'

DataGrout operates as a MCP gateway and control plane with agents connecting via its Conduit SDK, MCP, or JSON-RPC. The platform integrates with major SaaS applications including Salesforce, HubSpot, Oracle ERP, SAP, ServiceNow, Snowflake, and QuickBooks, and can connect to LLMs directly or through gateways like Amazon Bedrock and Kong.

Authors: Karin Sukonik, Salman Ladha, Ziad Ghalleb. Published: August 13, 2026.

This Wiz blog post addresses a critical security blind spot: developers' personal repositories where corporate secrets frequently leak undetected.

Key Findings: According to Wiz Research, 'verified secret leaks in 65% of the Forbes AI 50, and 56% of company-impacting secrets lived in employees' personal repositories' where traditional security programs lack visibility.

The Core Problem: Developers routinely toggle between organizational and personal GitHub accounts, often accidentally committing sensitive code or credentials to public personal repositories. Threat actors use bots to monitor public commits in near real-time, exploiting exposed secrets within minutes. The article identifies two accelerating factors: AI-assisted development increases code volume and reuse speed, while novel AI platform credentials leak disproportionately often—'four of the top five most frequently leaked validated secrets are for AI services.'

Why Traditional Secret Scanning Falls Short: Conventional approaches fail because they cannot see outside enterprise boundaries (personal repos remain invisible) or determine exploitability (a detected secret may be inactive or harmless).

Wiz's Solution: 1. Identity-based correlation - maps developer identities to their personal public repositories. 2. Attack path mapping - enriches findings through the Wiz Security Graph to show credential reach. 3. Exploitability validation - uses an AI 'Red Agent' to test if exposed secrets actually work. 4. Automated remediation - ties each leak to its commit and pusher for rapid, accountable fixes.

The approach shifts focus from isolated secret detection to comprehensive exposure management prioritizing actual risk.
